PREFACE


THE Essays of Synesius, his address to the Emperor Arcadius,
and the speeches that he delivered in Libya on the political situa-
tion, during the struggle between the cities of Pentapolis and the
barbarian tribes of the desert, although not so celebrated in an-
tiquity as the letters, and perhaps less well known to scholars of
to-day, are none the less of great value as bearing upon the evolu-
tion of philosophic thought in the latter part of the fourth century
and the beginning of the fifth. The present volume is an attempt
to make them more familiar to English readers. The task is not an
easy one, owing to the style of Synesius, which, as I have attempted
to show in the Introduction, is apt to run into obscurity in places,
owing to frequent use of ellipsis, and to the encumbrances that he
made for himself in an attempt to follow certain latter-day rules
of formal rhetoric. The precise value of these rhetorical points is
apt to escape us to-day, and they fill his pages with various un-
translatable plays upon words and subtleties of rhythm. I have
attempted to follow the Greek idiom as much as possible, some-
times at the expense of a more fluent rendering into English, as the
only way open to me of conveying to the English reader the un-
deniable personality of the author’s style. In decisions concerning
doubtful passages, I have every acknowledgement to make to the
experience and scholarly co-operation of Professor Souter, of the
University of Aberdeen, who has helped me with his advice and
assistance, and who has kindly consented to read the proofs of the
work. I wish also to express my thanks and gratitude to Dr. W. S.
Crawford, whose work, Synesius the Hellene, has done much for
the study of this author, for his generosity in lending me an
Original translation of the works of Synesius, which he prepared
to assist him in his own investigations concerning the essays and
hymns, and from the examination of which I have greatly profited.


vi PREFACE
My debts to this work are too numerous to permit of my acknow-
ledging them in detail.

The text that I have used in translating the prose works of
Synesius is that published in Migne’s Patrologia Graeca. This isin
part a reprint from the folio of Petavius and elsewhere a text estab-
lished by Krabinger, the talented scholar whose valuable work was
cutshort byan untimely death. The best as well as the latest edition
of the Hymns is that published by Professor Terzaghi,! who has
appended to a new text founded upon a further collation of the
manuscripts an apparatus criticus, and references to passages in
Greek authors comparison with which throws some light on the
shades of meaning implied in the language of Synesius. I have
attempted in the introduction to emphasize the points in Greek
history and culture that seem to me to throw light on the
foundations of the character of this latter-day Lacedaemonian, and
to disentangle some of the confused threads of Neoplatonism for
the benefit of those who have not had time to unravel them. The
essays and addresses have not been presented before to English
readers, and there has been a tendency to regard them as interest-
ing only to specialists on the decay and extinction of Greek litera-
ture under the later Roman Empire, or to philologists pure and
simple. I hope that a perusal of them will convince many that,
so far from this being the case, they are broadly human documents,
as intelligible to our own age as to any other. The object of the
notes, beyond giving some historical explanations, is to attempt
to trace the influence of previous writers on the mind of Synesius.
At the same time I have appended extracts from such Neoplatonic
philosophers as Proclus, Olympiodorus, and Simplicius, with a
view of showing to what extent the same trend of thought persisted
in the following centuries. Nicephorus Gregoras and Michael
Psellus under the later Byzantine Empire have still much in
common with the culture of the fourth and fifth centuries as


3 Srymesti Cyvenensis Hymui Metrici, ... dal Prof. Nicola Terzaghi, Napoli, 1915.

evinced in these essays and hymns. It is only by kceping these
facts in view that we can trace a certain cohesion and unity in
Greek culture which, under outwardly varying forms and through
gradual transmutations, has come down to our own times, and is
interwoven with many currents of thought in the present day,
possibly with all of them.


A. F.
LONDON, 1929.

INTRODUCTION
I


THE traveller who can find time, in these days of belated haste, to
return from Elcusis to Athens on foot, and to follow the road once worn
by the feet of pilgrims to the shrine of Demeter, may see at sunsct time
a sight which has, perhaps, no parallel in this modern world, either for
the perfect mirage that it presents to us of a past that is always present
in our traditional Western culture, or for the profound symbolism that
it conveys to the mind’s eye of the lasting, if transformed, vitality of
the spirit of Athens. Allof the great cities of antiquity have disappeared
so far as their outward semblance viewed from a distance is concerned.
Rome as we approach it through the wild beauty of the Campagna is
dominated by the great dome of Saint Peter’s, a monument of a later
period of civilization; the cattle graze to-day on meadows where once
stood the temples and marts of Carthage; but if we gaze at Athens from
the road to Eleusis, standing at a distance of some three miles from the
old town walls on an autumn evening, when the Acropolis, lit up by the
sun’s last rays, glows with incandescent splendour, and when Mount
Hymettus is turning rapidly to the deep blue of a distance painted by a
Titian or a Giorgione—at such a moment as this a living picture is con-
jured up by nature before our cyes, scarcely removed from that which
would have been displayed to their view in the days when Plato was
teaching at the Academy and Aristotle at the Lyceum, or when cight
centuries later Synesius visited Athens for the first time. This impres-
sion of the historic continuity of the city, when scen from a certain
distance, is due to the marvellous natural conf.zuration of the Acropolis,
which gives an unmistakable physiognomy to the town, and to the fact
that time has spared the outstanding features of the Parthenon, which,
illuminated by the decline of the sun, still glitters as it must have done
over two thousand years ago, however changed its hues may be, and
however maltreated its columns by the barbarities of war. As to
the town that has grown up, or lingered on beyond the Acropolis, it is
made up for the most part of white houses, probably indistinguishable
in their mass—when seen far away through the pines and olives that

28-1 B


2 INTRODUCTION


border the old road—from the walls and roofs that once sheltered
Athenian citizens; and such is the crown of wild olives that the ‘heir
of Time’, to quoté one of Synesius’ favourite phrases, has awarded to
these victors in games greater than the Olympian.

As we watch the last glow of the sun linger in golden warmth on the
Temple of the Virgin Goddess, we are insensibly reminded of the last
words in what is perhaps Plato's greatest work:

“Wherefore my counsel is, that we hold fast ever to the heavenly way,
and follow after justice and virtue always, considering that the soul is
immortal], and able to endure every sort of good and every sort of evil. Thus
shall we live dear to one another and to the Gods, both while remaining here,
and when like conquerors in the games who go round to gather gifts, we
receive our reward. And for ourselves, both in this life and in the pilgrimage
of a thousand years which we have been describing, may we fare well.’ !

The stream of time has taken us more than a thousand years beyond
the point that Plato foreshadowed as the goal of his pilgrimage, and
whether his successors have succeeded in keeping to the ‘Heavenly
Way’, I leave to the reader to determine; but he had one follower at
least who was worthy to make the pilgrimage which he adumbrates in
the great myth of Er, and that follower, always a Platonist at heart,
was Synesius of Cyrene, who flourished eight centuries after his death,
and most of whose works have come down to us. Looking at this still
beautiful shell of the city of the past with all the illusion of the sun ’s
last touch to vivify it, we are again irresistibly, if sadly, reminded of that
other sunset that was rapidly approaching Athens when Synesius
visited it for the first time at the end of the fourth century after Christ,
for its light which had so long illuminated the world was soon to be
extinguished in the earlier days of the sixth by the orders of the
Emperor Justinian.

The seat of the great University to which Greeks had flocked from
the ‘sprinkled isles’ of the Aegean, from Magna Graecia and Ionia, and
to whom, even in the fourth century B.c. as Isocrates? tells us, ‘all
other Greek cities were in comparison villages’, was sadly declining at
the time of Synesius’ visit to it. ‘It is nothing to be wondered at’, writes
Libanius to one of his friends some seven hundred years after Plato's

death, ‘if any man has fallen in Jove with the land of Attica, for the spot
is most beloved alike by those who have seen it and by those who have
seen it not’, and adds that though in his day the masters of thought had
become weak through luxurious ease, young men were in duty bound
to complete their studies in this privileged spot, so as to return to their
homes with at least a semblance of greater learning.’ Thus Athens still
stood high in the esteem of the Roman Empire as late as the fourth
century, Athens where, in the words of Gibbon, ‘the philosophic student,
according to the temper of his mind, might doubt with the Sceptics or
decide with the Stoics; sublimely speculate with Plato; or severely
argue with Aristotle.’ ”

But already the great beacon was beginning to wane, and it continued
declining until, with the death of Proclus at the end of the fifth century,
we come—to quote the same historian again—‘to a deplorable picture
of the second childhood of human reason. Yet’, he continues, ‘the
golden chain,’ as it was fondly styled, of the Platonic succession con-
tinued for forty-four years from the death of Proclus to the Edict of
Justinian, one which imposed a perpetual silence on the School of
Athens, and excited the grief and indignation of the few remaining
votaries of Grecian science.’ The last throes of the Academy, the
Lyceum, and the Stoa must have taken place in the year 529, a date
which carries us on to a point about one hundred and thirty-four years
later than the year of Synesius’ short stay in Athens. The course of
events, even at that time, must have pointed to the extinction of the
schools of philosophy to any mind sufficiently clairvoyant to sce the
inevitable consequence of the forces both religious and political which
the rapid spreading of the Christian Churches had introduced. Did
Synesius foresee the doom that in a little more than a century must
overtake the last vestiges of the Academy of his beloved Plato? I think,
decidedly not. The Hellenic philosopher who was later to become

4 INTRODUCTION


Bishop of Ptolemais, apparently saw no insuperable difficulty in
Christianity and Greek philosophy dwelling together harmoniously.
With buoyant optimism he imagined himself living, so far as religion
and thought were concerned, in that millennium where the lion and the
lamb shall lie down together. The world that he saw around him was
torn with strife and war; the Emperor Theodosius had died and had
left his great work of unification uncompleted; the Roman Empire in
the East and the West was trembling and uncertain, in the hands: of
young and worthless rulers; but in the precincts of the Temple, in the
aisles of the Christian Church, in the quiet chamber of the philosopher,
in the cell of the anchorite, here at least there must be peace.

The Bishop of Ptolemais calls on the Churches to pray for him in
several of his letters, in terms the sincerity of which I cannot doubt, and
the same Synesius, on the eve of his ordination, proclaims his belief in
the Platonic doctrine of the pre-existence of the soul. Was it not said
to Saint Jerome, ‘Thou art not a Christian but a Ciceronian’ ? Proclus,
half a century later, tells us that he regarded all religions as honourable
and as his own.' Had Synesius foreseen the death of the Schools of his
masters Plato and Aristotle, he could scarcely have written so heart-
lessly of Athens as he does in Letters 54 and 136, for his instinct would
have told him that the time was coming for her when

* as some green afternoon
Turns towards sunset, and is loth to die,’
the last life breathed in her by Proclus would struggle for its existence
in vain.

But when the sun of political freedom approached its decline at
Athens, thought, in the sense that thought was understood in the
golden days of the Academy or the Lyceum, was declining also, and the
twilight of mysticism was at hand; a change this, well expressed in
allegoric vein by Philo of Alexandria as follows: ‘What reasoning is in
us, that the sun is in the Universe. ... As long as our intellect shines and
pours itself into our whole soul, even as the effulgence of noon-tide, we

are self-contained and are not possessed. But when it declines towards
its sunset, then, as is natural, ecstasy falls on usand frenzy, for when the
divine light shines the human light sets.’ At the time when Synesius
made his first and only visit to Athens, a formidable rival to the more
ancient seat of learning had already reached its maturity. This was the
younger sister University of Alexandria, of whose tenets Philo was the
forerunner, and whose position in regard to the ultimate problems of
thought might be said to be enclosed in the one short sentence just
quoted. Thus a new star had arisen when that of Athens seemed paling
in the first century after Christ, a light which although at first only one
reflected from the original centre, had gradually increased in brilliancy
until, if we can credit Synesius, by the end of the fourth century it laid
claim to an even more dazzling intensity. Much had happened in the
world of thought and learning since the day when Philo of Alexandria
‘expressed the foundations of his faith in such lines as those above.
They point the way quite clearly to the growth of that Neoplatonism
which, two centuries later, was moulded in its definite form by the
Christian Ammonius Saccas, and his famous pupil the Hellenic Plotinus,
by whom it was carried to Antioch and finally to Rome, to receive there
an official acknowledgement at the hands of the Emperor Gallienus.
Why its direct founders did not come to Athens we do not know. They
looked to Plato as their Master, basing their doctrines on their own
mystical interpretation of -the Dialogues. It was even the dream of
Plotinus to establish a city which should be governed according to
Plato’s ‘Laws’. By the time, then, that Synesius had come to Athens
the Alexandrian School had in its turn imposed its way of thinking on
the Schools of the older city. Nestorius, the pupil of Iamblichus, is said
to have brought the later phase of Neoplatonism thither in the fourth
century, just as in the third Longinus, the pupil of Plotinus, had
brought the earlier. Neoplatonism had gone through three phases since
the days of Plotinus, but the current was in one direction; always to-
wards mysticism and away from rationalism; towards religion and
away from philosophy, a positivist might say. The first of these three
phases was that ushered in by Plotinus, who essayed to found in


3 Philo, Quis ver. div. heres, liii (vol. IIT, p. 60, ed. Cohn-Wendland).


6 INTRODUCTION


Alexandria a School of Metaphysics that should be at once rationalistic
and mystical. Porphyry and his other pupils, Amelius, Theodorus, and
Nestorius, continued his work without alteration. With minds of this
order, minds that alternately abandoned reason for faith and faith for
reason, the golden age of Ncoplatonism begins and ends. Iamblichus,
according to Jules Simon,’ marks the second period. With him theurgy
replaces ecstasy ; the evocation of spirits, demonology, and the mysteries
begin to supersede metaphysical speculation; the Schoo] assumes more
and more a sacerdotal character. Iamblichus and his circle, comprising
men such as Sopater, Edesius, and Chrysanthius, are more like the
hierophants of the mysteries than philosophical thinkers, for they were
men whose intellectual inspiration was being rapidly extinguished by
superstition. The third phase might almost be termed the political
phase. Neoplatonism, now struggling for its life, is at grips with Chris-
tianity,a force which had, after Julian’s unsuccessful] Hellenistic revival,
become openly hostile. Consider how strangely these forces had been
grouped in the third and fourth centuries and later. The great Hellenic
rhetorician Libanius was the master and intimate friend of such men as
St. Basil and St. John Chrysostom, and the founder of Neoplatonism,
Ammonius Saccas, had been born and bred in Christianity. All this is
matter of history, but at the moment when Synesius came to Athens
the exponent of the third phase of the doctrine was Plutarch, the son of
Nestorius, a native of Athens himself, and under his guidance the focus
of light seems to have passed from the younger city again to the older.
*Platarch the Great’, as his pupils insisted on calling him, eventually
passed on the torch to his disciple Syrianus, who in turn was succeeded
by Proclus. Such was the succession in ‘The Golden Chain’.

But alas for the glory of the great seat of learning at the end of the
fourth century! Synesius, fresh from the classes of his adored Hypatia
at the Schools of Alexandria, dismisses it with scant praise in a few
words written to his brother from Anagyrus. ‘In our day it is Egypt
which nourishes the offspring of philosophy which she has received
from Hypatia, whereas Athens, formerly the home of the wise, is now
only famous for its commerce in honey. And so that pair of Plutarchian


2 Juies Simon, Histoire de Ecole d’ Alesandrie, vol. 11. p. 190.


EARLY GREEK HISTORY 7


sophists attract the young men to the lecture-rooms not so much by
the fame of their discourses as by the pots of the honey of Hymettus.”
The Plutarchian sophists were probably Hierius and Archiades, the
former, Plutarch’s son, the latter the husband of his daughter Asclepi-
gencia, a woman whose fame as a teacher of philosophy was widespread
and who, according to Marinus, the successor of Proclus, communicated
to the latter a form of religion secretly evolved by her grandfather
Nestorius.” But although Athens, as well as Alexandria, had its great
priestess of philosophy, we hear nothing of her from Synesius. ‘In
future’, he writes ironically to his brother when about to set sail for the
great city, ‘I shall be relieved from the duties of bowing to the ground
when I meet men who come from Athens because of their Jearning.
They are, after all, only simple mortals like ourselves; they understand
Plato and Aristotle no whit better than we, and yet when they are in
our company they stalk about as demi-gods might amongst mules.”
These.carping remarks seem to betray an uneasy consciousness in the
mind of Synesius of some superior force in the more ancient seat of
learning, although he affects to throw it aside as an empty husk.
His studied avoidance of any allusion to the surpassing beauties of
architecture in Athens is also significant. He had an eye for works of
art, for he tells us that the Stoa had lost its famous pictures by Poly-
gnotus, but of the great temples and shrines he says nothing.’ This
paradoxical attitude in the case of a man whose mind was Greek to the
core, is only further evidence that in his own time,as in that of Libanius,
Athens was still supreme as the fountain-head of learning in the Roman
Empire, and that the student from Alexandria was somewhat jealous
of its prestige.

It would not be without profit here to inquire what were the deter-
mining forces which caused Athens to rise to this point of intellectual
supremacy, and to keep such a position in the civilized world for nearly
ten centuries. I must be forgiven for what mayat first seem adigression,

that I may place the facts and if possible some of the causcs before the

difficult even to the most imaginative of us to-day, to conceive of the

was an autonomous unit, which could of itself decide for peace or war,
and for whom other Greek cities must have appeared as countless as
those leaves of the trees to which the Ionian poet Mimnermus likened

Greece to-day, through Asia Minor, the islands of the Acgean, the

sovereign democracies, oligarchies, or tyrannies, might easily be out of
the ken of another, and by the very vastness of Hellas lost to the
knowledge of its fellow, living in a retirement broken only by the
trader’s ship or the advent of some new stranger, driven perchance
from his own city by political exile or crime. If we could imagine that
some Icarus more successful] than the legendary one should have taken
his flight from Larissa or the vale of Tempe, and moving southward at
some inconceivable height should find a central point from which he
might embrace in a glance every spot where Greeks had built a temple
to their gods, he would behold more than a thousand glittering cities
scattered from the Euxine to the Pillars of Heracles, from far Macedonia
to the sands of the Libyan desert, and a map of Hellas would be
extended before him that would resemble one of the star charts of
our modern astronomers. But this chart would be ‘ull of intermittcat
stars also. Some, of the third magnitude only, might suddenly blaze out
and become stars of the first magnitude, or, again, disappear entirely.
How often when reading Greek history, have we shuddered at the inti-
mation that ‘the city walls were razed to the groundand the inhabitants
sold into slavery’!> The condition of life then in these cities was dynamic

rather than static. The city was in a chronic state, in many cases, of
giving birth to new cities, cithcer from over-population or from that ever-
lurking enemy in its heart, ‘Stasis’—the word is untranslatable—and it
would throw out, at a given moment,a colony, that is to say a new city,
bound to the parent city by filial ties and claiming its protection.
Others again might be extinguished or deserted from natural causes,
sometimes only temporarily. ‘Let us leave the city’, says the Spartan
Archidamus, in Isocrates’ monograph, ‘send our parents, wives and
children to our kindred cities; they will be glad to receive them out of
gratitude to us for past bencfits and ties of blood. We will abandon our
city, and occupying the best strategic positions will fight the enemy by
land as well as by sea.’* Notice that the city means the group of men to
him, not the walls and buildings. It can even be dispersed for awhile
if the fortunes of war call for such a course. Its cohesion is moral, not
material. Thus our star map will be in a state of continual flux and
change like Heraclitus’ river. One could not travel through the same
Hellas twice.

There may be some of us who will remember reading Macaulay's
Lays of Ancient Rome for the first time in their boyhood, and who have
not forgotten the thrill they felt at the verses recounting the envoy of
‘The Thirty Cities’ to Rome. There was some image evoked in the
phrase ‘The Thirty Citics’ which seemed to call up in our budding
imaginations a world that was far removed from ours in its organic
structure, and a decentralization of forces that is difficult to grasp to-

latent, one that frequently caused its form of government to change
from monarchy to oligarchy, from oligarchy to plutocracy, from thence
to democracy, and finally perhaps to tyranny. The history of many of

the cities, as we read in Aristotle’s Politics, ran continuously in some

one thousand, if I may accept the estimate once given me by the late

Yet all these cities, politically independent though they were, except
to the extent that they had made for the moment shifting and ephemeral
alliances for greater security against each other,’ were linked together,
in a cultural sense, by their recognition of the same gods, by common
traditions of ancestry, by devotion to the shrine of the Delphic Oracle,
by their participation in the sacred games at Olympia, in which warring
Cities might take part under an inviolate covenant of peace, and lastly
im the possession of a language common to them all. There was a strong
bond of culture in religion and language, that made each one of these
thousand cities a participant in a larger community of racial sentiment,
and m an ever-present consciousness of a common ancestry, in the
remote past, an ancestry sprung from gods and heroes, and one that
made them all members of the great Hellenic race.? This consciousness
of an ancestry and destiny shared by all, under the gods, and sanctified
by the vatic utterances of the priestess at Delphi, is the golden thread
that runs through all Greek literature. It scintillates in Demosthenes as
brightly as in Homer or Pindar, and we have gleams of it in Synesius,
eight centuries later. It gave a wider horizon for the aspirations of the
Greek mind, but it never led the cities to permanent political cohesion.
Isocrates, it is true, made a determined effort to rally all the Greek
Cities in a combined movement against Persia. He dreamed of a great

Every citizen then of a Greek town had, as it were, two countries, one
his own city which meant to him, in the language of our own forefathers,
‘King and Country’, and another, standing behind this and ‘but dimly
understood’, the precious Hellas, the country of his spirit in a plane
nearer perhaps to the shadowy world below, where there would be no
cities or founding of cities. How deeply this Hellenic tradition affected
the mind and character of Synesius, living under the Roman Empire,
centuries after every Greek town had ceased to exist as a sovereign state,
we shall have occasion to remark later in greater detail.? Suffice it to say
for the moment that he came from the town of Cyrene founded by the
Lacedaemonians a thousand years before his birth, and that Cyrene
held his heart to the end. But there is more than this. The Greek city
was bound together by its very political independence. It was a perfect
dynamo of forces generated in its own market-place if it were a demo-
cracy, or in the public banqueting halls of its oligarchical rulers if it
were a timocracy or an oligarchy. Of settled peace, of security, there
was none. Each of our thousand cities knew not the day nor the hour
when it might have to struggle for its very existence, or which one of
the others it might have to summon to its side as friend, or to meet in
the field as foe. There were always distant rumblings of thunder on
its horizon; the call to arms might sound at any moment and the appeal
to think first of national honour and afterwards of ‘safety was always
on the lips of its orators. The city is, perhaps, not strong enough to repel
the forces of the antagonist. A force sent out to meet them has already
been destroyed. The farmers are then torn from their vineyards by their
own countrymen and are collected within the city walls; even the
greatest city of them all, Athens in her prime, Athens under Pericles,
did not escape this fate. It does not take any great stretch of the
imagination to picture the scene to-day, if we stand on the Acropolis
and look around us. Here an Athenian citizen at a given moment of the

Now all this tragic existence of the Greek city-states must have been
a strong element in the formation of personal character. But when in
the fullness of time the inevitable came to pass; when these states
running true to form to the end, met with the disaster that awaits all
polities which are incapable of durable alliance and cohesion against
their common enemy, when the Greek cities lost their independence
and, conquered in detail by the Macedonians, were finally administered
and governed by Roman prefects, or pro-consuls, a change must have
come over the whole aspect of life in a Greck town. Now at last there
was security and protection. The restless life of strife was at an end
under the reign of Augustus and, for many years following, the world,
and Greece with it, had peace. But alas for philosophic thought—


‘Peace amongst men and calm upon the sea,’ !


brought only stagnation to thought in the end.

‘In the first century of our era’, says Conybeare in his study of
Philo’s Contemplative Life, ‘the golden age of city life was already a
far-off memory. . . . The citizen of ancient Athens loved his city, because
he did so much for it by his own efforts; because he personally fought
and legislated for it. But for three hundred years before Philo was
born, the patriotism which can once more inspire the citizens of to-day,
had among the Greeks died out.. And as we turn over the pages of the
Ethics of Aristotle, we realize that man had already, even in his day,
not so much outgrown his surroundings, as discovered that the old all-
absorbing devotion to the city-state could not survive its independence.
For in them the life of contemplation is exalted above the life of action,
and a vague philanthropy is about to succeed to the intense and
passionate feelings of love or aversion which cemented together the
fellow-citizens of the preceding age.’? But although, as we shall see,
consciousness of the responsibilities and glories of civic life had become
extinguished in Philo’s time, in that of Synesius three centuries later,
the tradition, not all to the detriment of the vitality of thought,
still remained unclouded, and in the case of certain men was

capable of bursting out with fiery intensity. Any one must have been
struck by this who has read the letters of Synesius, and has admired the
sturdy patriotism evinced in them. Philo tells us that, ‘Market-
places, council-chambers, courts of law, and great crowded assemblies;
above all a life in the open air, one that is full of the heat of debate, and
moreover of action, of deeds that concern war and peace; these are the
only things fitted to men. . . . There are two kinds of states, the smaller
is ealled the home, the larger the city.’* The Hebrew of Alexandria has
very well expressed the conception of the Greek of the golden age.

But to return to the problem of the supremacy of Athens in the
world of thought. Of so many widely dispersed cities connected only
by identical language, religion, and tradition, there was every reason to
expect that a certain individuality should develop in each, that, being
independent, their institutions should push in different directions,
always under Delphi, be it said, and that out of the vast number some
should become more pre-eminent than others. The same law secms to
exist in regard to national units that is true for an assemblage of indi-
viduals. When a large number of individuals are gathered together at
any great centre of learning or art, the probability is that some one
of these should completely outstrip the others in the race, that he should
‘be regarded as standing head and shoulders above his fellows. The
greater the number of those engaged in the contest, the greater the
likelihood, a priori, of the towering man appearing. Now in the field of
competition amongst states the case of Hellas is unique in history. At
no other time have there been so many independent polities in exis-
tence, and therefore at no time has there been such variety in a given
type simultaneously. Variation is at the root of all evolution, and the
chances of the surpassing state appearing were so much the greater as
the number and differentiation of the states was more extended. The
case then and now was far different. A dozen or more countries of
Christian culture for us, a thousand and more of Hellenic culture for the
Greeks. A few considerations on our own centralized forms of govern-
ment will make it clear how in our own case competition in political
forms is limited.

16 INTRODUCTION


We know how towns in our own countries of to-day are apt to develop
traits of character which separate them from other towns, and to differ
in their handling of the problems of political legislation, but the fuller
progress of their individualism is curbed by the central government of
the country in question. If this central authority were once removed,
there is every reason to suppose that the towns would rapidly diverge
in their institutions, as in the temper of their inhabitants. One town
might have a law of voluntaty military service, another of conscription,
one of state control in all that in another would be given to individual
enterprise, and so forth. This is not practicable or desirable to-day, but
it grew up quite naturally in Hellas where the state was the city and
the city the state. If we turn to the first books in Plato’s Laws, we shall
find a dialogue between an imaginary Athenian citizen, a Cretan, and a
Lacedaemonian, which is most informing on all this side of Hellenic
development.

It is of course as impossible to solve the enigma of the intellectual
pre-eminence of Athens over the surrounding states, as to decide why,
out of many who have absorbed the same general culture and doctrines,
any particular individual rises to a pinnacle of excellence far above the
others, and assumes in turn an acknowledged position of leadership
amongst them ; but if our analogy between men and states is a sound
one, it will make it clearer why it was inevitable that ore or more of the
Greek states should have become the mouthpiece of the thought, senti-
ment, and aspiration that were latent in the others; latent in all the
loosely connected mass of Hellenic culture. It was inevitable in the
first place that all this culture should find a perfected form of expres-
sion. It was inevitable again that one or more of the city-states should
rise higher than the others in such power of expression.

No doubt one reason for the intellectual supremacy of Athens was
the position of the city as a maritime state, and the throbbing, changing
life of the Peiraeus which brought the city into contact with other states
in Greece through trade on the high seas. Then again the cause must be
sought in the social virtues of the Athenian people which made life in
Athens attractive to Greeks from elsewhere. Isocrates tells us that
Greeks from other towns were unanimous in declaring that Athens was
the only real city, and that it ‘would be rightly described as the town


EARLY GREEK HISTORY 17


of Hellas, not only on account of its size and its facilities in other
respects, but most of all because of the manners of the inhabitants; for
no people are more gentle and more sociable, nor are there any with
whom one could pass one’s whole life in a greater degree of intimacy
as far as daily contact is concerned’.’ This point bears out the state-
ments made in the speech of Pericles already alluded to and may help
us to understand the causes of the intellectual supremacy of Athens.
The engaging manners of the citizens and their civility to foreigners
attracted many philosophers to the city, men such as Parmenides,
Gorgias, Protagoras, and countless others.

There was another fact also that must have been largely contributory
to the growth of philosophy in Athens. This was the great part that
the Law Courts played in the life of the city, for the Athenians spent
much of their time in these courts listening to the speeches for and
against any case that might be in course of pleading; to such an extent
were their minds inclined to listen to argument. The result of this was
to raise the general level of mental acuteness, for the discourses of the
Law Courts prepared them for the discourses in the Academy and the
Lyceum. Any one to-day who should by chance read a public speech
of Demosthenes for the first time would probably be struck by this. He
would be inclined to say, ‘What an exceptional audience.’ People in our
time would quite fail to follow the subtleties of the Olynthiacs or the
complex threads of the ‘Impeachment of the fraudulent embassy’? But
so it was in Athens. The orator, the sophist, are always with you. Such
is the burden of Socrates in Plato’s dialogues ; his complaint being not
that the citizens were devoid of ideas on cthics and politics, but that
their ideas were those of the agora, the dicasterium, and the Sophists’
circle, ergo very apt to be unsound. At the same time it was the very
force which he decried that had made his pupils capable of following

in the sixth century in Ephesus; that Parmenides, the great pioneer of
metaphysical research, whose portrait Plato has so exquisitely drawn for

passed his life in the Greek city of Elea, not far from the Temples of

Athens had collected their threads of philosophy and had crystallized
their conceptions in the monumental works of Plato and Anstotle.

It was in one of these famous cities of Greek literary tradition that
Synesius was born, the city of Cyrene founded by Battus, according to
the legend, on the coast of Libya. Cyrene was precisely one of those
cities that, far distant from Athens, had evolved a high degree of per-
fection in literature and art. The beautiful Aphrodite recently dis-
covered there and now in the Museo delle Terme, in Rome, is an illustra-
tion, as are many other exquisite fragments of sculpture. It was the
home of Aristippus and of the poet Callimachus. The latter migrated to
Alexandria in the third century and is said to have been the librarian
of the Bruchium. He founded a school of rhetoric in a suburb of the city
called Eleusis, a fitting symbol this name of the mystical philosophy
that was to unroll itself in Alexandria.


II


Tue history of the school of Alexandria has been written by very
able men in the earlier part of the nineteenth century, by Vacherot,
Jules Simon, and others, and has of course been touched upon more
recently by Harnack, but they are all apt to exaggerate one point, in
ascribing the presence of all mysticism in the Neoplatonism that de-
veloped later in Alexandria to direct contact with the East. I do not
mean to underestimate the influence of such direct contact, but only
to protest against tke assumption that everything of a purely rational-
istic form must necessarily come from the Greek intelligence, and every-
thing of a mvstical form from the nations of the Orient. The old road
between Athens and Eleusis might instruct us better than that. The
very words ‘mystery’ and ‘mystic’ are Greek, and the cult of the Eleu-
sinian mysteries was as national to the Greeks as that of Serapis or Isis
seemed to the Egyptians. Are we to conceive that the Greek mentality,
so rich in every gift of the gods, was barren in so much as a whole phase
of man’s psychical nature is concerned? We have only to read one of
the choruses of Aeschylus to disillusion us of any such ideas. We must
ask ourselves whether the countrymen of this poet, or of the enigmatic
Pindar, were so sterile of mystical lore that they must of necessity
have borrowed from the religions of the East. Teiresias, the figure so
persistent in what Greek tragedies have come down to us, is a continual
reminder that mysticism was ever before the Greek mind.

So let us return to Eleusis, to the Eleusis near Alexandria this time,
and we shall find there about the middle of the third century B.c.
Calliimachus amongst his pupils. He will be surrounded by Erato-
sthenes of Cyrene, Aristophanes of Byzantium, and Apollonius of
Rhodes. This schoul was no doubt a reflected light from the University
of Athens. Clearly the ‘mountain streams of philosophy’ which Synesius
speaks of as ‘flowing from his masters Plato and Aristotle’! had made
the Libvan desert to bloom and had crossed the sea to join with the
waters of the Nile, even as the fabled river-god Alpheus flowed through
the Iunian Sea from Arcadia to unite with his beloved Arethusa in her
fountain in Sicily. a

unavailing. The tide was running too strongly against all thought that
was not impregnated with mysticism. In Athens itself not so much had
been changed since the advent of Pyrrho and the Sceptics; the stereo-
typed forms of philosophy were still undisturbed. But in Alexandria
hybrid forms had been in process of alternate formation and disruption.

Philo, the Jewish forerunner of Neoplatonism, had loomed on the
horizon with a system of allegoric interpretation of the Hebrew scrip-
tures, which sought to reinforce their authority in the minds of his own’
co-religionaries on the one hand, and on the other, to present, through
the symbolism which he read into them, a form of Judaism that would
be attractive to the mind of a cultured Alexandrian Greek. Whether
Philo can be called a fully-fledged Neoplatonist, is beside the mark.
What is interesting is that he was the first thinker to strike the chord
which seems to resound through the whole symphony of Neoplatonism,
a way of thinking which has been described by one of its admirers as
a ‘higher mode of apprehending God by spiritual intuition, which under
certain conditions culminates in knowledge of Him’.’ Here we begin to
touch on that later mysticism of Plotinus. We are at the parting of the
ways. We are no longer to ascend to the heavenly path by the ladder
of dialectic asin the Republic; intuition has supplanted reason, and
ecstasy logic. We have passed the point whcre we can ‘sublimely
speculate with Plato, or severely argue with Aristotle’.

But Philo, notwithstanding, is always slipping into the carlicr
Platonic doctrines, and frequently speaks with the voice of the old
Academy. ‘Those things which amongst men are called truth and
justice’, he says, ‘are symbols only, but those which are so with God,
are prototypes or ideas.’ Without attempting to disentangle the
somewhat confused threads of the web that Philo spun in the earlier
half of the first century A.D., it may be said here that the work creates
an atmosphere which is charged with both Hellenism and Judaism,
and in which the Hellenic spirit struggles with the Hebraistic with very

doubtful success. While he seems to have failed in his attempt to
strengthen the position of his own religion, Philo paved the way to that
merging of religious conceptions which is so characteristic of Synesius;
and the question that we must ask ourselves here is, whether the
Cyrenean had read his works. He never mentions Philo, but there are
passages in his essays which seem reminiscent of him. The most
interesting point of all in regard to Philo is the part that he played in
Neoplatonism by pointing the way to symbolism, that symbolism which
pervaded all philosophic literature after him, and finally invaded Athens
itself, where it may be found in full vigour, if such an epithet may be
applied to decadence, at the end of the fifth century, with Proclus.
Philo will always remain a landmark in the history of the school of
Alexandria. I say a landmark, because it is he who most clearly makes
evident the change of attitude that had come over the world at this
time towards thought in general. This change is most obvious in the
tendency to substitute mysticism for legitimate philosophical specu-
lation.

‘Speculation’, says Barthélemy St. Hilaire, ‘disquiets and troubles,
mysticism calms and rests, . . . it is the solid shore of eternity. To
borrow a comparison from the Areopagite, “It is this alone that permits
the sailor to drop the anchor of hope which is attached to the ship of
faith. This immovable ground once reached, the soul gives itself up
entirely to the love which moves it, stirs its depths, satisfies and over-
whelms it.”’! It is true that here and there a current of mysticism runs
through Plato's dialogues. Plato's horizon was so vast that there is
scarcely anything pertaining to the knowledge of the mindor tothe desires
of the soul, that he has not touched upon; but we feel that speculation
was his goal, speculation which is troublous and disquieting to the mind
(numquam quietat, inquietat potius), but which, by means of that very
unrest, seeks to raise it step by step, to the perception of the truth. As
Synesius writes in his Dio—*What could be more closely allied to mind
than reasoning, and what harbour could be more perfectly its home?
For wherever mind is, there is reason also."* Evidently he was a Platonist
at heart, from first to last, though not in the sense in which Plotinus or

even Philo would have understood the term. For with Plato the main
tide of philosophy set strongly towards the open harbour of reason.
“The immovable ground’ alluded to by the Areopagite is not Plato’s
paradise; the ‘ship of faith’ was not the vessel on which Plato had em-
barked, but rather the ship of reason; nor was ‘hope’ his anchor, but
rather demonstration. ‘Truth is militant’, said Mill, ‘and can only
establish itself by controversy’, and Plato’s dialectic is little else than
a model of controversy; one might almost say a monologue of contro-
versy, for it always seeks the counter-argument on the part of the
reader. It invites, to quote a French expression, the ‘retour sur soi-
méme’. The founder of the Academy, at all events in the works that
have come down to us, never drew up a formal philosophic system.
This was reserved for his great pupil Aristotle, in whom, in spite of his
divergences and his attacks on his master’s ‘theory of ideas’, we can
always recognize the mind first formed in Platonism.' Even his ‘uni-
versals’ have been identified by some commentators with Plato’s ‘ideas’.
Whatever traces of mysticism there may be in Plato, in Aristotle we
find that all tendency to mysticism has disappeared, and that the area
of speculative inquiry has shrunk ; he aims at finality; all human know-
ledge is to be not only demonstrable but demonstrated. A few more
such sledge-hammer blows, and pure speculation as well as mysticism
would have been extinct, but the followers of the Stagirite were not
strong enough to deal them. Thought for the moment had annihilated
thought. At this time the minds of men had found quiescence not as yet
by dropping ‘the anchor of hope from the ship of faith’, but by leaning
on the ‘ipse dixit’ of the master.

It was in such a world as this that Synesius, the pupil of Hypatia,
was born in the last half of the fourth century. I have advanced else-
where’ the opinion that he was in no wise a mystic by nature. His mind,
so far as we can judge of it in his letters, was a distinctly reasoning and
inquiring one, his character open and direct, his heart warm and
passionate in devotion to family, country, and friends. Intellectually
he turned to the natural sciences, to physics and chemistry, as well as
to philosaphy. He loved hunting and manly sports. One can scarcely
find a trace of the mystic in the very clearly-cut image that rises before
our eyes as we read those letters of his which so charmed the later days
of the Roman Empire. The allusions to his native town Cyrene are
particularly fresh. We seem in them to look across the chasm of cen-
turies which divides them from the city where Callimachus wrote his
hymns or where Arcesilaus made ready his chariots for the Olympian
races. We seem to be taken back to the Greek city when he speaks of his
native town Cyrene or of his Lacedaemonian ancestors. We feel at once
outside the Roman Empire. The Greek city that we were considering
a moment ago, and which was the self-centred unit of Hellas, seems to

divine and of the nature of gods, be sure that they must be grateful

Aurelian and his party had saved the Eastern Empire from the Goths,
or so at least thought Synesius. We in our day would at once have

more patriotic citizen than Synesius, as we shall sce presently when we
pass in review his great address to the Emperor Arcadius. When about
to take the field against the Ausurians he writes to his brother, ‘I
must certainly set out to meet these audacious men just as I am, and

make trial of them, what manner of men they are who pretend to laugh

We in our day have been schooled to ‘think incontinents’; but not so
Synesius. He thinks in cities. The old spell of the ‘thirty cities’ is still
upon him. When he writes to congratulate his friend Aurelian for the
great services he has rendered to the state, he instinctively thinks first,
not of the Empire which concerns himself more directly, for it includes
his beloved Cyrene, but of his friend's city, Constantinople, the guardian
spirits of which must needs rejoice. His outlook on life was still that
of the Greek city, his own city; * the foundations of his mind had been
laid in Cyrene where the traditions of the school of Aristippus were
probably not extinct. When he went later to study at Alexandria, it
was as one formed already in a more old-fashioned and secluded spot
and one which may easily have been Icss affected by the trend towards
mysticism that was now in the ascendant elsewhere.

There are some natures that, once fully developed in youth, are little
affected by stronger influences amongst which they are thrown later in
life. Synesius seems very little affected intellectually by his residence
at Constantinople. Most. commentators show surprise as well as regret
that he never makes mention in his letters of the great events in which
he must have more or less participated. In his cryptic history De Provt-

serenity was quite undisturbed by the events he had witnessed. ‘Pytha-

Obviously because it was not his own city. It was his friend Aurelian’s
city or any one else’s you please, but not his. He carries Cyrene about
with him as a tortoise its shell. He only puts his head out to watch
what is going on about him from time to time. But every Greek city was

to think, and that the mainspring is to be sought in the traditions of

Western Empire forty years later. The charm of his works proceeds
from the intimate touch that he had the art of establishing with his
reader, and they are invaluable also in the indirect evidence that they
give us concerning the iritellectual movements of his time; for however
insular he may have been, however wedded to the past, his works must
unwittingly betray something of what was present at the moment when

chiefly on the sphere as the form supreme in the universe. ‘If you agree
with my own estimate of the work,’—this is in substance what he says
to Ni —‘make it known to the Greeks.’ The last phrase is signi-
ficant. Greek was the literary language of the age as well as the
spoken language of at least the whole Eastern Empire, so that anybody
who cared to read at all must have read Greck. But we notice that he
asks his friend not to make his book known to the world, but to make it
known to the Greeks. That Greek town ofhis origin always possessed his
soul. The other races of the world were still only barbarians to him, and
this six hundred years after Zeno the Stoic had, first amongst the Greeks,
conceived of a more international outlook on life, and had written as if
the world were equally open to Greeks and to other races,' the loyal
Roman citizen, for this Synesius certainly was,remained always aGreek,
and it is for the Greeks alone that he writes; the others do not signify.
He seems never to have taken the trouble to acquire the Latin tongue.
We may learn then from our examination of this letter at Icast three
things. First, that the author of these essays was himself by his
thoughts and imagery a Platonist, second, that while he lays claim
to intimacy with the Muses of poetry and philosophy, he is conscious
of being at times only a popular writer, and feels uncertain about the
place of his works in literature, and finally that he writes for Greeks
and Greeks only. Would he have regarded even such men as Plotinus
or Ammonius Saccas as Greeks? I think it very doubtful, although, as
we shall see, in one of his works, On Dreams, he was palpably influenced
by the Exncads. We must therefore always attempt to approach his
work from the point of view of the Greek philosopher or rhetorician.
In trying to assign to his works their true place amongst those of his
century or of all time, we must not lose sight of the fact that they

cover the field of oratory, literary criticism, his own conception of the

equals. A writer who touches‘so many chords on the lyre of the Muses
must be criticized with the indulgence accorded toversatility. It would
be rather breaking a butterfly on the wheel to make a profound and
searching analysis of his philosophy. Such an attempt could only result
in the conclusion that it was a reflection of Plato with stray elements
that had floated in to him from the Gnostics, from the Neoplatonists,
from Philo and from the Stoics, and that these echoes are more or less
happy as the case may be. To ask what his place is in the general history
of thought would be as absurd as to put the same question in regard to
Montesquieu or Lord Chesterfield. It would be to court an answer in
the negative. Neither did he nor the writers just mentioned ever profess
tohave founded asystem of philosophy; but theinterest we take in them
as writers suffersin noway from this fact. We take delight in their works
notwithstanding; and they give us a marvellous sidelight on their epoch
and the current of thoughts by which they were surrounded. Now, if
we are to understand Synesius better, it will be well to go back a little
and trace the history of thought in the schools of Alexandria from the
point where we left it with Philo to the time when Hypatia the Platonist
was holding her courses of Iectures there, Hypatia, whose pupil and
devoted friend Synesius became.

All the time that Neoplatonism was in a process of crystallization,
Christianity was developing and was, as we have seen, pushing itself
in every direction as a political force. Though it was compelled to lay
the foundations of its own theology, it could not remain indifferent to
the influences of all that Neoplatonists were thinking and writing. The
hypostases of Plotinus approached the doctrine of the Trinity too
closely, even before it had received its final and definite form in the
Council of Nicea, for the Fathers of the Church to pass over such an
analogy altogether. And so it came about that the doctrinaires on
either side became, as we have seen, friends and enemies at the same
‘time. We have seen how this struggle finally ended in later days by
the gradual absorption of the Neoplatonists, one by one, in the Church.
But this process of absorption took place individually rather than


36 INTRODUCTION


collectively, and implied in no way a disavowal of the fundamental
conceptions of Neoplatonism amongst those that remained attached
toit. What rendered this easier was the fact that even if Christianity was
not directly imitating the theology of Plotinus or of Porphyry, never-
theless in its ultimate decision concerning the creed it was not so far
removed from the point of view of those philosophers as to render it
difficult of comprehension to any Neoplatonist, so much did the two
systems of theology resemble each other when viewed only externally.
This made it easier for a Neoplatonist to enter the Christian Church.
How then were matters progressing at the end of the second century ?
Vacherot, in speaking of the Christian school at Alexandria, says, ‘Under
the enlightened direction of St. Clement and of Origen it entered into
communication with all the great schools and the great doctrines of
Alexandria. Origen went himself to the lectures of the founder of Neo-
platonism, and on the other side, the Platonic philosophers came to
listen to Origen. Things had got to such a pitch that in this general
mélée doctrines became effaced and schools. were recognized only
with difficulty. We come across a number of teachers concerning whom
we know not whether they are Christians or pagan philosophers.”! As
to Origen, ‘he lived’, says Porphyry, ‘in the most intimate exchange of
ideas with Plato’, but Origen, that noble and enthusiastic character,
ends by making an enemy of his own bishop, Demetrius. He is expelled
from the Church, excommunicated, tortured, and dies an exile from the
City of light and learning. ‘If we wish to understand the Alexandrian
Fathers,’ continues Vacherot, ‘we must always think of the Gnostics, of
Philo, and of Platonism.’ ‘What need had they to look beyond?”
Gnosticism was the most dangerous enemy that Christianity had yet
encountered on its path. We are now well into the third century, and
nevertheless its influence is still making itself felt. Christianity carried
in its own bosom this germ of a possible disruption, but the origin of
the germ is quite obscure. St. Paul ptobably is speaking of it in the
first letter to Timothy when he alludes to ‘a false wisdom’ which had
begun to spread and which was a menace to the Church. It came from
Samaria in Syria in the form of legends of a miraculous personage
called Simon the Magus, who was—so the Gnostics in that country

pretended—the incarnation of God Himself," that is to say, of the

wished to draw the Church into an acceptance of their own doctrine.
The matter gradually became an open heresy.

Gnosticism as a doctrine signified a superior form of knowledge ac-
quired by an instantancous revelation, one that the Gnostics held to be
supernatural. Harnack defines it as ‘an acute Hellenization .. . of
Chris. .nity’. If this be the case, we can only say that the Hellenic
spirit had enormously changed since the days of the Academy and the
Stoa; but is it really the Hellenic spirit that was the mainspring of the
Gnosis? I should be inclined to doubt it. The Greck spirit has always
been more inclined to reasoning than to supernatural and sudden illu-
mination. I am aware that here I am touching upon controversial
ground and raising the whole question as to whether Plotinus and all

of the opinion that they were, and one eminent critic of the Alex-

were only a ‘kind of splendid digression’ from the normal current and
development of Greek thought.?

There are still, as I mus. remind the apologists of Neoplatonism,
lovers of Plato and of his unapproachable works, who hold that he was
largely misunderstood by Philo and by all his successors, and that in
the words of F. C. Conybeare, ‘at the bottom he is a concrete thinker,
to whom the sensible and the ideal, or rational, are ultimately one and
not two.’

Be this as it may, Gnosticism seems to have been an exaggerated
development of a great force that existed everywhere in the world at
large at that moment and was particularly rife in Alexandria. It was
the culmination of that mania for religious syncretism which in the
beginning of the second century had become a veritable obsession, and
threatened at one moment to absorb Christianity and disperse it in its
own raging waters. The Church was forced to struggle for its own inte-
gtity, but at the moment which we have been describing, that interesting
moment in Alexandrian life when Origen was receiving the Hellenic
philosophers, it was strong enough in the consciousness of its own inde-
pendence of action and sufficiently confident in its ever-increasing
power to have no further fear of Gnosticism. If therefore Alexandria
was the whole world for the Fathers of the Church as well as for the
Hellenic philosophers at this time, and if the tradition of the great
University city constituted such an interdependence of intellectual
forces; if the great centre was coloured by Christianity, Gnosticism, and
Neoplatonism at the same time, not to speak of indigenous cults such as
those of Isis and Osiris, is it surprising that Synesius a century after-
wards should be in no way disconcerted at the metamorphosis of an
Hellenic philosopher into a priest of the Christian Church, precisely the
change which he made in his own life? There is nothing in all this to
excite so much surprise as it has awakened in the minds of his bio-
graphers. The thing which is really extraordinary is that Christianity
and Neoplatonism preserved so long their independent positions; that
Christianity succeeded in not being completely contaminated by
Gnosticism, and was able to escape the universal tendency towards

confusion of doctrines. Synesius the idealist, dreamer, and poet, the
dilettante in literature, though full of force and action as a man, was by
his very objective and contemplative nature quite prepared to make a
transition which seems to us, in our age, an extraordinary one, and which
carried him to the dignity of the see of Ptolemais. His biographers
are in despair as to what explanation to give of such a phenomenon, but
the matter will not be so difficult to understand if we once succeed
in placing ourselves in imagination among the streets and market-
places of the fourth-century Alexandria, amidst the religious and philo-
sophic currents which crossed each other everywhere, mingling and
sometimes clashing, and which formed a vast whirlpoo! in which friends
and foes alike were often incapable of distinguishing each other. As to
Synesius, his most devoted friends, his brother Euoptius, Herculian and_
Olympius, they who formed with him what he called ‘the sacred quartet
of friendship’ passed eventually, all of them, into the Christian Church.

Neoplatonism was more than a philosophic system: it had really
become a form of religion. Plotinus its great Apostle preached—there
is no other word for it—asceticism, fasting, the mortification of the
flesh, prayer, all these were preparations for a state of ecstasy in which
the soul might disengage itself from fleshly bonds and unite with God.
Concurrently with all this he gives us in the Enneads a sort of philo-
sophic criticism impregnated with the higher mysticism, at times poeti-
cal, frequently very obscure, and one in which a rationalist would soon
despair of finding the thread of sustained reasoning. The transcendent-
alist on the other hand will tell us at once that the important matter is
not reasoning at all, but intuition; that his High Priest can only give
us the voices that come to him from within. We shall be told that the
‘great inspired’ are more valuable than logicians. I am ready to agree,
if the field of philosophy is not the field of demonstration, or of specula-
tion, but is a matter of inspiration only. In that case,.obviously, all
philosophy will reduce itself to a purely personal formula, and that
formula can be no other than this: ‘Seek out your High Priest, the in-
spired oracle.’ It really seems as if, after all these centuries, we were
coming back with Plotinus to the Pythia at Delphi.

The admirers of Plotinus, however, will not be slow to assure us that
we are not to take the Enneads in the form in which they have come

down to us, as giving adequate expression to his doctrine. We are
to understand that he kept his papers very carelessly, that the work
before us is a conscientious but rather desperate attempt on the part
of his pupil Porphyry to reassemble scattered documents, which at no
time were other than notes destined to be expanded into a more finished
‘production, and that the lack of logical cohesion which many complain
of in the Enneads is due to this fact. We seem, therefore, to be in need
of two anchors of Hope for our ship of Faith instead of one; the first
being the hope that Plotinus really was inspired, the second that the
pages before us are actually his inspirations and not merely garbled
notes. How much of the work before us represents Plotinus, and how
much Porphyry? Did Porphyry edit what Plotinus left behind him to
the extent of reconstructing the whole system, and if so, was he com-
petent to do so? Did he understand the doctrine himself? Who shall
resolve this double star of Plotinus and Porphyry? The more limited
mind of the rationalist might ask whether it is a double star or a double
obscurity, and might watch with consternation the spectacle of one
transcendental philosopher trying to set in order the house of another.

cpon pure thought, even upon contemplation. It no longer feels its body, it
no longer feels that it is enclosed in a body. .. . The soul loses everything,
even the consciousness of its own pure essence, and thus prepared unites
itself to the Good, purely by virtue of its presence. Out of this irresistible
attraction is born that love which disturbs the soul and urges it to the
bosom of the Good. The soul then melts away there and is absorbed so
completely that it has no longer even the consciousness of the presence of
God within itself. Once arrived at this height it can only now descend;
-hought itself is a fall when the soul has arrived at this point of love. The
moment that this divine fire penetrates it, riches, fortune, science, virtue,
beauty, intellect, all these leave it cold and indifferent, and this is ecstasy.
.-- But why cannot the soul remain without return in this ineffable union
with God, when it has once had the happiness of reaching that point?
The reason is that the body solicits it without ceasing and tears it away
from its divine intercourse that it may plunge it again in the life of the
senses. It is rot until after death that the union of the soul with God can
be constant and durable.’ !

little doubt that its subsequent development in the works of such men
as Iamblichus, Aedesius, Maximus, Sallust, or Chrysanthius was the
inevitable consequence of the school of Plotinus. Mystery having
become the established divinity, the proselytes of Neoplatonism were
soon dissatisfied with the official form of worship. They betook them-
selves to the invocation of the host of demons and divinities that
Plotinus had never denied, but which he had always held aloof from as
one who sought to raise himself to the One, through the two lower
hypostases of Soul and Mind. Another element had now entered, in the
shape of theurgy. It was Iamblichus, the Syrian, who was the high-
priest of this second phase of Neoplatonism. Plotinus, while tolerating
_all the time-honoured beliefs of the Grecks, ‘had said to his disciple
Amclius, when urged by him to approach the gods: “It is for them
to draw near to me” (Porph. Vit. Plotin. c. 10)... What need had
he to invoke gods of an inferior order, he whom philosophy had already
elevated to the One’?* But this was not sufficient for Iamblichus. He
gave himself up to mysteries not merely in theory but in practice; his
disciples regarded him as endowed with supernatural powers.

Porruyry, the great pupil of Plotinus, had been, in the words of
Jules Simon, ‘the last defender of philosophy and common sense’. With
Iamblichus began the reign of something akin to ‘spiritualism’ in the
modern sense of the word, but one in which the personages evoked were
gods and heroes, not ordinary mortals as in the séances of its acolytes
of to-day. But as the field of the mysterious increased in magnitude,
mysticism proper diminished, for, paradoxical as it may appear at first
sight, the spirit of mysticism is a contrary one to that of spiritualism.
The former comes of an exalted form of religious longing, a passionate
desire of the soul to penetrate things impenetrable, the nature of God,
the enigma of life, the problems of time and eternity. It comes, indeed,
from an extreme of passion, one that failing of a solution in measured
reason, breaks through its philosophic trammelsand seeks toattain itsend
through the inconceivable path, the direct and instantaneous separation
of the soul from the body through ecstasy. But of what use were the
ladders of dialectic or the occasional liberation of the soul by fasting
and contemplation to those who had found a still shorter road to
paradise, those who without the stern abnegations and labours of the
ascent to a phase of union with the One and the Infinite, could remain
on earth and summon the gods of Olympus to commune with them on
easier terms’ The one conception is obviously lofty and spiritual,
the latter is material, and conceived in a crudely anthropomorphic
sprit.’ Neoplatonism, in passing over so lightly the traditional and
polytheistic beliefs, in admitting them either directly or by implication,
had left the way open to the entrance of the very forces which were now
to destroy its own exalted inspiration. Was it not, to use its own
imagery, being pulled down by the demons to the darkly lowering abyss

But even with this poison sapping its vitality, Neoplatonism produced
minds of no mean order. Did it not,when at its last gasp over a century
later, present the world with the acute. Simplicius, with Olympiodorus,
with Damascius? At the moment, with Iamblichus and his followers,
it has passed to a second and an inferior phase. But these Neoplatonists
hoped for a polytheistic restoration. This restoration was destined to
take a political as well as a philosophical form. With the emperor
Julian a new force had now come into play, one that might well have put
a different face on history. In a time of dramatic changes at the Imperial
court of the Roman Empire, none of these could comparewith the advent
to the throne of this young acolyte of philosophy and learning, one who
had, a mere boy, discarded the mantle of the philosopher for the breast-
plate and lance of the soldier, who had risen almost at once to the com-
mand of an army, who had carried the Roman eagles anew through the
battlefields of Gaul; who had crossed the Rhine repeatedly with all his
forces, had defeated the seven kings of Germany in one great battle, and
had finally been proclaimed Emperor by his troops, literally borne aloft
to the throne on the shoulders of an enthusiastic and cheering soldiery.

Hymas, the writer of Dreams, be identified with the orator who ad-

either of the mystical, the first phase of Neoplatonism, or of the

phases. In the most important crisis of conscience in his life, he seeks
to evcke no spirits or divinities, he addresses himself in an unmistakable
sprit of monotheism to One God and One only. In this he never wavers.
It is true that he attaches great importance to dreams, and even other
auguries of the future, but he defends them from the standpoint of the
natura] phenomena of the universe, and in a sense that Aristotle could
scarcely have taken exception to; whereas Julian was completely in the
hands of the charlatan Maximus, who professed to be a worker of
miracles, and amongst these to possess the power of animating marble
statues, like Pygmalion. He belonged rather to the last and most de-
cadent phase of Neoplatonism.

The life of Julian offers a very interesting comparison with that of
Synesius. They both lived in the same age; Julian died two or three
years later than the probable date of the birth of Synesius. Both were
men of a high degree of education and culture, men who had known the
university life of Alexandria and Athens. Both were past-masters of
the rhetoric of their day, and both have left a number of letters which
yield to no others in the history of literature, either in felicity of form,
or in the interest of the matter which they contain. Both seem to have
been born orators, both drew their inspiration from the works of the
Greek philosophers. Both were, in their different ways, extremely
original men. The one, Synesius, was brought up entirely outside the
Christian Church; the other nominally as a Christian, but in point of


FROM PLOTINUS TO JULIAN 53


fact as a pagan. The title of ‘Apostate’, with which Julian was sub-
sequently dubbed by the Christian writers, is rather misleading. He was
in reality entirely educated by his tutor, Mardonius, a philosopher who
was an ardent upholder of the old religion. His cousin Constantius,
who was responsible for his bringing-up, seems to have been entirely
devoid of all principle and capable of every crime; so that the un-
fortunate orphan lived in perpetual fear of assassination. In fact, it is
probable that it was only due to the goodness of the Empress Eusebia,*
who was very fond of the child, that he ever grew up at all. Mardonius,
his tutor, apparently instructed him secretly in the Greek religion, ex-
‘ horting him to stand by the faith of his ancestors. His words fell upon
a mind naturally disposed to the same end. Julian kept his religious
convictions to himself until he came of age, which was not surprising,
as he lived continually in the shadow of sinister court intrigues, and
to have taken any independent line of action might have been in his
case a fatal step. Although, therefore, brought up nominally within the
pale of the Church, he was precluded from coming under any influence
that might have inclined him to Christianity. The case of Synesius
was entirely different. ‘Brought up outside the pale of the Church’,
as he tells us himself, he began with paganism, and only later in
life was brought over to accepting the Christian faith, possibly
from motives which we should be inclined to describe as political. He
was pushed towards his conversion to Christianity by his friend
Theophilus, the Primate of Alexandria, who was determined that he
should be Bishop of Ptolemais; and after elaborately explaining to the
great prelate that he made every reservation of conscience on certain
points of Christian dogma, he consented to be ordained a Bishop. His
real position in regard to Christian doctrine seems to have been quite
identical with that of certain ‘Modernists’ of to-day, who apparently
regard Christianity as essentially the same as the Neoplatonic doctrine.

The character of Synesius, as it appears in his letters, is certainly a
“very winning one. You cannot read these without getting to like the
man for his qualities of heart, his charitable feelings, and his sparkling
wit; whereas the character of Julian is somewhat antagonistic. There
is in the Emperor a vein of bitterness which appears here and there,

and a lack of power to get into intimate touch with the reader, in
spite cf his very considerable literary abilities. Both men might have
gone much further as writers, if they had lived. ‘Julian’, says Alfred
Croiset, ‘who died at the age of thirty-three, does not seem to have
reached his full development as a writer. He certainly had in him the
stuff of a thinker, an historian, a moralist, and a satirist, and above all
of a man, a man whose true nature is always breaking through the con-
ventional forms of the literature of his period. Even his prejudice and
his violence of sentiment might have contributed to make him still
moe original. He did not live long enough to disengage himself from
the influence of his masters, and to become entirely himself.’ Synesius
was more happy in this respect, his more malleable nature seems to have
developed quite easily and harmoniously both in his literary work, and
his life in general. He had the golden touch of an amiable and benevo-
lent nature, which is reflected in such works as the Praise of Baldness,
and in that singularly mysterious and fascinating essay On Dreams. But
his literary power is much more flexible than Julian's, for he is capable
also of very stern and very fiery invective, which comes out with quite
startling intensity in the tirades which he launched at his great enemy,
the Roman prefect, Andronicus.

Some of Synesius’ letters remind one irresistibly of those of Julian.
There is a certain aroma that emanates from them, which is reminiscent
of these. Take, for instance, the letter 153, in which Synesius writes to
his friend Pylaemenes as follows:

*A letter comes to us from you every year, as though the seasons them-
selves brought it with them, and this fruit is perchance sweeter to me than
that which the circling months and the husbandmen bring to maturity. You
would do me an injustice if you deprived me of the joy I find in this. Change
your mind, then, and send me, this year at least, an abundance of letters.’

Compare this with Julian’s letter to his great friend Maximus:

“I sleep with your letters as though they were healing drugs of some sort,
and I do not cease to read them constantly, as though they were newly
written, and had only just come into my hands. Therefore, if you are
willing to furnish me with intercourse in letters, as a semblance of your own
society, write, arid do not cease to do so continually. Or rather come, with
Heaven's help, and consider that while you are away I cannot be said to be


alive, except in so far as I am able to read what you have written.’
(Letter 12, ed. Wright.)

Compare these last two letters. Julian seems to be on the defensive,

We have now, with the death of Julian, come to the probable date
of the birth of Synesius, for I quite agree with Crawford that he must
have been born not later than 360. By the time that he arrived at man-
hood, the last perturbations of the attempted Hellenistic revival of
Julian had subsided, and Neoplatonism, relinquishing any hopes of
becoming a world force politically, had, as we have seen, entrenched
itself behind the barriers of its own erudition and traditions. Again the
centre of gravity had shifted in the world of thought, this time from
Alexandria to Athens. Plutarch, the master of the great Syrianus, was
teaching at the Academy. We have seen with what scant respect
Synesius alludes to him and his disciples. And yet it was Plutarch whose
influence on the last hundred years of the school of Athens was most
important, as we gather from those of the Golden Chain who succecded
him, Syrianus, Proclus, Marinus, Isidore, Hegias, Damascius, not to
speak of others who followed, such as Olympiodorus, Simplicius, and
Philoponus, all of whom quote him. The fact that Synesius passes over
him so lightly is only another instance of his aloofness from Neoplaton-
ism as an established system. He remains a free lance to the end. He
plucks the flowers of philosophy wherever he finds them, and after
weaving some garland, as the fancy of the moment takes him, he lets it
fall lightly to earth. We should be wasting our time if we attempted to
seek an established system in his works, and herein lies much of their
charm. He was very proud of his capacity to speak with the voice of
another writer, as he tells us in Dto (p. 1161 A):

This was probably his first work, and one written in verse, prized, as he
