enough. The scholars of our more immediate past were so impressed by
the changes in the Greek language after its golden age that they went
rather to the extreme in depreciation of all literature that succeeded it.
At present we seem to be undergoing a reaction against our traditions
of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Greek that a century ago
‘was regarded as hopelessly debased in form is now having a better place
assigned to it in the estimation of scholars, and some later writers who
in the past were deemed entirely out of the race seem to be now receiv-
ing consolation prizes. How then does Synesius stand as a master of
Greek style? for that he aspired to be one we know from his own words.
The question is not an easy one to answer. Are we to compare him with
the Attic models of the golden age? Evidently this would be absurd;
his Atticism is purely relative. We can best compare him, perhaps, with
Julian, with Iamblichus, with other fourth- or fifth-century writers.

Dionysius of Halicarnassus analysed the canons of criticism in
hterary style as they existed in his own time, four centuries earlier,
and perhaps the most interesting passage in his celebrated work on
rhetoric is the following:

“The strongest style of all is that which has the most frequent pauses and
harmonious transitions, where one thing is said within, another without,
a period; where one sentence is made up of more, and another of less,
clauses; and where, of these very clauses, one is shorter, another longer, one
artiessly simple, another closely studied; where now one, now another
rhythm, predominates, where all manner of rhetorical figures occur, and
where also the pitches of the voice, termed accentuation, are diverse, and
conceal (what would otherwise produce) satiety.’!

In other words variety and antithesis were the qualities that he gave the »
first place to. All this comes under the head of what we should call
flexibility of style. But the rhetoricians of the first and second centuries
vefore Christ, ever since the days of Aristotle in fact, had multiplied the
classification of figures of speech and forms of logic employed in literary
style, until the canons of style had become complicated, and so rather
clipped the wings of the literary aspirant, somewhat as in French poetry
infinite subtleties enchain the freedom of metre together with rules of
prosody, frequently arbitrary, and complex rhythmical laws founded on
usage and precedent. All these limitations, while giving an unmistak-

able distinction and perfection of form to poems written in the lan-
guage, at the same time tend to contract the possible field of expression.
One result of this is that at the present day in France ‘vers libres’
are gaining ground, and blank verse is increasing to the detriment of the
time-honoured rhymed metres. The elaborate edifice of rhetorical form
in metre that has been built up since the days of Clément Marot show
signs of crumbling, because it no longer inspires the poet to express
his thought. Forms of metre that were originally spurs to thought
become by their over-development and excessive complication drags
upon it, and there must then ensuc either a breaking away to completely
new forms of expression, or a decadence into lifeless formalism. There
seems to be a Jaw in the history of both literature and the plastic or
pictorial arts, in virtue of which the most perfect results are obtained
at a moment when the critical facultics are dormant, before the icy
finger of analysis has dissected the delicate fibres of the works of art,
and has rendered the artist conscious for the first time of the laws that
until then he was unconsciously obeying. The critical faculty in man
is the inverse of the creative, and we might parody an old proverb, with
sufficient justice, by saying that when criticism comes in at the door
creation goes out by the window.

The history of Greek rhetoric and oratory, not to speak of philosophy,
bears an unmistakable resemblance to that of Italian art in its great
days. First there is a slow and cautious development, but full of the
seeds of life, criticism or analysis at this period being completely in
abeyance; then at a given moment and with vertiginous rapidity. as
Athene leaped clad in full armour from the head of Zeus, the perfected
works are born; a golden efflorescence of art in Italy, the day of the
great masters of painting and sculpture, in Athens the day of Thucy-
dides, of Plato, of Aristotle and the Attic orators, all this in a mar-
vellously short space of time. The succeeding period is that of sterility
in creation and activity in criticism. Analysis of the great works has
taken the place of production of them. The master of rhetoric reigns
supreme in the university, the academician in the studio. The spon-
taneity of art has disappeared with the classification and explanation
of its methods, with the supremacy of the lecture-room in Athens, and
the activities of the Eclectics in painting in Italy. Even in the days

of Socrates the sophists were preparing their fatal work in Athens and

But, it may be asked at this point, how does all this bear upon the
works of Synesius? Simply to this extent, that in considering the
literary style of any writer of his time or the centuries preceding or
immediately following it, we must remember that the writer was
oppressed by the schoolmaster. He was hemmed in on every side by
the rhetorician,the grammarian, and thesophist.' He wasnota freeman.
He was gazed upon by a thousand eyes, not of the starry vault of
heaven,as in Plato's verse, but by those of a very earth-born Argos, who
took human form clothed in the dark or the white mantle, as the case
might be. This was the atmosphere in which he lived, and this atmo-
sphere must have increased his difficulties very much as the refinements
of a rhetorical prosody, to return to the first illustration, must increase
the difficulties of the French poet of to-day. These limitations were
ever present before his mind, and it is perhaps due to this that the letters
of Synesius seem to us to surpass his purely literary works in point of
style. In the letters to his friends he was more emancipated, he did not
have the critic continually before his eyes. How could a man move

anaphora, diatyposes, hyperbata and polyptota’ of ‘Longinus’,? not to

classified. Even Cicero in his own time tells us that ‘the schemata as

cannot be said for Plotinus, whose style seems in so many places wilfully
and perversely distorted. Must we then look for the key to all this in
the corruptions of the text? I do not think so. I am more inclined to
accept Dionysius’ estimate of the causes that determine this sudden
involution of a writer’s style into obscurity, namely the desire to
indicate as many things as possible in as few words as possible, and the
consequent over-stepping of the limitations of language. In the case of
Thucydides this frequently takes the form of a change of construction
in the middle of a sentence, in the case of Synesius in the continual use
of ellipsis. We cannot say in the case of the latter that ‘brevity is the
soul of wit’, if by wit we mean the comprehensible.

But further than this, the position that a clear mind must express
itself clearly, in literary form, is scarcely tenable. Any one who has read
the letters of Robert Browning must acquit him of any obscurity or
confusion of thought as a man, but this did not prevent him from
writing much that is unintelligible to a reader who has not given up some
time to the study of his style. In the same way the late Henry James


FROM PLOTINUS TO JULIAN 67


wrote romances that are models of clearness and directness of style,
while other of his works belong clearly to the esoteric if not the unintel-
ligible school. Now it is of course true of poets, and prose writers alike,
that they may purposely adopt obscurity of style in order to create an
atmosphere suitable to the artistic effect at which they are aiming, but
we cannot suspect Thucydides, the first of historians, of playing such
notes on the lyre of Clio as this. The obscure passages in his work, as it
stands before us to-day, are certainly not artistic. They are, on the con-
trary, jarring, discordant notes, in an otherwise completely harmonious
narrative, the foundations of which have been profoundly considered
and consistently established. In his case, at all events, obscurity, from
whatever cause it proceeds, cannot have been intentional; but there are
cases in literature where this point is not so obvious, and where the
work of art has been left in an enigmatic condition so far as the inten-
tions of its author are concerned. We might quote Plotinus as a case in -
point, or in modem literature Browning's Sordello. It is not always easy
to separate difficulty of apprehension on the part of the reader from
deliberate mystification, or again from a failure in the power of expres-
sion on the part of the writer. There are therefore in the case of any
more or less obscure literary documents of antiquity three factors at
least to consider: the possible corruptions in the text, the possibility of
the obscurities having been intentionally introduced for artistic pur-
poses, as in the choruses in the Agamemnon of Aeschylus, and finally
- the possibility that the writer has failed in an attempt to express himself
clearly. There is also a disturbing factor in cases where technical terms
are employed. In the case of Aristotle the bulk of his works is so large
that we have been able, by a comparison of passages, to establish with
tolerable certitude the shades of meaning to be attached to such words.
But in the case of Synesius the works are so smal! in compass, that it is
not easy to proceed in this way, and we lack sufficient contemporary
evidence to help us. The work that I have chiefly in mind in making
these observations is the Dreams. Throughout this, in some respects
the most interesting that Synesius has left us, all the elements enumer-
ated come into play. The subject, as he viewed it, is a mysterious one,
for he was without the lights of modern psychology; the text certainly
seems corrupt in places, the tone of his inquiry into the subject, the

of the Dreams, it will be sufficient to indicate,at the opportune moment,
passages where it seems to me that intricacies in the thoughts to be
expressed have combined to obscure the meaning.

Greek language grew older, the element of quantity, that is to say the
Jength of time involved in enunciating a syllable, which had always
been the foundation of its rhythm in prose gs well as of its metre in
poetry, seems to have grown enfeebled, and the pitches of the voice
which the later grammarians attempted to stereotype by writing
accents over the vowel. sounds, apparently became intensified. There
must, therefore, have gradually arisen an ever increasing gap between
the spoken language and the language of literature. This language of
hterature was slipping little by little into the position of a dead lan-
guage, so far as its sounds were concerned, and it was inevitable that
sooner or later there should be a change in the rhythms of prose com-
position to accord with the change that had come over pronunciation.
As has already been said, Himerius, the rhetorician, and Themistius
were the first writers to introduce new laws of rhythm founded on the
accents and discarding the quantity, and more particularly to fix upon
certam recognized forms of terminating sentences, clausulae, as gram-
marians style them, the bases of which are the intervals of unaccented
syllables between the two last accented syllables in the sentence.
Synesius is almost enslaved by these artificial laws of clausulae, not to
speak of other modes of rhythm, a profound study of which will be
found in the works of Meyer, Maas, and Terzaghi. The most interesting
results obtained by the latter scholar is the discovery, for I can call it
nothing less, that Synesius became more and more under the domina-
thon of fixed Jaws in the clausulae as his literary experience ripened.
In his earlier works, Professor Terzaghi concludes, he shows a strong
tendency to follow the Jaws of accentual clausulae, but in the end this
tendency becomes a fixed law to him, as we see in his later works.
What is probably his earliest literary work, the letter to Paeonius,
contains 16 per cent. of clausulae that are violations of Meyer’s law;
his latest, the Praise of Baldness, contains only 3 per cent. The facts
speak for themselves. After the first work (to Paeonius), the others,
that is to say, Egyptian Tale, Dio, Dreams, Catastasis, and the Praise
of Baldness, taken in this their presumed historical order, show a contin-
ually decreasing percentage of violations of the law, or irregularities,
as we should call them. The percentages would then be as follows in
the order given: 16 per cent., 12°17 per cent., 11 per cent., 10°5 per cent.,


FROM PLOTINUS TO JULIAN ot


7°88 per cent., 3°17 per cent., 3° percent. But apart from the clausulae,
Terzaghi finds other figures of style, such as isotonism, parallelism,
rhyme, homoeoteleuton, &c. So we sce that the style of Synesius, which
seems Careless enough at first sight, is really vastly complicated by all
these considerations that he has in view, and all these points of rhetori-
cal rhythm that he is seeking to work up to. Of course, all the effects,
whatever they may be, attained by such means, must inevitably be
lost in a translation. The reasons given by Professor Dewing for con-
cluding that in all writers earlier than Himerius there is no approxima-
tion to this accentual scheme, are, of course, founded on exhaustive
statistics. He finds that no preference is shown in them for the set of
regular accentual forms made out by Meyer. While Himerius all this
time was using the accentual rhythm in his prose writings, Themistius
was at work on the accentual laws of clausulae, and was putting his
principles into practice. But the observance of such laws he can find
in no earlier writers. Synesius must therefore have been one of the
first to base his style upon this new system, which on the one hand
linked the literary style closer to the elements of popular speech, while
on the other hand it increased the artificiality of literature, and may
have made it more unintelligible to the ordinary layman. This last
point, however, it would be very difficult to determine. But all this
is quite in the tradition that we are beginning to establish concerning
all Synesiana. Whatever path we pursue in any attempt to analyse his
style or to trace his thoughts to their origins, we are faced by some
unexpected paradox and are as far from the solution as ever. He is
impalpable, and nowhere more so than in this fascinating and quite
untranslatable essay on Dreams. It moves in the finest, the most rare-
fied atmosphere of Athenian mentality, whatever reservations we may
make as to its Atticism in point of style. Joubert was certainly right
in saying that ‘even the dregs of Greek literature in its old age offer us a
delicate residue’. It is precisely this delicate residue that defies analysis.
‘The Greek’, Synesius says himself, ‘is on the whole superior to the
Barbarian’, and we quite believe him.’ The Barbarian takes up philo-
sophy or literature as an occupation or distraction, so he tells us, but
to the Greek it is his whole life, once he has passed the portals of the

temple of the Muses. So we see in perusing the letters of Synesius, that
the obsession, for it was scarcely less than this, of philosophy,. was
ever-present in some chamber of the conscious or sub-conscious mind ;
and his mind must have wandered far in the field of whatever literature
was accessible to it, and must have been well stored with reminiscences
even of other authors than those from whom he quotes.

But the faculty of improvising so easily the style and thoughts of
other writers, which he describes so nalvely, and not without a touch of
vanity, in the passage quoted a moment ago, is proof of an imaginative
mind; and imagination, the author tells us in Dreams, is the most
important function in the intellect of man. However that may be as a
general principle in psychology, it is certainly true of Synesius. He is
under the spell of ‘phantasia’—I raiust be allowed the Greek word, for
it conveys a shade of meaning all its own. He arises in the middle of
the night, and pens.a work that is fantasy itself. His own identity
disappears in that of others who control his hand, as he tells us, and he
finds himself in a state of complete detachment. Even the history of
his own time, the events he witnessed in Constantinople, all these he can
only see, or at least describe, in a framework of some mythical past in
Egypt, where the actors on the stage are no longer Aurelian, Caesarius
or (perhaps) Arcadius, but Osiris, Typho, the High Priest; the whole
court of the Emperor is peopled with phantom courtiers. The world
past and present becomes a fanciful one when he, the man of action,
gives rein to the impulses that move him to a world of images crystal-
lized by his imagination ; that world in which as in a finer element of the
spirit we are entranced by the visions of others, so that, as in the words
of Browning's poem:
“Whatever they are we seem,
Imagine the thing they know;
All deeds they do we dream :
Can heaven be else but so?’2

This supreme power of the imaginative faculties linked to a warm-
hearted nature tends to a dreamy idealization of his friends, but also
to a very real and active consciousness of their necessity. in his actual
life. He essays in vain to cultivate philosophic self-sufficiency. After
reproaching his friend Herculian for pining after him too much: in his
absence, he ends by gracefully admitting his friend’s point of view:
‘Why do you lament and drench your letters with your tears’, he writes
at one moment (Ep.140) ... ‘it is womanish or childish to love those
things through which the demon is able to rob us of the fruits of our
plans.’ But later he confesses to him (Ep.146) that there has been for
long ‘such a flood of enchantments’ in his letters, that he has ended by
giving way to the same state of feeling himself. ‘You see me to-day’,
he continues, ‘such a man as I at one time reproached you for being.
Has the illustrious Herculian done me great benefit in thus making my
soul depend on himself, and in compelling it to descend from the heights
of philosophy?’ This passionate feeling for friendship is one of the
forms that his idealism in philosophy takes. It is Platonic in its essence.
The phrase ‘give yourself up to philosophy’, which persistently recurs
in those letters written to his dearest and most intimate friends, is more
than a mere formula. It is a burning appeal to them to seek to partici-
pate with him in the forces that he feels to be the illuminating principles
of his own life." Here there is no appeal to the degenerate phases of
Neoplatonism, to theurgy or necromancy. He does not exhort his
friends to invoke deities or communicate with spirits; neither, be it
remarked, does he ever speak of a state of ecstasy as the object of a
philosopher's life. This alone.would be-sufficient to separate him from
the Neoplatonist proper. He is eager that his friends should share with
him in the greater light that comes from abstract thought, and should
establish a still deeper community of friendship thereby. For him the
one great fellowship that he sought was in thought. The ‘sacred quar-
tette’ to which he half playfully alludes, and in which his brother
Euoptius was to share, is only a form of his one desire.

of which Synesius has given a version in the Egyptian Tale. Nothing

Roman Empire was, with his accession to the ‘throne of massive gold’
in Constantinople, divided for the first time into an Eastem and

East was placed in a setting of truly oriental magnificence, to judge
from the words of St. John Chrysostom, and those of Synesius himself.
Surrounded by a whole phalanx of guards and courtiers, he appeared
in public in a golden chariot drawn by white mules, the very animals

resplendent with precious stones. ‘For you’, says Synesius, ‘even the

your waggons and merchantmen bring you from all the ends of the
earth... for it is not kingly to halt in the enjoyment of luxury even
in the soles of the royal sandals.’ (p. r080 B-C.)

This exaggeration of the outward pomp and circumstance of royalty
was, by the irony of fate, coincident with the time when the pillars
which supported the imposing edifice were themselves crumbling. The
great Theodosius had scarcely been borne to his last rest, when the
Goths flamed up in the North, and before the end of the winter of 395,
the erstwhile auxiliaries of Rome were moving in the direction of
Greece. Their leader Alaric poured his barbarian hordes over the
harvest lands of Boeotia. His progress was a veritable column of smoke
by day and fire by night’, as village after village was lit up by the torch
of the savage soldiery, who massacred the male population and carried
off whatever they found of youth in the womanhood of Greece, to share
‘in their rough barbarian life. Even Athens escaped only by payment
of a ransom that impoverished the city. There is a grim contrast in

this picture of a young, weak, and wavering Emperor passing his hours

which he makes an eloquent appeal, perhaps really directed to the

Is it possible that the downfall of the Barbarians to which Gibbon
alludes was hastened by the address which Synesius scems to have
delivered a year before it occurred? The sudden panic which seized
upon the Goths in the imperial city, their attempted flight, their
clashing with the citizens within the walls; all these events which he
recounts in allegorical form in the Egyptian Tale, have never been
satisfactorily explained. Given the extraordinary tension of fecling
that had come to prevail in the city between the foreign mercenaries
and the citizens, it might well be that the words of Synesius fired the
train. All things considered, this address will always rank as the most
important of his works. A comparison of it with the indictment of
Andronicus and the Catastasis would suggest that he was an orator by
natural bent; he shows equal power whether in the line of invective or
in that of persuasion. It would seem to us that so brilliant an entrance
as this successful address must have given him to the life of the court
at Constantinople, might have tempted him to go farther in a political
career. But his heart was evidently in his own country. The one city
always claimed him, and despite the triumphal return to power of his


78 INTRODUCTION


friend Aurelian, he soon shook the dust of the imperial capital from his
feet. It would be interesting to know whether the strange story that
he has given us under the title of the Egyptian Tale, and which is so
dramatic a history of these years under a thin disguise, was written
when he was at the court of the Emperor, or later. The incident of the
literary passage of arms with Typho, whoever he may have been, has
certainly all the aspect of a real scene, one that was actually enacted.
But it is perhaps the essay on Dreams which is the most fertile in
those thoughts that form the keystone to the edifice of his views on
psychological problems, and certain passages are very significant as
seeming to give evidence of a dim perception of factors in the analysis
of the actions of the conscious mind which it has been reserved for
modern times to elucidate more completely. His distinction between
the imaginative power in man and the lower animals is particularly in-
teresting. His conception is that imagination is the collective sense-
perception in which all the local sense-perceptions are united, and
which in the lower animals serve the ends of reason. In man, as
associated with the intellect, it becomes the higher reasoning faculty;
for, he says, we cannot form thoughts at all without the imaginative
element coming into play. Given that imagination is the sense of senses,
it is this super-sensorial faculty that passes the percepts to the intellect
in a form intelligible to it, and the result of this union is the act of
reasoning in the brain. ‘Imagination is like a mirror’,’ as he puts it in
his metaphorical language, ‘in which things are reflected which have
their seat in the soul... . We have no consciousness of the acts of the
intelligence, unless the imagination reveals such consciousness to us.’
And it is by force of this faculty, therefore, that man becomes conscious
that he is a thinking being (cogsto; ergo sum). Synesius finds in dreams
his clearest evidence. In this state, which is purely psychical, we do
not actually see, for our eyes are closed, nor do we hear, touch, smell or
feel pain; but all these sensations we experience nevertheless. These
sensations then must come from the super-sensorial faculty that is
Conjoined with the brain, and this faculty is none other than what we
call imagination. To leave imagination behind and enter into pure

It is interesting to observe how the Platonism of Synesius interprets
a tentative psychology founded on observation and reasoned hypo-
thesis. He begins, always in the language of poetic similes, to define
the imagination, that ‘perception of perceptions’, as the ‘first body of
the soul’, and speaks of it as ‘lurking there in its fastness and directing
the government of the living being ag from a citadel, for about it
Nature has constructed all the functions of the brain. Hearing and
sight are not senses, but only subservient organs of the common sense-
perception, like door-keepers of the living being, who announce to their
mistress (i. e. the super-sensorial imaginative element), the things per-
ceived outside, and from which the external organs of sense receive
knocks at the door. And this is the perfect sense-perception in all its
parts, for it hears and sees with its whole spirit and has power over all
the remaining (senses). It divides its powers, assigning one to one
place, and another to another. These powers stretch out from the
living being, each one separately, and, like straight lines radiating
from a centre, return to and meet in the centre again, all of them
one in their common root, though many in their outgoings. .. . But
the perception without an intermediary is more divine and nearest to
the soul.’ From all this it follows that the life in dreams, as being
one raised from a participation in the lower category of perception to
the imaginative faculty alone, by just this step stands so much nearer
to the life of mind, pure and unadulterated, and (for he pushed his
conclusions to this logical sequence also) approaches more closely to
the life of the soul after death. As our waking life is to our dreaming

life, so is our dreaming life, if I understand him aright, to our future

This is the end of the all too short incursion that Synesius has made
into what might be termcd moder psychology. Like some psy-
chologists of the present day, he is attempting to cross the ditch
that separates mind and matter. His solution is the postulating of this
principle which he calls ‘phantasia’, and which makes the long sought
bridge. It belongs to neither mind nor matter, but is nearest to cach.
It is, in his own words, a ‘no man’s land’ (the term used is a military
one), that lies between the ‘unreasoning and reason, the bodiless and
the body, and is a boundary common to both, and through it the divine
elements (i.¢c. mind and soul), are brought into contact with those
furthest removed from them (matter). And for this reason’, he says,
‘it is apprehended by philosophy with difficulty, for it borrows any-
thing that is suitable to its purpose, taking it from cither of the
extremes, as it were, from neighbours, and so images in one nature
things that dwell far apart.”

Looking back at all this from the vantage ground, if it be such, of
over fifteen centuries, it is safe to say that we are no nearer the solution
of the problem than in the days of the philosopher of Cyrene. All
attempts to break down the dualism that exists between consciousness
and what lies outside it, have failed. Science again, in another field,
has, so far, been unable to bridge the chasm between living and lifeless
matter, between the organic and the inorganic. Olympiodorus, at a
later period than Synesius, feels the same diflicultics. He is not content
with the explanations of Aristotle. He cannot, he says, agree with the
Peripatetics, that sense-perception is the principle of knowledge. ‘The
inferior cannot be’ the cause of the superior. Sense-perception is like
a messenger or a herald,” he goes on to say, repeating here the words of
Plotinus, ‘its réle is to awaken the spirit to attain knowledge.’ But how
does it awaken the spirit, or through what agency? Through imagina-
tion, Synesius would answer, through this super-sensorial faculty that
he has described to us. The messenger is a messenger indccd, but not a

Synesius next proceeds to tell us what an important part the study
of dreams has played in his own life, and how it protected him in the.
troublous and dangerous days of his mission in Constantinople. There
is an interesting parallel in the third hymn, where he gives thanks to

art which consists in the observation and interpretation of a positive

he says, ‘assert that sense-perception creates memory, memory experi-

maintains that this art is one purely personal to cach individual. He
laughs to scorn the innumerable books which profess to give rules for
interpreting dreams. These images, reflections, as he calls them, of the
future, differ with every person, and no gencral laws of interpretation
can be devised. They are part of the realm of positive law, but a law
that has infinite variations. Proficiency in reading these signals of the
future can only be attained by continual practice, observation and

revealed in sleep.

The picture of the universe in the story is an undeniably gloomy
one; man lives in a valley of fear, the carth scems peopled with the
demons of matter whose whole function is to destroy. This one con-
ception of the maleficent spirits that lurk in the dark places of the
earth and draw the soul of man down to its destruction, is as firmly
embedded in this paganistic imagery of the Providence, as it was in the
Christian imagery of the Middle Ages. There is a breath here such as
we catch in Orcagnas’ Triumph of Death, and in many works of art
before the Renaissance in both painting and sculpture. The same view
of man’s destiny is to be found in Dante, and has been passed on in
some form or other to modern times, a strange legacy that the poly-
theism of Greece and Rome has left us, and which was accepted in all.
its essentials by the early Christians. Even in building their church
whose tapering spire pointed to heaven, the architects of the Gothic
cathedrals could not escape giving their testimony to thiscult of demono-
logy, and the forms of grotesque spirits may still be seen mingled with
the soaring columns and pinnacles of living stone that carry aloft their
message of redemption, The grinning faces of the demons of matter
still look down from the towers of Notre-Dame on the island of the
Seine, on the very spot which the Emperor Julian knew as Lutecia,
and where the Imperial diadem was forced upon his brow; they still
brood over the city of Strasbourg, and rail at us from the heights of
Rouen cathedral. To what an extent this conception of the universe
was ever present to the mind of Synesius, appears in his letters in many
places, and in his other works also, nor could he refrain at times from
attempting to offer some explanation that might satisfy the cravings
of his soul to reconcile the powers of darkness with the powers of light.

This passage illustrates very well the spirit in which he has written
his Dio. There is something very buoyant, something full of hope and
inspiration in this delightful essay on the value of literature and style,
and on their relation to the higher life of tte philosophic mind. Druon
and Crawford agree in placing the date of its composition in the year
403, not long, it would seem, after his marriage. His first son was soon
to be born, and we can easily imagine how the paternal heart, of which
he gives such touching, and even tragic evidence 1n his letters, must
have thrilled with the expectation that filled him at this period. “These
criticisms concerning Dio have occurred to me’, he writes, ‘in connexion
with this son of mine who is soon to be born; for it was at the moment
when I was perusing his works that the oracle prophesying the birth
of a son was revealed to me.’ This name Dio means very little to-day,
even to those fairly well-read in Greek literature, and is a case the more
to remind us of the uncertainty of the survival of any literary reputa-
tion. At the time in which Synesius wrote he seems to have been looked
upon as a great master of rhetoric, and it is this writer whom he has
selected as a guide for the budding talents of his son, when the time
should come for him to devote himself to literature. He seems to have
no doubt that he shall have a son to instruct worthy of his own powers.
And this is only another evidence that the vein of thought which we
encountered in Dreams was a reality to him, and a part of his nature;
the conception of a world in which the past and the future are indisting-
uishable, and where the presage of the future has the same authority
as the memory of the past. ‘Already’, he says, ‘I have the feelings of
a father; I long to live with my son, to have him by my side to instruct
him; he must know what I think of every writer and of every book; I
shall introduce my favourite authors to him, and criticize them one by
one. And among them Dio of Prusa shall have a foremost place, both.
for the style of his work and for their substance... . my son will learn
to love him, although without placing him in the same rank as the real
kings of philosophy.”

Synesius, the gay and laughing philosopher, shines on us agz.in in the
pages of the Praise of Baldness. Here his predecessor, Dio oi Prusa,
is the foil of his wit. Dio had written a eulogy on Hair, in the rhetorical
taste of an age when any paradox in literature was prized, and when
the more absurd the subject, the greater honour the writer had in
displaying his ingenuity in handling it. Dio praises hair as the scat of
man’s might and intellect. Synesius, centurics later, reverses the
decision, and extols baldness. It will be noticed that he never loses an
opportunity in his letters and elsewhere, of deriding the sophists and
would-be philosophers by whom he is surrounded, for the ostentation

which they make of their beards, and men who wear long hair are

they shine out for a few brief months, and then disappear for ever.
And so he rings the changes on his theme, until even the heavenly
bodies can no more escape the shafts of his wit than the army of
Alexander, which he tells us was routed by the Persians, who pursued
their enemies, and caught them by their long flowing hair, until the
great Macedonian drew off his forces, and saved the fortunes of the day
by handing his troops over to the barbers. Thus he diverts his readers
by leading them through an amusing labyrinth of absurdities, not
without wit and a decidedly original vein of satire all his own. Like his
forerunner, Julian, he shows the powers of the satirist, but his satire
is more kindly than Julian’s. We miss the biting sardonic vein that
rans through the Afisopogon and the Caesars. Julian’s touch is heavier
than that of Synesius. He was everything but a poet.

That Synesius was a poet by temperament, there can be very little
doubt, but his Hymns fail to display this side of his nature to the best
advantage. One reason for this seems to be that he has tied himself
down to a metre that is scarcely fitted for conveying the mingling of
religious sentiment and philosophic or theological divagations that he
wishes to.express. The metres resembling those of the Anacreontea which
he employs were the form of verse used by the Gnostics, whose sect, or
rather sects, for there were innumerable forms of them, had long fallen
from the important position which, as we have seen, they had occupied
in the days of Valcntinus or Bardaisan. Nevertheless they had left
a certain literature behind them and they still perhaps continued to
write. The short lines of verse, then, were the official form so to speak
of Gnosticism.

Here we are faced with another problem. Why should Synesius have
adopted a manner of versification that would have stamped him in the

eyes of the world as a Gnostic? There is no allusion to Gnosticism in his
works, but this is not the only trace of the Gnostics that we find in them.
Inspeaking of Providence, Crawford makes the following very just obser-
vations (p. 80):


*‘Synesius extremcly complicates his psychology by maintaining that
souls spring from two different sources. Some, he says, come from above;
some from below. There are, therefore, those which are fundamentally
good, and those which are fundamentally bad. The destiny of souls is to
return to the region whence first they came. The bad lodge in suitable
hiding-places; the good, if they have preserved their character and kept
themselves free from pollution during the time of their earthly sojourn,
flow back along the same course as that by which they came, and are re-
absorbed into their proper source. .. . The origin of Typhos and his final
doom exhibit a belief in the baldest dualism. The Persian doctrine of an
almost equal Ormuzd and Ahrimazn, the Spirits of Light and Darkness ever
in conflict from the very first, is not more opposed to the Neoplatonic con-
viction of unity in all things than Synesius’ tale of Osiris and Typhos.’


He further very pertinently remarks in a foot-notc, ‘Is there here a trace
of Alexandrine Gnosticism? One is remindcd of two of the three classes

on their works. (Robertson, vol. i, p. 79.)’ After showing the contra-
dictions to the doctrines of Plotinus and his followers that this way of

work On Providence and elsewhere, ‘is generally displaying a view of

was undoubtedly his view, and one certainly not shared by Plotinus or
any of his followers. I have always maintained that the Cyrenean
philosopher was not a Neoplatonist in the common acceptation of the

simply gathered into his net whatever other. doctrines pleased him,
He is not at one with Plotinus in any way, although he sometimes
quotes him, and shows his influence in certain passages of Dreams.
But there seems to me to be more than a trace of Gnosticism in his
conception of the source of the souls. It is practically identical with
the doctrine of Valentinus set forth in Crawford’s note, and icads

one to suppose that Synesius had woven views of the Gnostics into his

cated. The same voice is audible in the //ymns,as in the following lines:
*Peace, audacious lyre, I entreat, pause; reveal not the mystcries to the
people at large, mysterieswhich are celebrated without initiation; gothou
and tell of the things here below; silence covereth those above’ (H. 1.)

As we advance in the Hymns, the grim spectre of matter and its
demons overshadows us. He prays to the Unknowable, Unspeakable
Father to chase away from his soul the hound of the soil, the demon of
earth. ‘Let him flee, let him leave me, the demon of matter, the power
of sufferings, who builds his fortress-wall against the path that leadeth
above, who violateth the aspirations that seek God... . grant to my
soul oblivion of its passions to the end that I may complete the life that
comes with destiny after the chains that weigh us down to the carth,
a life purified of matter, even unto Thy halls and unto Thy bosom,
whence outwelleth the fountain of the soul.’ (H. IV.) But if Synesius
had been influenced by the example of Gnostic writers, it must always
be borne in mind that Gnosticism had an influence on the early Christian
Church itself. Its literature was rich in hymns, and once Synesius had
adopted this form of poetical expression, it was inevitable that he should
be attracted to these examples, even if for no other reason than that
of following a model which lay ready to his hand. To raise the question,
as has so often been done, of the orthodoxy of Syncsius, or to specu-
late as to whether he could be regarded as essentially a Christian
writer, is to involve oneself in contradiction, because the factors of
the problem are themselves uncertain. What I mean is that, agcord-
ing to the doctrine of the Neoplatonists, he was scarcely. one of them-


96 INTRODUCTION


selves, nor was he orthodox according to the doctrines of Christianity,
if we take the Hymns as expressing his real tenets. Whether he was
orthodox from the point of view of the Gnostics it would be impossible
tosay. There were such innumerable ramifications of Gnostic thought,
and so many sects of them, that the term ‘orthodoxy’ could have no
meaning in regard to them. They were like the ‘two and seventy
jarring sects’ mentioned in Omar Khayyam’s poem. But the followers
of Plotinus had a more clear-cut conception of their belicfs and aims, -
although it had considerably changed, as we have scen, since the
death of the founder of their system, and had sadly deteriorated. It
had become the opponent of Christianity, and its struggle to maintain
its life had tended to crystallize its conceptions into an unmistakable
form of religion (for I can see it in no other light), a form that has
captivated certain thinking religious minds to such an extent that
the formerly despaired-of reconciliation between Neoplatonism and
Christianity is again talked of to-day in certain quarters as the only
salvation for the Church. Such a thinker as Eucken has expressed him-
self to this effect very clearly, and a high authority to-day on the works
of Plotinus, not merely sees nothing irreconcilable between the doctrine
of the pagan philosopher and that of Christianity, but even goes so far
as to say that it is of the first importance to the religious life of
Christians. As to the soundness of all this, I express no opinion; I am
only pointing to facts which are significant of the trend of a certain
section of religious sentiment to-day. After an interval of sixtcen cen-
turies the same dream of a millenium has begun to be an obsession
again, and this to minds of a high order. Whatever may be said on
the merits of this conception, although syncretism in the precise sense
that it existed in the first centuries after Christ may not be operative
Bail callaiabs in an altered form is still living. It no longer
; to construct a mosaic of beliefs taken from different forms of
religion,but rather to discover an identity of belief in ascending to the
metaphysical root of each. The Timaeus of Plato, the Enneads of
Plotinus, the Gospel of St. John, would (there is no other explanation
of the statements made to us by the school in question), come under
a common source of inspiration. Could the position be better stated
than in the words of Ogniben, the Pope’s Legate, in Browning’s play,


CRITICAL APPRECIATIONS 97


A Soul's Tragedy: ‘New truths, old truths, Sirs, there is nothing new
possible to be revealed to us in the moral world: we know all we
shall ever know; and it is for simply reminding us, by their various
respective expedicnts, how we do know this and the other matter, that
men get called prophets, pocts, and the like. A philosopher's life is
spent in discovering that, of the half-dozen truths he knew when a
child, such an one ts a lie, as the world states it in set terms; and then,
after a weary lapse of years, and plenty of hard thinking, it becomes
a truth again after all, as he happens newly to consider it and view
it in a different relation with the others; and so he restates it, to the
confusion of somebody else in good time. As for adding to the original
stock of truths,—impossible.’ This seems to chime very well with
the reflection made by St. Augustine, to the effect that all the great
truths embodied in Christianity had always been known to man since
the very beginning of the world, and that the revelation of Christ
was only the Divine seal and endorsement of them."

There are two tendencies observable to-day amongst the modernists
in the Church, but they rather point in the same direction. The one is
towards this incorporation of the doctrines of the Neoplatonic philo-
sophers, the other towards the formal renunciation of the old-time
teleological explanation of the universe, and the adoption of the evolu-
tionary conception which has sprung from the discoveries of modern
science. The protagonists of this double movement again seem to show
a certain sympathy for each others’ views, so that a new coalition of
thought in regard to religious doctrines is a possibility of the future.
Such a movement would again attempt a reconciliation between the
rationalist point of view and the theological. Theology, which Huxley
in the nineteenth century described angrily as a ‘false science’, would
be rehabilitated in the eyes of the rationalists and evolutionists of the
twentieth. Christian and Hellenic theology would be consolidated on
some new basis which would admit also of the cardinal principles of
modern science, the principle of development, and the universal reign

- Now all this contains a lesson in regard to our estimate of Synesius.
If the minds of churchmen and prelates in the present day can find
religious doctrines and beliefs so malleable, is it surprising that any onc
who was first a philosopher and finally an ecclesiastic in the fourth
century should show similar tendencies? Griitzmacher has described
him as a ‘religious phenomenon’, but I fail to sce that he was more so
in all essentials than the extreme modernists of to-day, or the Christian
scientists who resemble in many respects the gnostics. To ask whether
Synesius was orthodox, in the sense in which orthodoxy was understood
at his own time, is easily answered by referring to the letter in which
he informs the primate of Alexandria that he makes various reserva-
tions, and sufficiently important ones, concerning the dogmas of the
Church. Nothing could be clearer. He admits, like an honest man,
that he is not orthodox. This, however, did not prevent Theophilus
from insisting on his taking holy orders; nor was there anything in
these reservations as to the Platonic doctrines which he held, that
would compromise his position as a Christian in the eyes of the modern-
ist of to-day, or, from their point of view, render him unfit for a
bishopric. History is only repeating itself if we look a little below the
surface. In the work on Providence, as we have seen, he attempts to
reconcile Divine intervention with the laws of nature, and here again
he approaches currents of thought of the present day. He reduces the
‘action of Providence’ to an occasional intervention that takes the form
of the introduction into the world of souls kindred to the divine,—to
the ‘gods’ in the story—inspired men we should call them perhaps; but
the moral, as I have pointed out, is that man’s real Providence is in his
own hands, though he is, to a certain extent, predestined by his inheri-
tance, or as we should say, by heredity. If I am right in my reading of .
the allegory, nothing could be more rationalistic. He is evidently at
grips with the same problems that areoccupying us to-day, andalthough

I should be almost inclined, therefore, after weighing the somewhat
contradictory evidence that his works contain, to describe Synesius as
a fourth-century modernist, but one whose literary taste and imagina-
tive temperament are always Icading him into by-ways of imagery
derived from other religions than his professed one. This again we have
ample precedent for in more modern times. There is an unmistakable
pagan clement in Dante, who not only invokes the supreme deity of
paganism in a passage beginning ‘O susnmo Giove’, but continues ‘Che
fosti in terra per noi crucifisso’, and the Lusiad of Camoens is full of the
mingling of Christian and pagan imagery. Milton himself is not exempt
from this confusion of the imagination. ‘What is really disconcerting
to the student of Synesius is not so much his mingling of pagan imagery
with Christian, as his apparent ignorance, or studied neglect, of Chris-
tian theology, and his silence in reference to any of the works of the
Greek Fathers of the Church. It is difficult to imagine that he had
never seen any of the works of Clement of Alexandria, of St. Basil, or
of St. John Chrysostom, and it is difficult to understand why he seldom
makes any allusion to the gospels or the Pauline epistles, although, in
the impeachment of Andronicus and elsewhere, he not merely quotes
the Old Testament, but, what is more important, scems thoroughly
imbued with its spirit. In this work at.all events he speaks with the
voice of a Hebrew prophet. It is true, on the other hand, that his
silence regarding the Hellenic wniters of his own century, such as Julian,
Themistius, or Himerius, is equally unaccountable, particularly when
we consider that he adopted a system of clausulac that seems to have
been introduced by these two rhetoricians. If Synesius was some
apocryphal writer, whose date we were attempting to fix by internal
evidence derived from his works, and if these were not full of historical
allusions that would be conclusive in any case, we might, by following
the line of argument pursued by Rhys Roberts and other commentators
on the Pseudo-Longinus, very well decide that he could not have
belonged to the fourth century at all, for he quotes none of its writers.
This is only another instance of the baffling problems that beset us.

But as to the origin of his inspiration, nothing could be clearer. It


100 INTRODUCTION


rests upon Plato. This docs not preclude the influence at times of
Plotinus and of the Gnostics; but the main current seems to me plain
enough. Whatever his sources were, he tried to bring them into a closer
touch with his own age. However the matter may be regarded in our
own day, there is no doubt that the Greek Fathers of the Church were
conscious of some inspiration that distinguished Plato and his works
from other pagan literature. Later on, as the world approached the
Middle Ages, this influence was obscured by that of Aristotle, whom
the schoolmen, little imaginative and inclined to formalism, turned to
as their standard of knowledge. But the necessities of the Church,
struggling for the domination as well as the illumination of the souls
of men, had forced it into a war with friend as well as foe, and its con-
sciousness of an inspiration closely resembling its own, though not
identical, that runs through the works of Plato, had to be suppressed
in the polemics which the clashing with Neoplatonism gave rise to.
There had been also a side of the philosophy of Zeno and the Stoa,
which had long been preparing the ground for the fruition of the Chris-
tian ideal, in the perception that Zeno first gave voice to, of the equal
claims of all men to justice, whether Greek or Barbarian, and the
complete separation of religious from national or racial ideals; the first
conception of an affinity of all men on purely moral grounds that led
to the Christian conception of a brotherhood in Christ. An interesting
document concerning the international spirit of early Christianity may
be found in the letter to Diognetus, a work of uncertain authorship that
was erroneously ascribed to Justin, a writer of the second century, but
which is possibly of earlier date. Speaking of the Christian communities
he says:

“The Christians are separated from other men, neither by frontiers nor
language nor customs. . . . They have, each one of them, a country of their
own, but they are as it were sojourncrs in it... . Every foreign land is their
own country and every country is to them a foreign land. . . . They say
prayers on the earth, but they are citizens of the heavens; they are born in


the flesh, but they live not according to the flesh... . In a word, what the
soul is to the body, the Christians are to the world’ (c. 5).


Can any one reading this fail to be reminded of the last words in the
ninth book of the Republic (§92): |


CRITICAL APPRECIATIONS 1or


Glaucon, ‘I understand; you mean that he will be a ruler in the city of
which we are the founders, and which exists in idea only; for I do not believe
that there is such an one anywhere on carth.’

Socrates. ‘In heaven there is laid up a pattern of it, methinks, which he who
desires may behold, and beholding may take up his abode there. But
whether such an one exists, or ever will exist in fact, is no matter; for he
(i.e. the just man) will live after the manner of that city, and of no other.’


Again, could anything be clearer than the unity of inspiration to be
found in these two passages, the one by the Christian writer of the
second century, the other by Plato himself?

We have now madc the pilgrimage of a thousand years shadowed in
the last words of the Republic. We have passed through the portico
of the Stoa; aloof with Epicurus, we have looked down upon the ‘flam-
ing ramparts of the world’; we have dissolved ourselves with the
atomists, we have reconciled the Hebrew and the Hellenic inspiration
with Philo, we have accepted universal doubt with Pytrho, we have
railed with Clement, and floated on the waves of ecstasy with Plotinus;
we have been amazed at the fantastic dreams of Valentinus and Basil-
ides, we have stood by while Proclus was calmly blowing on the expiring
embers of Hellenic thought at Athens.


*So to save the sced of fire, that he might not perforce scek it elsewhere’ ;


we have marked his successors Damascius and Simplicius, still subtly
commenting on Aristotle, and then after the great blow, we have seen
the smouldering torch passed on to the theologians in Byzantium,
where, with Psellus, Platonism revived in the tenth century. Again the
words of the Republic surge up irresistibly: ‘Adeimantus added: *’Has
no one told you of the torch-race on horseback in honour of the goddess
which will take place in the evening?” ‘With horses?” I replied; “that
is a novelty. Will horsemen carry torches and pass them one to another
during the race?”’’

Even at the risk of being taken for disciples of Proclus, and of laying
ourselves open to the anathema that Gibbon hurled at one whose life
‘exhibits a deplorable picture of the second childhood of human reason’,
we shall, I think, read into these words something of a prophetic nature.
For in all the intricate web of the tangled skein that we have been
seeking to unravel, the golden thread woven by Plato is always present,


102 INTRODUCTION


hidden at one moment, at another glittering in the sun, that sun which
to him symbolized ‘the idea of good . . . parent of light and of the Lord
of light in the visible world, and the immediate source of reason and
troth in the world of mind’.

Ah, masters of theology, of metaphysics, whether in Athens or
Alexandria, in Antioch or Byzantium, you have explored the heights,
you have sounded the depths, you have peopled the chasms of the earth
with demons and have drawn down souls from the stars. Has anything
appeared on your horizon that was not first illumined by the lamp
lit by Plato in the city that was once the ‘eye of Greece’? We are again
on the old road, the road that leads from Eleusis to Athens, the road
that had always bridged the chasm which separated the East from the
West. Could Svnesius have made the pilgrimage of a thousand years,
not in the shadowy region spoken of by Plato, but upon this earth, he
would have found himself in the new springtime of the master he had
followed, at the first budding growth of the Renaissance of Hellenic
thought in Italy, in the world of Ficino, of Pico della Mirandola. The
drama that he speaks of in De Providentia is still moving towards an
unknown destination. Can we, in these later days, do better than to
take his advice, ‘to sit quietly and watch its different acts as they
develop successively before our eyes upon the stage’?

“Time, the incorruptible witncss,
Comes to enlighten us in the end.’

5. No term has ever yet appeared in any place that grasps the

All men, everywhere, methinks, celebrate the goodness of God,
ts alike peoples that are wise and peoples that are foolish. In this at
least all agree with one another, and speak with the same voice,
however they may differ in all other respects in their notions of the
Divine element, and however they divide His pure and indivisible

20 undisputed good does not yet disclose to us the throne of God in
real existence. That is only gathered from events that follow;
for the Good does not come to our hearing as absolute, but as a
relative good to those for whom it is an efficacious force and by

25 is an attcmpt to signify further that God is the cause of the good.

16. Now the warlike king may be above all a man of peace, for
to him alone who is able to inflict injury upon the evildoer is it
given to keep the peace. For my own part I should say that the
king has, all in all, gained most applause as a peacemaker who,
although desiring injustice to none, is nevertheless provided with 5
the power to escape injury at the hands of others; for if he does
not war, he will certainly be warred against. Peace is a happier
state than war, because the preparations of war are actually made
with a view to peace. The end in view would justly be preferred
to those things which exist on its account. Thus it is well that the 10
king give himself up to each half of his command in turn, that body
politic divided into two estates, that of the armed men and that of

civic rights. He will visit again and again in his tours as many
races and as many cities as possible; and whatever portion of his
Empire he does not reach, even to that he will devote his atten-
tion in what is apparently an effective and excellent way.

a2 «1. Pattostratus of Lemnos, in composing the lives of the
sophists who had preceded him, divides them into two classes at
the beginning of his treatise; first the sophists in the exact sense,
and second those who, although really students of philosophy, had
nevertheless been classified as sophists on account of their reputa- 5
tion for beauty of language. He gives Dio his place amongst these,
as also Carneades the Athenian, and Leo of Byzantium, and
many others who passed their lives in the profession of philosophy,
but had accustomed themselves to a sophistical form of style; and
again he accounts amongst these Eudoxus of Cnidus, a man at first 10
known as one of Aristotle’s disciples, but also well versed in astro-
nomy, at least as much of the art as was cultivated in those days.
For our part let Dio through all his works be a sophist, even as he
is said to be, in virtue of the range of that ‘tongue of gold’ which
he possessed, if any one chooses to consider the cult of oratory an 15
achievement proper to the sophist. The nature of this, indeed, we

#113 shall examine a little later. If we consider his aims, Dio should
neither be placed alone nor with the men just mentioned, but
rather with Aristocles, although he is to be contrasted even with
him. Both of them changed their earlier attitude, but Aristocles 20
was a man who from being a philosopher and an earnest one at
that, and one whose brow was knit with thought, ended among
the sophists, and not only indulged in every luxury, but even
reached the culminating point.

After spending the bloom of his youth in the advocacy of the 25
Peripatetic views, and in publishing treatises for the Greeks with
all the philosopher’s enthusiasm, he fell a victim to sophistic
opinion to such an extent that he repented him when an old man
of the very seriousness of his youth, and in his contests shook the
lecture-rooms of Italy and Asia with his declamations. Moreover 30


DIO 149


he had given himself over to the cottabus and introduced flute
girls at dinner parties, and besides gave public banquets.
Dio, however, from being a senseless sophist ended his life as a
philosopher, and favoured in this rather by fortune than by his
gs own judgement, has himself given us an account of that good ::36
fortune. So it was the duty of one writing his biography to
describe the flaw in the man and not simply to reckon him thus
with Carneades and Eudoxus. Whichever of their subjects you
take, it is a philosophic.one handled in a sophistical way; that is to
10 say the style is wantonly, withal cunningly, set forth, and brings
in much of the element of grace. In this way also by men whom
they fascinated in speech by the beauty of their phrases, they were
deemed worthy of the title of sophist, but it seems to me that they
themselves would have repudiated this and would have declined
35 it if offered, since philosophy brings such an expression into con-
tempt, for Plato had just risen up against the name. But Dio
showed forth brilliantly in each of these two walks of hfe re-
spectively, and is at war with himself in his subjects, publishing
speeches setting forth these opposite ways of life. Now we should
zo not, methinks, pass over in silence the facts concerning this man,
least of all on account of the discrepancy found in his speeches.
As to what Philostratus says in the following passage, when he
absolves him from blame for composing a panegyric on a bird
called ‘a parrot’, on the ground that it is the part of a sophist not
as to scorn even such a subject, in all this he seems to confute himself,
for he announced to us before that this man is one of the slandered,
inasmuch as, though all the while a philosopher, he is dragged
into being a sophist; for he speaks as follows:
‘The ancients described as sophists, not only those of their
30 rhetoricians who made loud speeches and were brilliant men, but
also those of the philosophers who expounded their thoughts in a
fluent style. In behalf of these latter we ought to speak first, for
although they were not sophists but only seemed so, they have


150 DIO


passed under this designation.’ Then he distinctly enumerates the
men who are philosophers, amongst these Dio, and others after
Dio, and in taking leave of the last of them, says: ‘So much for the
philosophers who have the reputation of being sophists,’ only |
saying in another way the same thing, namely, that not being s
sophists they usurped that name. And yet in the meantime he
admits, it would seem, that he is in doubt in what rank of his
chorus to place this man, for he is really very expert.

What then did you say at first, and what afterwards? was it that
the one thing is, and the other only appears to be? For my part I 10
do not split hairs over these contradictions, and I am willing to
admit that Dio was really a philosopher and only played at
sophistry, as long as he shall be found gentle and compassionate to
philosophy, and has nowhere done her violence or marshalled
against her reckless and evil-minded words. But this man of all 15_
the sophists had behaved with the greatest effrontery to philo-
sophers and philosophy. The reason for this, I think, is that since
a nature full of power was allotted to him, even the practice of
oratory made him speak the truth, for he was persuaded that it
was better to live according to the views shared by the generality 20
of mankind than to live according to philosophy. It follows from
this that his works directed against the philosophers are carried
out with great attention to expression and shirk no brightness of
language. The work addressed to Musonius also was another of

that law which does not permit us to make additions in books. On

let it make trial of its own strength and not entirely cling to the 10
syllables.

For just as any other problem becomes a source of satisfaction
to us if our perplexity over it exercises our invention; thus also
the mind, compelled to weave that which is missing into the
sequence of what is read, and not resting entirely on vision, makes 15
practice in venturing upon a similar work by itself. At the same
time it accustoms itself not to belong to others but to itself, for
these books containing errors seem to seek out the mind that is


superior to mere eyesight.


16. The teachings of Pythagoras prescribed this to quite young 20
a363 Men, at one time making trial of the natural bent of each of them,
at another time esteeming this a preparatory exercise even more
suitable to boyhood than the assumptions of plane geometry, for
it is no great task to adapt a letter, a syllable, perchance a
phrase, or if you will a whole period, and again to employ conve- 3§
niently what is in the book. This is quite like what happens in the
case of the fledglings of eagles. The parents take the eaglets when
they are just ready to fly, and bearing them aloft let them go on
high, as if permitting them to use their own wings. Then in a
moment they take them up again, for they foresee the weakness 30
of their youth, and this trial they repeat frequently until the
young have learned thoroughly how to fly.

Now I shall never indulge in youthful boasting before any man,

but about these truths, at least, I will boast in your presence. Oft-
times I do not attempt to await the conclusion of a book for any
good it may do me, but rather‘do I lift up my eyes and procced to

s exercise mysclf in the narrative, not hesitating in the least but
yiclding to the opportune moment; and pretending that I am
reading straight on, I recite out of my own head whatever it seems
to me should follow, and I test what has been thus said in the
light of what has been written. Oft-times I find that I have
10 happened upon the same sense and even the same form of ex-
pression (as the author). On the other hand, I have occasionally
made a happy shot at a thought, although missing the phrasing
itself, and have produced what quite resembled the harmony of
the work. And even if the thought was different, it was at all events

1g Such as would befit the writer of the book, and one which he would
not have rejected if it had come into his mind. I know that on
one occasion I was holding in my hands a volume of the noble
and classical order, and when certain men who were present asked
me to read something aloud that they might listen to it, I pro-
20 ceeded on this wise. And as opportunity arose I would invent
something new and would add an explanation of it, not, by the
god of eloquence, that I had rehearsed it, but that, when I came
upon it’ in this way, I fell into harmony with the author’s
thought and language. Straightway a great: shout of applause
2s arose and there burst forth clapping of hands; they werc praising
the man who wrote the book and not least on the ground of the
additions themselves; to such an extent has the deity made my
soul a soft surface to bear the impress of the stamps of diction,”
and if I had directed my attention by this exercise to uncorrected
30 copies of books, nature would have conducted my mastery to this
point when I made the attempt. A certain sound} continues with

Page 112, 1. 31. #2 the case of your own sive. The admiring language
that Synesius uses in regard to Theodosius is amply sustained by the
judgement of Gibbon (Decline and Fall, cap. xxvi): ‘From the innocent
but humble labours of his farm Theodosius was transported, in less’
than four months, to the throne of the Eastern Empire; and the whole
period of the history of the world will not perhaps afford a similar
example of an elevation, at the same time, so pure and so honourable.
The princes who peaccably inherit the sceptre of their fathers claim
and enjoy a legal right, the more secure as it is absolutely distinct from
the merits of their personal characters. The subjects, who, in a monarchy
. . - acquire the possession of supreme power, may have raised them-
selves, by the superiority either of genius or virtuc, .. . but their virtue
is seldom exempt from ambition .... But the most suspicious malignity
cannot ascribe to Theodosius, in his obscure solitude of Caucha, the arts,
the desires, or even the hopes,.of an ambitious statesman. . . . in the
public distress his superior merit was universally felt and acknowledged.
... What expectations must have been formed of his abilities to en-
courage the hope that a single man could save, and restore, the empire
of the East! Theodosius was invested with the purple in the thirty-
third year of his age. The vulgar gazed with admiration on the manly
beauty of his face, and the graceful majesty of his person ....’

The battle of Hadrianople, in which forty thousand Romans fell, was
not, however, as Gibbon reminds us, avenged by any decisive victory
on the part of Theodosius, and the consequences of this defeat to the
Roman arms were even greater from a moral than a material point of
view. Gibbon finds a passage from St. John Chrysostom (tom. i, p. 344,


188 NOTES


ed. Montfaucon) containing an anecdote concerning a Gothic chief who
“was heard to declare . . . that he was astonished that a people who
fled before him like a flock of sheep could still presume to dispute the
possession of their treasures and provinces’. But although Theodosius
did not immediately reverse the fortunes of war, the prudence and
judgement with which he handled a difficult and even alarming situa-
tion have won the highest praise from the historian, in whose words
‘the great Theodosius, an epithet which he honourably deserved, con-
ducted himself as the firm and faithful guardian of the republic’.
Establishing a system of garrison fortifications, and probably what
we should describe in these days as chains of blockhouses, he contrived
to restore the confidence of his troops by making sporadic attacks on
the enemy at favourable moments and retiring to inexpugnable posi-
tions. ‘The deliverance and peace of the Roman provinces’, to quote the
same authority again, ‘was the work of prudence rather than of valour:
the prudence of Theodosius was seconded by fortune; and the emperor
never failed to seize, and to improve, every favourable circumstance.
..- An army of conquerors was broken into many disorderly bands of
savage robbers; and their blind and irregular fury was not less perni-
cious to themselves than to their enemies.’ What is most admirable in
Theodosius is that all this time he was in the grip of a long and relentless
malady to which he eventually succumbed in the year 380. But
perhaps the greatest piece of statesmanship in his life was the way in
which he enlisted on his side the power of the Gothic king, Athanaric,
who, when he finally was received by the Roman Emperor in Constan-
tinople, was made to exclaim, ‘Indeed, the emperor of the Romans is |
a god upon earth; and the presumptuous man, who dares to lift his hand
agaist him, is guilty of his own blood’ (‘Deus, inquit, est sine dubio
terrenus imperator, et quisquis adversus eum manum moverit, ipse sui
sanguinis reus existit.’ Quoted by Gibbon from Jornandes, c. xxviii.)
On the death of Athanaric, a short time after this, his followers and
army took service in a body under the Roman Emperor, and this
adhesion of the Visigoths saved for the moment an otherwise dangerous
situation. We see, however, that Synesius is against all traffic with the.
Goths and Scythians, in spite of the example of the Theodosius whom
he so highly lauds.

Plato also in the Republic, Bk. I, makes a good deal of play of the
simile of the shepherd and the sheep in the long diatribe that Thrasy-
machus pours out to prove that justice is only the law of the stronger.
Cf. p. 343, where he says to Socrates, ‘You fancy that the shepherd
fattens the sheep with a view to their own good, and not to the good of
himself or his master; and you further imagine that the rulers of states,
if they are true rulers, never think of their subjects as sheep, and that

they are not studying their own advantage day and night... . Consider
further, most foolish Socrates, that the just is always a loser in com-
parison with the unjust’, &c. Socrates, in replying to Thrasymachus,
comes back to the simile of the sheep in these terms: ‘For I must remark,
Thrasymachus, if you will recall what was previously said, that although
you began by defining the true physician in an exact sense, you did not
observe a like exactness when speaking of the shepherd; you thought
that the shepherd as a shepherd tends the sheep, not with a view to
their own good, but like a mere diner or banqueter with a view to the
pleasures of the table; or again, as a trader for sale in the market, and
not asa shepherd. Yet surely the art of the shepherd is concerned only
with the good of his subjects... and that was what I was saying just
now about the ruler.’ (/bid., p. 345.)

Page 118, 1. 8. as if I had set up a statue. The simile of the statue is
used by Plato in reference to the ideal state described in the Republic,
420C: ‘Suppose that we were painting a statue and some one came up
to us and said, Why do you not put the most beautiful colours on the
most beautiful parts of the body—the eyes ought to be purple, but you
have made them black—to him we might-fairly answer, Sir, you would


ON KINGSHIP 195


not surely have us beautify the eyes to such a degree that they are no
longer eyes; consider rather whether, by giving this and the other
features their due proportion, we make the whole beautiful. And so I
say to you, do not compel us to assign to the guardians a sort of happi-
ness which will make them anything but guardians’, &c. Synesius,
evidently inspired by this passage, proceeds to describe the various
portions of the duties allotted to a king, and calls his representation a
statue that he is modelling. Plato returns to the same simile in the
Politicus, 277A: °...in my judgement the figure of the king is not yet
perfected; like statuaries who, in their too great hastc, having over-
done several parts of their works, lose time in cutting them down,so too
we, partly out of haste ...and also because we imagined that a
king required grand illustrations, have taken up a marvellous lump of
fable and have been obliged to use more than was necessary.’


Page 118, 1. 22. establish a monarchy in his soul. This phrase and the
thought underlying it are again obviously inspired by Plato’s Republic.
Cf. Rep. 576 E: ‘Tyranny is the wretchedest form of government, and
the rule of a king the happiest.’ On the same page he has already said
that ‘as state is to state in virtue and happiness, so is man in relation
to man’. The conception throughout in the Republic is that true king-
ship is the rule of the higher moral forces over the lower and the sub-
jection of the absolutely evil forces in the soul; that the soul of man is
a microcosm of the state. Cf. Shakespeare, Julius Caesar, Act II, Scene
i, line 67:


And the state of man,
Like to a little kingdome, suffers then
The nature of an insurrection.


The drift of the long argument in the Republic is to show that the state
is only the expansion of the self-government of the individual. The
conclusion is pithily expressed in p. 592 A, where Socrates, in answer to
Glaucon’s objection that the ‘just man’ such as he describes will never
be a statesman, replies: ‘By the dog he will! In the city which is his
own he certainly will, though in the city of his birth perhaps not,
unless he have a divine call.’ (See the Greek on page 197.)

‘Of what sort ?’

ON KINGSHIP 197


in all this, he calls his knowledge wisdom, and makes of it a system or
art, which he proceeds to teach, although he has no real notion of what
he means by the principles or passions of which he is speaking, but calls
this honourable and that dishonourable, or good or evil, or just or
unjust, all in accordance with the tastes and tempers of the great brute.
Good he pronounces to be that in which the beast delights and evil to be
that which he dislikes; and he can give no other account of them except
that the just and noble are the necessary, having never himself seen,
and having no power of explaining to others, the nature of either or the
difference between them, which is immense. By heaven, would not such
an one be an outrageous educator?’ In general the comparison of the
unrestrained passions in an individual to the turbulence and irresponsi-
bility of the mob is fairly common in Plato.
