NOTES ON DIO


PHILOSTRATUS of Lemnos, sometimes described in antiquity as
Philostratus of Tyre or of Athens, was not mercly the biographer
of the sophists, but their eulogist. Descended from a family of
sophists in the island of Lemnos and born during the last third of the
second century a.D., he wrote a work that might be described as a
panegyric of all men who had, like himself, become distinguished in the
rhetorician’s career, but he includes under the designation of sophist
such Athenian orators as Isocrates, Aeschines, and Antiphon. The
philosopher has less importance in his eyes than the rhetorician. He
was a protégé of the empress Julia Domna and her husband the
emperor Septimius Severus. The empress spent much of her time at
Antioch, where she surrounded herself with scientists and men of letters.
An excellent résumé of what can be gathered as to the facts of his life
will be found in Mrs. W. C. Wright’s introduction to Philostratus’ Lives
of the Sophtsts in the Loeb Series.

Dio Chrysostom of Prusa, the subject of this essay, had a vast repu-
tation in the second- and third-century days of the Roman Empire, and
we can see from the ternts in which Synesius speaks of him that this
reputation had not waned in the fourth. ‘As for Dio of Prusa,’ says
Philostratus, ‘I do not know what one ought to call him, such was his
excellence in all departments; for, as the proverb says, he was a “‘horn
of Amalthea’”, since in him is compounded the noblest of all that has
been most nobly expressed. His style has the ring of Demosthenes and
Plato, but Dio has besides a peculiar resonance of his own... and it was
combined with a scrious and direct simplicity of expression. ... That
he had also a talent for writing history is proved by his On the Getae; he
did in fact travel as far as the Getae during his wandering as an exile.’

He was born at Prusa, in Bithynia, about the middle of the first
century A.D. He travelled a great deal, going from one town to an-
other very much as did the sophists in the days of Plato. He visited
Rhodes, Ilium Novum, and Egypt, coming back from time to time to
his native city, where he married under the reign of Titus or Vespasian.


212 NOTES


Owing, however, to the execution of a great friend of his in Rome
(Flavius Sabinus, according to Emperius), he fell into disfavour at

‘court and was exiled. Philostratus says, ‘I cannot call his sojourn with
the Getic tribes an exile, for he had not been ordered to go into exile.’
Dio himself, in Ov. xlv, 1, however, uses the word ¢vyj,

This expatriation, whatever may have been its origin, lasted fourteen
years. He wandered about Greece, now no longer as the brilliant sophist
surrounded by admirers of his eloquence, but disguised as a vagabond
and unknown. In the school of adversity he had become a serious
thinker instead of a specious rhetorician. It is to this change in his
intellectual life that Synesius alludes. But after so many years of
wandering (rocovrov xpdvov mAavnbeis, as he expresses it in Or. xl. 2) the
death of his enemy Domitian befell in the year 96. And here, according
to Philostratus (Vist. Sophist. p. 488), a dramatic scene took place in one
of his journeys near the Danube, for when he saw the garrison beginning
to mutiny on receiving the news of the emperor’s assassination, he
stripped himself of his rags, like Odysseus at the climax of the Epic, and
beginning his harangue with the famous verse (Od. xxii. 1)

avrap 6 yupywOn paxdwy modvpntis ’Odvaceds,
‘he revealed’, says Philostratus, ‘that he was no beggar, nor what they
believed him to be, but Dio the sage: he delivered a spirited and ener-
getic indictment of the tyrant, and convinced the soldiers that they
would be wiser if they acted in accordance with the will of the Roman
people.’ After this he returned in triumph to Rome, where the new
emperor, Nerva, received him with every mark of affection. But Dio,
alas, fell ill at Rome, and Nerva died before accomplishing anything of
importance for his friend. Fortune, however, smiled upon him from
this time forth, and after returning to Prusa and taking up various
public works there, he again after a time felt the old unrest possess him,
and took again to travelling from one lecture hall to another, speaking
before enthusiastic audiences at Tarsus, Alexandria, and many other
places, not now as a sophist, but as a philosopher. Two of his speeches
“On Kingship’ (wept Bacweias) were delivered before the emperor
Trajan. His admirer Synesius was perhaps stirred by his example when
he wrote his address to the emperor Arcadius. It is to this latter part


ON DIO 213


of his life that his political speeches belong, and in these Dio appears
more as a statesman than as a philosopher. In them he trics, and it
would appear with a certain amount of success, to arrange difficulties
that had arisen between various cities in Bithynia and elsewhere. This
is only another evidence of the vitality of the Greek city, politically,
under the Roman Empire ; of the tradition of a former independence
that these once autonomous states could never forget, and upon which
I have insisted in the introduction to this volume as throwing light on
the mentality of Synesius. ‘These speeches,’ says Maurice Croisct
(Histotve de la Littévature grecque, v. 476), ‘although less well known
than the Moral Treatises, are greatly to his honour. In them he shows
himself at once an honest man and a clever one. . . . Like Plutarch, he
feels, and says with effect, that the best way for the Greeks of his time
to lighten the strain of the Roman domination is to give it no cause for
a harsh intervention in their affairs through useless political agitations.’
The orations show Dio in the light of a patriotic Greek in whom the
cultural elements of Hellenism had never become divorced from the
political. The passionate lover of Plato and Demosthenes, bred in a still
Greck city and speaking the language of the masters from his infancy,
could scarcely free himszlf from the aspirations of an indestructible
Hellas that is interwoven with all that they have written. It is easy to
see why Dio was such a favourite author of Synesius. The one writer in
the first and second centuries, and the other in the fourth and fifth, were
at heart and perhaps unconsciously, Greeks of the golden age. What is
admirable about them both is that, notwithstanding this, they showed
themselves most loyal supporters of the Roman Empire. |

Dio, like Synesius, was very frank and fearless when addressing an
assembly of citizens. He takes the part of a critic quite freely, somewhat
as his inspirer Demosthenes did before him. ‘I would praise you more’,
he says in speaking tothe people of Alexandria, ‘if you spoke deliberately,
if you could be silent, and if you thought rightly’ (Or. xxxii. 2, ed.
von Arnim, vol. i, p. 267). This faculty for telling his audiences blunt
home truths was, however, conjoined with such great charm of per-
sonality that he succeeded in winning their applause even in his most
caustic moments. “The persuasive charm of the man’, says Philostratus,
*was such as to captivate even men who were not versed in Greek


214 NOTES


letters. An instance of this is that the emperor Trajan in Rome set
him by his side on the golden chariot in which the Emperors ride in
procession when they celebrate their triumphs in war, and often he
would turn to Dio and say, “I do not understand what you are say-
ing, but I love you as I love myself ”’’ (Lives of the Sophists, p. 488).
‘This mcident’, says Prof. W. C. Wright, from whose edition of Philo-
stratus my quotations have been taken, ‘is improbable and is not else-
where recorded. That Trajan understood Greek is probable from
Cassius Dio, Ixviii.3 . . .; cf.also lxviii.7 and Pliny’s Panegyric, xlvii. 1.’
The story, however improbable, is worth quoting as showing what an
impression the charm of Dio’s manners made upon his contemporaries.

The 3foral Discourses, to which allusion has been made, were, perhaps,
the most famous of Dio’s works; some of them might be termed lay
sermons. These d:atdfecs were popular amongst the public and its
philosophers and mentors of the period, but as Maurice Croiset has
very pertinently pointed out (Hsst. Lt. Grec., v. 479), the discourses
of Dio are sharply distinguished from such work as was current in his
day by the fact that he addressed himself ‘not to pointing out the
errors of mankind in general, but those of the audience before whom he
was speaking, so that he discoursed to them of their present needs,
warned them of the dangers that they were incurring, and showed them
practical means of averting these’. In a word, his aims were those of
one who sought to educate the city populations in his day, and for many
years he seems to have had great success in this path, showing courage
as well as oratorical talent in his efforts to instruct. The moral principles
that he taught were chiefly those of the Stoa, as Synesius tells us here,
though Platonic and other influences enter into his work also, but the
Hellenic tradition is always presented in its purity and unclouded by
any Asiatic symbolism.

His works may be divided into three groups, the sophistical, written
m the first period of his life, the political, and finally the ethical or
moral. The last two belong to the period after his exile. A great part
of his works has been lost, although many of these existed in the time
of Synesius. We now possess a collection made after the fifth century,
containing eighty pieces, a certain number of which are incomplete.

Carneades, the founder of the New Academy, born at Cyrene in the


ON DIO 215


year 213 B.c., was, like Dio, both a philosopher and an orator. It was
he who, following upon Arcesilas, crystallized the floating conceptions of
the decadent Platonists and Atomists of his day into the doctrine of
‘probable opinions’. This was only the logical outcome of the rejection
of the absolute idea, the sheet anchor of the whole Platonic system.
Scepticism as to the existence of any absolute truth was the mainspring
of his views on philosophy. All approximations to truth were to be
regarded as tentative and relative. Philostratus dismisses him with a
few words as one who shouid be enrolled amongst the sophists, although
his mind had been formed in the philosophic mould, adding that his
power as an orator led him to the highest degree of proficiency. We see
in Philostratus how clear-cut, in his day, was the distinction between
philosopher and sophist, and Synesius seems to feel this also. ‘Study
philosophy’ is the advice that he is always giving his friends in his
letters, but he excludes rhetoric in general, at least such rhetoric as
leads to practice in the law courts. He would have his dearest friend
Pylaemencs attach himself ‘not to the rhetoricof the bar, but to that right
and noble rhetoric that even Plato himself . . . does not try to prohibit’
(Letter 103). ‘You yourself admit’, he saysa little later, ‘that philosophy
in itself is worth more than rhetoric.’ For Synesius there was evidently
rhetoric fair and foul. The rhetorician par excellence in his eyes was the
sophist, and the sophist was anathema to him, as we sce in the last
passages of De Insomniis and in the Letters passim. He had made the
old enemy of his master Plato his own. Dio and Carneades at least had
absolution from him, for they were philosophers as well. Of the last it
will be remembered that he was sent to Rome by the Athenians on a
political mission. Michael Psellus, writing in the eleventh century at
Byzantium, drawsan equally sharp distinction between the sophist and
the philosopher; cf. Chronogr. lib. vi, cap. 41: éwpaxws 5¢ crt Svo

Leo of Byzantium, again, was a pupil, in his youth, of Plato, if we
can trust Philostratus, and became identified with the sophists owing


216 NOTES


to his brilliant successes as an orator. Philostratus tells anecdotes
that turn upon his reputation for wit and his powers of persuasion.
Eudoxus of Cnidus was another product of the Academy, according to
the same authority, who became famous for his oratory and who was
also dubbed with the title of sophist. Diogenes Laertius speaks of him
as ‘astronomer, geometer, physician, and legislator’. He represents him
as a pupil of Archytas. ‘Sotion,’ he adds, ‘in his Successions of Philo-

Synesius has, again, presumably drawn his information as to the
life of Aristocles of Pergamos from Philostratus, who describes his
change of life m the following passage (Lives of the Sophtsts, p. 567): ‘So
long as he was a student of philosophy he was slovenly in appearance,
unkempt and squalid in his dress, but now he began to be fastidious,
discarded his slovenly ways, and admitted into his house all the
pleasures that are afforded by the lyre, the flute, and the singing voice,
as though they had come begging to his doors. For though hitherto he
had lived with such austerity, he now began to be immoderate in his
attendance at theatres and their loud racket. When he was beginning
to be famous at Pergamon, and all the Hellenes in that region hung on
his oratory, Herodes travelled to Pergamon and sent all his own pupils
to hear him, thereby exalting the reputation of Aristocles as though
Athene herself had cast her vote. His style of eloquence was lucid and
Attic, but it was more suited to formal discourse than to forensic argu-
ment, for his language is without acrimony or impulsive outbreaks on
the spur of the moment. And even his Atticism, tested by comparison
with the language of Herodes, will seem over-subtle and deficient in the
qualitics of magnificence and sonorousness.’ ‘Herodes Atticus’,as Philo-
stratus calls him, was a wealthy sophist who established himself in
Rome under the emperor Nerva (Phil. Vst. Soph. p. 548) and whose
lectures Aristocles attended there. It is evident that in the second
century, through which Synesius is for the moment threading his way,
the philosopher affected the ‘simple life’,and the sophist became the man
of the world, courted by. all and always in the limelight. But there was
more than this. The sophist became the statesman. Cities that had
grievances to settle with other cities would bring them up before the


ON DIO 217


emperor's council-chamber at Rome, and then each city would choose
an advocate (ovvduxos) to defend its case. What more likely than that
they should choose the famous sophist whom they knew so well, whose
words they had hung upon at the theatre, by whose arguments they
were spellbound, as their beloved Dio Chrysostom tells them reproach-
fully, and whose voice they greeted with thunders of applause. Just
as Horace tells us that in his day Roman citizens had gone mad over
‘belles-lettres’ and a dilettante mania for writing verses, so in the
second century the Greek-speaking world in the Roman Empire had
gone mad over rhetorical demonstrations of oratory and sophistical
casuistry. Here again we are only in face of the same tendencies that
Socrates, in the mouth of Plato, reproaches the Athenians for giving way
to in the golden age of literature in Greece. History is only repeating
itself. In thought, in philosophy, Carmeades is only another Protagoras.
*Man is the measure of all things’ for the one, and truth is only approxi-
mate probability for the other. The only difference that the lapse of
five hundred years had brought was that the rhetorician was more
supreme than ever, that the rhetorician was the sophist, and the sophist,
whom Plato in his great dialogue is so anxious to draw out of his lurking-
place, had become the statesman; as much at least as the statesman
could exist for Greek cities shorn of the golden fleece of their bygone
autonomy. .

Page 151,1.7. The funeral oration of Aspasta. This speech is recited in
Plato’s Menexenus (236 B) by Socrates, who tells his friend that he has
learned it from the lips of Aspasia. ‘Yesterday I heard Aspasia com-
posing a funeral oration . . . partly improvising and partly from previous
thought, putting together fragments of the funeral oration which
Pericles spoke, but which, as I believe, she composed.’ It will be seen
from this extract that Plato claims no originality for the speech, which
is one that in any case would have been scarcely worthy of him. It
belongs to the domain of rhetoric pure and simple, and it has always
puzzied the commentators on Plato that he should have written such
a dialogue. By some it has been regarded as apocryphal, although

Burnet and most scholars of to-day accept it. Jowett refers to Plat.
Menex. 235 D and a short quotation from Aristotle (Rhetoric, i. 9. 30) as
an evidence of its authenticity. Synesius’ example of the antithesis
between the style of the statesman and that of the rhetorician is happily
chosen.

Page 153, L 8. in exchange for those of the ‘Euboean’, It is unfortunate
that four of the works of which Synesius speaks in terms of admiration
have not come down to us amongst the orations (so called) of Dio
Chrysostom. We have the ‘Euboean’ and the four orations, ‘On King-
ship’; but not the “Tempe’, the ‘Memnon’, the ‘Parrot’ or the
*Gnat’, nor, again, ‘The Attack on the Philosophers’. ‘The Euboean’
iS a very pretty story written to point the moral of the value of the


ON DIO 221
simple life in poverty and in rural surroundings in comparison with the
life of the city. The author describes a voyage that he took with some
fishermen in a small boat and tells us how he was shipwrecked on the
coast of Euboea. Going alone into the interior he meets a sturdy hunts-
man who befriends him and takes him to hishome in the hills, where he
comes into contact with a handful of people living a patriarchal life
with a few cattle to furnish them with the necessities of food, and
occupying themselves also with hunting wild game—a mixture, this, of
the primitive, agricultural, and venatorial phases of existence. The
huntsman narrates to him their history; how their fathers were the
shepherds of a wealthy man in the past, but one who fell into misfortune
and lost his lands, and whose flocks and herds of cattlewere driven away
and sold; howhis own father remained on the spot bivouacking with his
family in tents and managed to live off the country by his own industry.
At a given moment, however, the city which was near to them on the
sea-shore sunimoned them to renderan account of what they were doing
on land that properly belonged to the State. So he was compelled to go
down to the coast with the official who had been dispatched on this
errand and to explain his position. Then follows a very bright descrip-
tion of the town life that the rustic sees for the first time; of his astonish-
ment at the sight of the quays, the shipping in the harbour, the crowdcd
agora. A heated debate follows in the popular assembly. He is accused
of paying nothing to the state in taxes, and has only to say in his defence
that he has nothing to pay. Finally another orator takes his part and
succeeds in convincing the assembly that the city only owes gratitude
to a handful of people who occupy land that the city has never been
able to do anything with and who prevent it from becoming a total
desert. So all ends well, and he is finally dismissed with marks of
appreciation. There is a vein in this charmingly told story that reminds
one a little of Rousseau: the same notion that man left to himself and
outside of the corrupting forces of civic life is by nature good, that
civilization brings chiefly evil in its wake. The people in the hills of his
story represent poverty (zevia), but they have all the wealth of nature
as their portion and are filled with generosity and goodwill towards
men. The town-dwellers are torn with avarice and malice, despite their
possessions. The story ends with some general considerations on the

happiness (epi wevias wpovlépeba cizeiv ws ovx dxopa alr} Ta mpaypara

Synesius shows discrimination in selecting the Eubocan out of the
numerous essays by Dio that must have Leen known to him. Those
that have come down to us are very unequal in literary value, nor is it
easy for us to-day to understand the hard and fast line that he draws
here between the ‘sophistical’ and the ‘philosophical’ style of Dio.
Presumably the essay on hair quoted in the Calvitsi Encomtum would
come under the former head.

The Rhodian, of which he speaks a page or two later, is a long and
tedious diatribe on the impropriety of demolishing public statues, of
which there was a superfluity in his day.

The Trojan, mentioned in the same passage, is an attempt to show
that the Greeks never succeeded in taking Troy. It is full of amusing,
paradoxical arguments. -


Page 153, 1.9. he praises the Essenes. The Essenes were a sect of
Jewish ascetics in Palestine who practised a communistic form of life
and devoted themselves to agriculture and various forms of manual
labour. Pliny (Naturalis Historia, v.§ 73), after describing the Dead Sea,
continues as follows: ‘On the west side the Essenes avoid the baleful
shore line. They are a race by themselves, more remarkable than any
other in the wide world; they have no women, they abjure, sensual love,
they have no money, and they live among palm-trees. Still their
membership is steadily recruited from the large number of people who

resort to their mode of existence because they are wearied of life's
' Struggle with the waves of adversity. In this way the race has lasted,
strange to say, for thousands of ages, though no one is born within it;
so fruitful for them is the dissatisfaction for life which others feel.’

Philo, as quoted by Eusebius in his Preparation of the Gospel, draws a
somewhat similar picture of them (viii. 11); ‘Our lawgiver’, he says,
“trained an innumerable body of his pupils, who are called Essenes, to
partake in those things, being, as I imagine, honoured with this appella-


ON DIO 223.


tion because of their exceeding holiness. ... There are no children among
the Essenes, nor youths nor persons just entering upon manhood,
since the dispositions of all such persons are unstable. ... Noone among
them ventures to acquire any property of his own, neither house, nor
slave, nor farm, nor flocks ... but they bring them together into the .
middle as a common stock... . There are some of them who are devoted

to the practice of agriculture, being skilful in such things as pertain to

the sowing and cultivation of lands; others, again, are shepherds or cow-

herds and expcrienced in the management of every kind of animal;

some are cunning in what relates to swarms of bees; others, again, are

artisans and handy craftsmen. ... Again, perceiving ... what is alone or

at least above all things calculated to dissolve such associations, they

repudiate marriage; and at the same time they practise continence in

an eminent degree, for no one of the Essenes ever marries a wife’

(Yonge’s transl., vol. iv, p. 219). Philo again (Quod Omnis Probus liber

sit, 12, §§ 75 ff.,) mentions the Essenes as follows: ‘Syria Palaestina, too,

is not barren of exemplary wisdom and virtue.... There is a portion

of those people called Essenes in number something more than four

thousand. ... These men in the first place live in villages, avoiding all

cities on account of the habitual lawlessness of those who inhabit them,

... there is not aslave among them; they are all free... . Their ex-

penses are all in common, their garments belong to them all in common,

their food is common to them all, since they all cat in messes, . . . those

who are sick are not neglected because they are unable to contribute to

the common stock ...,’ &c. (ibid. vol. iii, p. §23, corrected).

Josephus speaks of the Essenes as having spread for the first time
in the second century B.c. (Jos. Ant. xiii. 5,9). Traces of Pytha-
goreanism, Orphism, even Buddhism, have been attributed to their.
cult by various scholars, but the exact nature of it remains obscure.
W. M. F. Petrie considered them identical with the Therapeutae, a sect
of Egyptian ascetics who inhabited the shores of lake Mareotis and
whom Synesius seems to allude to in chapter ten, but this view has not
found acceptance. I find no reference in the Eubocan to the Essences.

Aristides, born in A.D.129, is the sophist and philosopher whom Synesius
has in mind here. His birthplace is Hadrianoi,in Mysia. He studied rhe-
toricat Pergamus under Aristoclesandafterwards at Athens. Hetravelled
when a young man and delivered his first oration in Alexandria. Suffer-
ing for many years from a seemingly incurable malady, he sojourned
chiefly between Smyrna and Pergamus. Inthe latter cityhe spent much
of his time at the temple of Aesculapius, and it was there that he used
to receive visits, when asleep, from the god of healing by the medium
of dreams. One only has to read Synesius’ On Dreams to realize the in-
terest that such works as Aristides’ Sacred Discourses must have had for
him, for these speeches (07. xIvii-lii) treat of his favourite subject,
the intercourse of man with the gods in dreams. ‘These discourses’,
Philostratus writes (Vst. Soph. ii. 9, trans. W. C. Wright), ‘served him
in some sort as a diary, and such diaries are excellent teachers on the
art of speaking well on any subject. And since his natural talent was
not in the line of extempore eloquence, he strove after extreme ac-
curacy, and turned his attention to the ancient writers; he was well
endowed with native ability, and purified his style of any empty
verbosity’. Synesius has this passage in mind in his essay On Dreams
(De Insom. 1316, Migne) when he says, ‘We shall therefore see fit to
add to what are called daybooks what are termed nightbooks’, in
other words the very diary that Aristides kept. Again in chapter
thirteen (p. 1317) he advises ‘every man of leisure’ to ‘proceed to write
a narrative of whatsoever happens in his waking and sleeping states’.

Page 158, l.10. Vestal Virgins. Syncsius, no doubt, alludes here to the

Roman Forum. This house was occupied by them until the middle or
the end of the fourth century, when they were finally dispersed and the
order abolished, as we read in Zosimus (v. 38) ; it is therefore probable
that they were still in existence at the moment when Synesius wrote
this essay.

Page 160, 1.30. men of foreign race,&c. It has been thought not quite
clear whether Synesius has in mind in this passage the Therapeutae
or the Essenes mentioned by him in chapter three, but probably he
refers to the latter, as he says nothing about agricultural labour. Again,
the phrase ‘pass their lives apart from each other’, would scem to
indicate the former, who lived each an ascetic in his separate hut (Philo,
De Vita Contemplativa, cap. 3). A great storm of controversy has raged
over the actual religion of the Therapeutae. Flinders Petrie regarded
the Therapeutae, who lived on the borders of Lake Mareotis, near Alex-
andria, as of the same persuasion as the Essenes, and us being in fact an
identical cult whose doctrine came from the Buddhists of India.
Eusebius introduced an element of confusion into the question by mis-
taking them for early Christian monks (cf. F. C. Conybeare, Philo
about the Contemplative Life). Asa legend existed in his day that St.
Mark the Evangelist preached the Gospel in Alexandria, he jumped to
the conclusion that the ascetics who lived near Alexandria must have
been descended from his converts. He even assumes that Philo Judaeus
had met the apostle Peter when in Rome and had become imbued with
the spirit of his teaching. Philo had written the Contemplative Life, in
which he makes a eulogy of the virtues of the Therapeutae and describes
their fasts, vigils, and mortification of the flesh, speaking of them by
implication at least as co-religionaries of his own. It was, nevertheless,
with this document as to their original history before his eyes that
Eusebius formed the opinion that they were from the beginning con-
verts and disciples of St. Mark. St. Jerome and others followed Eusebius
in this. The error so propagated continued until the days of the Re-
formation. Then controversy arose. Monasticism as an institution
began to be attacked. The Church pointed to the sanctity of the
cloistral life having been endorsed by the Evangelist Mark himself, as
witnessed by his converts, the Therapeutae. Baronius, at the end of
the sixteenth century, defended the Catholic point of view against
Scaliger, who had attacked the validity of the argument of Eusebius.
Bellarmine responded to the Protestant writers with arguments from
Dionysius the Areopagite, the pseudo-Dionysius already exposed by
Scaliger. Montfaucon, in the beginning of the eighteenth century,
again tried to prop up the crumbling fabric of Euscbius’ views in the


228 NOTES


matter, but was replied to with effect by Bouhier, and so the struggle
was continued. But now the controversy entered a new phase. The
deists, such as Bolingbroke and Voltaire, as Frederick Conybeare
pointed out in his excursus on the authorship of Philo’s Contemplative
Life, profited by the exposure of the unsoundness of the Eusebian
tradition to ask ‘what became of the claims of Christianity to be an
entirely new revelation? If men had already by their unaided efforts
made themselves so like the primitive Christians, that the fathers them-
selves could not distinguish them therefrom... what became of the
supposed necessity for an incarnation of God, and for the gift of the Holy
Spirit?’ (Philo about the Contemplative Life, F.C. Conybeare, p. 325 f.).
So the dispute went on, until towards the end of last century Gractz
and Lucius reopened the whole question on a new basis (v. Lucius, Dse
Therapeuten, Strasburg, 1880). In spite of the extravagance of the
views of the latter, he succeeded in converting to him, at least at first,
such distinguished scholars as Schiirer, Ad. Harnack, Hilgenfeld, Hatch,
Robertson Smith, and others. Lucius tried to show that Philo’s Con-
fem plative Life was a latter-day forgery. He proceeded on the gratuitous
assumption that the early monastic institutions were being attacked in
the third century and that the work in question had been forged by
some unknown hand with a view to their rehabilitation. All this line
of argument was finally shattered by the appearance of Frederick Cony-
beare’s scholarly and exhaustive work on the subject (Philo about the
Contem plative Life, Oxford, 1895), in which every thread of the intricate
maze of evidence that Graetz and Lucius had concocted to support their
theories was followed up and shown to be worthless. Dr. Paul Wend-
land’s work on Philo was also contributory to this result. Conybeare,
with his great knowledge of Armenian, was able to establish the gross
- improbability of the hypothesis of Lucius, that the forgery he assumes

had been intercalated in the text of Philo by the time when Eusebius
must have read it, that is to say, at the end of the third or beginning of
the fourth century ; and to this purpose he published the Armenian text
ts extenso, and showed what its derivation must have been. In the
“Armenian version’, to quote from his work (p. 331), ‘we have a witness
to the text of the De Vita Contemplativa not later than A.D. 420, and
very probably made from a text much older’ (the italics are mine). In the


ON DIO 229


Latin Version we have another witness of the same age.’ Conybeare
explains in a foot-note that he has put down the old Latin Version to
as late a date as possible. He then quotes Pitra’s Analecta Sacra to show
that there is presumptive evidence that the Latin Version of the De Vsta
Contem plativa belongs tothe age of Tertullian. ‘Inthe Eusebian extracts’,
he continues, ‘we have excerpts taken from it before the year 315. Now

. the Greck MSS. and the old Latin all flow from one archetype; the
Armenian and the Eusebian texts from another and independent arche-
type. But the Greek text was already an old and much-worn text when
the Latin version was made, for the Latin reflects many of the corrup-
tions characteristic of its congeneric Greek texts; andon the other hand,
some of the Greek texts, especially Cod. JLaurent. Plut. X,cod.xx,con-
tain a tradition which, in order of derivation, is much older than that
of the Greek text from which the Latin was translated. It follows that
the text of the Greck MSS. had already had a long history before the

history which cannot be crushed into the short period which Lucius’

old Latin and existing Greek texts, can have converged only at a point
in time long anterior to A.D. 300.’

It will be seen from this that the mind has the power first to think and
reason, while turned to what is within it, and second to see by a certain
perception and comparison (intuition?) what is above it, and so is one.
The first state is that of reason, the second that of this complete unity
ofthe mind, which comes from repudiating reason and submitting to the
passionate power that is within it. This last state prepares the way for
union with the One. In this wise Plotinus adumbrates the real nature
of his religion, for such indeed it is, the preparation of the mind for a
passionate flight to a union with the Eternal. One is inclined to ask,
taking the argument in these last passages, in conjunction with the
distinction between Greeks and Barbarians which Synesius introduces
here, whether he does not mean to imply that the philosophy of the
Egyptian Plotinus was not the philosophy of his Greck masters, Plato
and Aristotle. To ascend gradually to the conception of the first cause,
of the good, by training in dialectic they would have regarded as the
orthodox teaching of philosophy. It is true that unquestionable autho-
rities on Plotinus, Bouillet and Mackenna amongst others, have con-
sidered that this matter of ecstasy bulks too large in the prevalent
notions in regard to the author whom they have so ably commented
upon. But the passages I note seem to me to leave little doubt that
this absolute casting off of the trammels of reason is the goal of his
philosophy or religion. In Enn. vi. 9. 1x he is even more explicit in
describing the state of one carried aloft by ecstasy: od ydp rs dxweiro

Page 181, L 14. And even if the thought was different, &. A very good
example of the sort of talent which Synesius ascribes to himself may
be found in the translation of Boethius written by King Alfred the
Great in the ninth century. The King was not satisfied with trans-

of his own invention, writing in the style of the author he was trans-

translation proper. Some of the sallies of King Alfred introduced in
this way are doubly interesting, for they give a glimpse on the one hand

Writing in the same style as his great model. An edition of this work in

with King Alfred's intercalations in italics, so that the work which is
of his own creation can be compared with that of the Latin philosopher.

Diphilus was a contemporary of Menander, and a writer of plays much

Thus the idea came to me of praising those who make a cult

In my own case no such calamity has as yet happened. True,
I was at first vanquished by the argument, but I think now that
Dio was a man clever enough in speech, though one who had
nothing to say, and yet went on speaking through a superfluity
5 of power; and that he would have shown himself to far greater
advantage if he had chosen to praise the very opposite case,—
namely, that of my own head! For what might not a man
resourceful in difficulties have accomplished, if he had fallen in
with a subject suited to his powers? But now that he has both
ro hair and skill, he employs his skill on his hair. How roguishly
he has insinuated himself in this essay! For in this discourse of
his there is no other lover of hair who beautifies it with a reed
save only himself, and it is with this very reed that he has written
his discourse. But if I in turn am bald and withal able to speak,
15 and if the one subject is found more noble than the other, or if
I am inferior to Dio, why, then, should I not strip for the
contest and make trial both of myself and of my argument, to
see if after all I could transfer the reproach to the men adorned
with hair?
zo I will speak then, neither making a vigorous and trenchant
preface such as orators arm their fighting speeches with, as men
arm triremes with beaks, nor first sounding, like Dio, a clear
measured prelude to the speech like a harpist’s overture, such as
—‘ After rising in the morning and praying to the gods, as is my
25 custom, I attended to my hair; I happened to be unwell at the
time, and it had been too long uncared for.’ While he is thus
going through the evidences of carelessness, he is bringing us,
without our being conscious of it, to the point of praising him for
the care he takes of his hair. This is what the clever fabricators
30 of speeches do to us; at one moment they charm us, at another
they astound us. Now I can grasp facts as well as any other man,
but am not addicted to rhetoric. I have been practising two arts
all my life,—the culture of plants, and the training of dogs against

the most fearless of wild beasts, and these fingers of mine have been
rubbed against shovels and hunting-spears rather than reeds;
unless by reed you should mean the reed that is an arrow, instead
of the author’s.

So now it is not to be wondered at if my fingers have clung to 5
that one. I shall never disgrace my ancestral rusticity, nor shall
I come on the scene rounding off little periods, forewords, and
preludes or the like. I shall pursue what I consider the best course,
even for the nature of a rustic, by setting the naked expressions
of thought in full view. I shall fight, with facts as weapons, only 10
by turning the pitch of my voice from argument to vehemence,
from the Dorian note, as they say, to the Phrygian. But I need
breath adequate to my undertakings, breath which, I prophesy,
my heart will render me in abundance.


5. My argument, then, will lay it down that of all men a man 15
who is bald has least reason to feel ashamed. For what matter
it if his head is bald, so long as his mind is shaggy, as was the
case with the descendant of Aeacus, whom poetry sang of? This
man cared little enough for his locks of hair, which, actually, he
presented to a corpse; they are indeed a sort of corpse, a life-

1176 less portion attached to living beings. Thus those animals
who are the more deprived of intelligence, are clothed with hair
all over their bodies, whereas man, inasmuch as his lot in life 1s
more brilliant, is the most bare of this natural burden. But that
he may not boast of having no taint of fellowship with what is 25
mortal, he is covered with hair in a few places. He, therefore,
who has no hair anywhere is to the normal man what man is to the
brute. And just as man is the most intelligent, and at the same
time the least hairy of earthly creatures, conversely it is admitted
that of all domestic animals the sheep is the stupidest, and that 3c
this is why he puts forth his hair with no discrimination, but

14. Nowas to the man who thinks with Dio that hair is much
more fitting to men than to women, is he not taking up a position
quite opposed to the evident facts of the case?

For what sort of reason is there in allotting to the destiny of
the stronger what weakens its very possessors? Assuredly a dis-
tinction has been made both by nature and by custom. By
custom, inasmuch as hair is not esteemed beautiful in all males
nor in all places, nor at all times in the same males; for the
Lacedaemonians adopted long hair after Thyrea,? whereas the
Argives, before Thyrea, wore their hair long. There are plenty
of nations who have not adopted it in the past, nor do they to-day.
But always and in every place it has been thought a beautiful
thing for each woman to make the care of her hair a most serious
affair. The woman does not exist, nor has ever existed, who has
submitted her head to a razor, unless on account of some ill-
omened and horrible calamity, if so be that time has brought such
misfortune. For my part I have never seen or heard of such an one.
Then again nature is in harmony with custom: for no woman who

their hair-nets conceal this, for our comedies pierce all such subter-

THE EGYPTIAN TALE
(DE PROVIDENTIA)
PREFACE


Tus has been written in the days of the sons of Taurus, and 1209


the first part here presented was read as far as the riddle of the
wolf, precisely at the moment when the inferior man was ruling,
after coming into power through a division in the state. The
§ ensuing part was woven into it after the return of the better men,
who begged that this history should not remain incomplete amidst
misfortunes; but that since those things which were foretold
according to God seemed to be in course of fulfilment, it were
better in dealing with the same subject to go on to more happy
10 fortunes than those already recounted. From the moment, there-
fore, in which the overthrow of the tyranny was already in
progress, the story followed the sequence of events. And it is
worthy of no ordinary wonderment in all this that the handling
suffices for many subjects. Many doctrines which up to this
15 moment remained undecided, have found room for investigation
in this story, and each has been examined in detail. Lives are
described therein which are to be taken as examples of vice and
virtue; the narrative contains a history of contemporary events;
and this story has been fashioned and embellished throughout
20 with a view to its utility.


PART ONE
1. The legend is Egyptian. The Egyptians are remarkable for
their wisdom. Perhaps, therefore, this, which is only a legend,
might signify, enigmatically, something more than a legend, for
the very reason that it is Egyptian. And if it is not a legend, but
25 sacred history, in that case it would be all the more worthy to
be set forth in writing.
2878.2 F


1212


276 DE PROVIDENTIA


Osiris and Typho were brothers, and came of the same parents.
Now the relationship of souls and that of bodies is not one thing
and the same. It does not belong to souls to be born on earth
from the same parents, but rather to flow from the same fountain.
And the nature of the universe furnishes two kinds, one luminous, 5
and the other indistinct, this last gushing forth from the ground,
since its source is somewhere below, and leaping out of the earth’s
Cavities, if perchance it might so compel the divine law. But
the former is suspended from the back of the Heavens;?* for it
is indeed sent down that it may order the earthly lot, but it is 10
enjoined upon it that when descending it should take great care

1213 lest, while it is arranging and ordering disarrangement and dis-
order, it should itself by its propinquity be infected with dishonour
and disorder. Now a law of Themis has been established which
announces to souls that, whichever one of them has been ac- 15
quainted with the furthest confines of existence and has withal
kept guard over its nature and remained inviolate, that such a
one, I say, should flow back again by way of the selfsame road,
and be commingled with its own source, just as it is a necessity
of nature that those who have in some way set out from the other 20
part, should be lodged in the abysses that are akin to them.

‘Envy and Anger there dwell, and there tribes of other misfortunes

Wander about through the gloom in the meadow of infatuation.’?


2. Of souls there are those which are well-born, and those
which are ill-born, in such wise that it might befall a Parthian 2s
to be related to a Libyan, and that those whom we call brothers
should be in no wise near to one another in kinship of soul,

a fact which was indicated in the case of the two Egyptian boys
from the moment of their birth, and when they were adult was
shown quite clearly. For the younger, born and brought up as by 30


1 Cf. Plato, Phaedrus, 247 C.
2 Empedocles, Fragment 121 (Diels, Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker’, i. (Berl.

a divine destiny, even in childhood’s days was fond of listening,
and fond of fables, for the fable is the child’s treatise on philosophy;
and as he grew, he always desired training which was in advance
of his years. He gave ear to his father, and whatever wisdom was
§ known to each, all that he hungered after, eager to seize first upon
all knowledge at once, in puppy fashion, as, of course, all natures do
which promise great things. Such natures show impatience and
start before their time, already pledging themselves to the beloved
goal. Then again, long before his adolescence he was even more
10 sedate than a well-bred man of mature age, and he listened with
modesty, and when he himself had, on occasion, to speak, whether
to ask about what he had been listening to, or with some other
purpose, every one would have noticed him hesitating and blushing.
He always made way for the older Egyptians, and gave up his
15 Seat to them, and this although he was the son of the ruler of
the great kingdom ; and respect for those of his own age was ever
with him, for it was pre-eminently in his nature to care for the
feelings of men. It was indeed difficult at that period of his life
to find a man in Egypt for whom the boy had not obtained at
20 least one benefit from his father.
The elder brother, Typho, on the other hand, was, in a word,
a downright boor. All knowledge he hated with his whole heart,
both so much as was Egyptian, and also foreign learning,
teachers of which the king had placed at the disposal of his son
25 Osiris; and he laughed the whole business to scorn, as though it
were idle and calculated to enslave the mind. When he saw his
brother conducting himself in an orderly way, and leading
a modest life, he thought this cowardly, inasmuch as no one saw
him striking a man with his fists, attacking him with kicks, or
3orunning in a disorderly fashion, withal that he was nimble,
without any spare flesh, and with a body that was a ight burden
for the soul therein. Then again, Osiris did not gulp down drink,
or give way to peals of vulgar laughter, which shook the whole 1216


278 DE PROVIDENTIA


body, such as his brother indulged in every day, for Typho
deemed these the only acts worthy of a free man, namely to do
whatsoever one chanced to desire at a given moment. He was like
no one of his race in character, nor indeed like anything human,


and he did not, to put it in a nutshell, even resemble himself, for 5


he was a compound of every kind of evil. At one moment he
seemed to be stupid, and a mere cumberer of the ground,’ only
keeping from his sleep long enough to fill his belly and to take
other provisions for the route of slumber; at another he would
neglect the moderate necessities of nature to indulge in gross
horse-play, and to annoy his own equals in age and his elders.
He admired strength of body as being the ultimate good, but he
used it ill, wrenching off doors, throwing clods of earth, and re-
joicing if any one was hurt thereby, or if he had done any other
mischief, as though this bore witness to his prowess. He flamed
up with untimely lust, and was violent in seeking amorous
encounters. Further, envy of his brother smouldered within him,
and hatred of the Egyptians, because they, the people, gave
honour to Osiris, both in speech and in song, and at home in
their common religious rites, all, everywhere, prayed of the gods
that every sort of good thing might be his. Such was the man and
so regarded. Then again, Typho took to himself bands of senseless
boys, for no other reason (since it was not his nature to care for
any one in his heart) than that he might have some partisans who
did not hold the views of Osiris. It was easy enough for any one
to win this man’s good graces, and to get from Typho anything
that young men desire, by merely whispering something tending
to calumniate Osiris. So from childhood did the respective
characters of the two foretell the difference of their lives.

6. Now the king is appointed by the Egyptians in the following
way. There isa sacred mountain near the great city of Thebes, and
just opposite to it another. The Nile flows between the two. Of 10
these mountains the one described as opposite is the Libyan, and
on this it is the custom that the candidates for the royal dignity
should take their abode during the preparatory period, to the end
that they may perceive nothing of the choice. But the sacred
mountain is the Egyptian one. On the summit is a tent for the 15
king, and by him are collected as many of the priests as are versed
in the great wisdom. This arrangement extends to all that have
precedence, for it distributes the positions at the ceremonies
according to merit. A first circle is composed of these of which
the king is as it were the heart. The soldiers occupy another 20
circle next to this. These then still surround the peak, which on
the widely extending mountain is another mount; it is like a nipple
standing up, thus keeping the king in full view even of those
encircling him at the farthest distance. And they to whom it is
permitted to be present at the spectacle, surround him, taking 25
possession of the ground at the base of the nipple. These are they
who only applaud what they perceive; the others have authority
over the election. As soon as the king has been invoked, and those
also to whose office this belongs have moved the whole assembly
of priests, as if the divinity were present and were assisting in the 30
proceedings of the election, the name of one of the candidates
for the kingdom being then announced, the soldiers raise their


THE EGYPTIAN TALE 283

s to twenty hands, and the acolyte counts as ten. Then a second

are common to all, but it was no labour for him to condescend even

THE EGYPTIAN TALE 295


he demanded out of respect for wisdom that such a man be inde-

10 for malignity not assuaged by virtue is rather inflamed by it. If to

the deeply groaning brother suffered over the reign of Osiris.

1. From this point the actions of the gods begin to be manifest,
for all things were now full of all manner of evils from every
quarter, and a belief in Providence had disappeared from the mind
of men, their impious conjectures being largely sustained by the

s events witnessed. On the one hand no human agency appeared
anywhere to assist them, for the foreigners were using the city as

a camp; on the other hand, the commander of these was stricken
with terror during the night, the Corybantes, I suppose, attacking
him, and by day panic uproars took possession of the troops. The
ro frequent occurrence of this reduces them to a state of frenzy and
causes them to lose their wits. They wandered about, alone or
in company, all as if possessed by the nymphs’ delirium, at one
moment attempting to draw their swords, and behaving as about
to deliver an immediate attack, at another, on the contrary,
1§ claiming pity and asking to be spared; or again, springing up, they
seemed alternately like pursuers and pursued, as though some
hostile force had been secretly conveyed into the town. But in
the city there was neither weapon, nor any man to use it; the
people were an easy prey offered up by Typho. So this also is very
20 Clear, that a god is needed even by those well prepared for war,
unless their preparations are to turn out useless, and that victory

is from no other source: at the same time one deprives the
victorious cause of its due in foolishly supposing it to be
probable that the better prepared man will win. For when our
25 plans turn out to be successful, a god seems to us superfluous,
and disputes the honour of a victory that was already prepared
by ourselves. But if no one intervenes to produce the result, and

if the unseen alone is responsible, we hold nothing short of a refuta-
tion, not stated in words, but in evident fact, of the views of those
30 who disbelieve that the gods care for mankind. Now something
of this actually took place on that occasion. Here were the bold,

Enough has now been said about this, but another question
wrapt up in it seems to demand further consideration. That in
various places and in various periods of time thesame events should
have often taken place, that old men should have become spectators

either from books or from their grandfathers’ tales, this seems to
me the most incredible thing, and if it 1s not to remain incredible,
it is worth while that a cause should be found for it. Let us speak
then, when we have found the proper cause, for perhaps a philo-
sophic truth is neither small nor very easy. We must regard the 30
universe as a single whole completed in its parts; we shall then
think ofit asconfluent, and animated by the same breath, for in this

way only could it save its unity, and we shall not represent its parts

one unless they are knit together by nature? They will act on

s act and others will only be acted upon. Proceeding therefore on
this hypothesis to the subject of our examination, we should
logically make the happy body moving in a circle, the cause of
what happens here below.’ Both are parts of it and they have some
relation with each other, and if generation functions in the things
1o about us, the cause of the generation is in those things above us,
and from thence the seeds of what takes place come here. Now

PREFACE


IT is an old tradition, I think, and quite in the manner of Plato,
to conceal the profound thoughts of philosophy behind the mask
of some lighter treatment, that thereby whatsoever has been
acquired with difficulty shall not be again lost to men, nor shall
such matters be contaminated by lying exposed to the approach 5
of the profane. This end accordingly has been most zealously
pursued in the present work, and whether it attains this end, and
whether in other respects it is wrought out with distinction after
the manner of the ancients, let those decide who shall approach
it in a spirit of loving labour. 10


1. If dreams are prophets, and if the visions seen in dreams are
riddles of their future fortunes to anxious men, they would in that
case be full of wisdom, though certainly not clear. In sooth their
lack of clearness is their wisdom.

fair things,

‘The gods have set sweat.’?

that God differs from man, as does man from the brute. But

[ 2. Let the foregoing be proof that divinations are amongst the

The scholar reads these, and he is a scholar who learns by his
natural bent. One reads some of them and another reads others,
one reads more and another less. In the same way one reads them
by syllables, another reads the complete phrase, another the whole 15
story. In like manner do the learned see the future, some under-

It must needs be, I think, that the parts of this great whole, since
it all shares one feeling and one breath, belong to each other.
They are, in fact, limbs of one entire body, and may not
the spells of the magicians be even such as these? Obviously, 30
for charms are cast from one part of it to another, as signals
are given, and he is a sage who understands the relationship


CONCERNING DREAMS 329


of the parts of the universe. One thing he attracts to himself

s another part suffers also with it, so a pain in the finger settles in
the groin,' although there be many organs between these parts
which feel nothing.
This is because they are both portions of one living organism,
and there is that which binds them one to the other more than to
1o other things. Even to some god, of those who dwell within the
universe, a stone from hence and a herb is a befitting offering;
for in sympathizing with these he is yielding to nature and is
bewitched. Thus the harp-player who has sounded the highest
note does not sound the sesquioctavus next, but rather strikes
15 the epitrite and the nete, a heritage of to-day from a more
ancient state of harmony. But there is in the cosmos, even as in
human relationship, a certain discord also; for the universe is not
one homogeneous thing but a unity formed of many. There are
parts of it which agree and yet battle with other parts, and the
20 struggle of these only contributes to a harmonious unity of the
whole, just as the lyre is a system of responsive and harmonious
notes.* The unity resulting from opposites is the harmony both of
the lyre and of the cosmos.* Archimedes the Sicilian * asked for a
point of support outside of the earth wherefrom he might prop
25 himself against the whole earth, for he said that as long as he was
himself upon the earth he had no power over it. But the man,
howso great his knowledge of the nature of the universe may be,
once placed outside of it, could no longer make any use of his
wisdom. He uses the universe against itself ; accordingly his touch
30 with it once lost, he will watch it in vain, and lifeless symbols only

g. Yet I have narrowly missed incurring a charge of ingratitude ;

of divination must be applied, for its genesis was, so to speak,

its development is most obscure. Now its character is as follows.
From all that nature possesses, all things that are, that have come
into being and that shall be (since this too is a phase of existence),
from all these things, I say, images flow and rebound from their
substance. For if each perceptible thing is form coupled with
matter, and if we discover an escape of matter in the combination,
reasoning shows that the nature of the images also is canalized,
so that in both cases perceptible things renounce the dignity of
real being. Now the imaginative pneuma is a powerful reflecting
mirror of all the images that flow off in this way.’ For, wandering
in vain and slipping from their base, on account of the indefinite-
ness of their nature, and because they are recognized by no being
of real existence, whenever these fall in with psychical pneumata,
the which are images indeed, and have a seat fixed in nature, then
they lean upon them and take their rest as though at their own
hearthstone. Of those things, therefore, which have come into
being, inasmuch as they have already passed into the activity of
existence, the images sent forth are distinct, until in the fullness
of time they become faint and evanescent. Of existing things,
inasmuch as they are still standing, the images are more tenacious
of life and more distinct, but those of future events are more in-
definite and indistinguishable. For they are the advanced waves
of things not yet present, efflorescences of unfulfilled nature,

what more fascinating? These induce even fools to pay heed

lived ten years beyond adolescence to stand in need of any
other diviner, shameful that they should not have accumulated
an abundant store of technical principles. It would be a wise 25
proceeding even to publish our waking and sleeping visions and
their attendant circumstances; the wise thing to do, I say, unless
the culture of the city is like to be too rustic for so novel an
enterprise. We shall therefore see fit to add to what are called
‘day books’ what we term ‘night books’, so as to have records to 30
remind us of the character of each of the two lives concerned ;
for our argument already laid it down that a certain life exists in


CONCERNING DREAMS 355


imagination, at one moment better, at another worse than the
intermediate, according to the relation of the pneuma to health
and disease. If in this way, therefore, we make profitable the
observation by which the art is developed, and if nothing slips

5 our memory, in other respects also the result will be a refined
pastime; it will be paying oneself the compliment of a history
of one’s waking and sleeping moments.

As to those who occupy themselves with public speaking, I do
not know any other foundation to replace this as a compre-

10 hensive basis for exercise in the power of speech ; for if the sophist
of Lemnos’ says that the day books are good teachers of effective
oratory on every subject, for that they do not overlook matters
of lesser importance, but compel one to go through the trivial and
the serious alike, is it not worth while to value night books as

15 a subject for oratory?

Any one can see how great the work is, on attempting to
fit language to visions, visions in which those things which are
united in nature are separated, and things separated in nature are
united, and he is obliged to show in speech what has not been

20 revealed. It is no mean achievement to pass on to another some-
thing of a strange nature that has stirred in one’s own soul,
for whenever by this phantasy (of dreaming) things which are
expelled from the order of being, and things which never in any
possible way existed, are brought instead into being—nay, even

25 things which have not a nature capable of existence, what con-
trivance is there for presenting a nameless nature to things which
are per se inconceivable? Again, it (the phantasy) neither makes
these forms appear numerous and all present at the same moment,
nor yet does it present them after an interval, but exactly as the

30 dream itself might have them and pass? them on to us; for we
believe whatever it wills us to believe. To survive at all and with-
out cutting a sorry figure amidst all this, would be proof of a

masterly rhetoric. It conducts itself wantonly even against our

Now in dreams one conquers, walks, or flies simultaneously,
and the imagination has room for it all; but how shall mere
speech find room for it? So a man sleeps and dreams; he sees 15
a dream, and arises from it still sleeping, as he thinks, and shakes
off his dream while still recumbent. He philosophizes a little on
the vision that has appeared to him, according to his knowledge ;
and this is a dream, but the other is a double dream. Accordingly
he believes it not, and thinks that now he is awake and that what 20
appears to him is really alive. Forthwith a fierce struggle ensues,
and a man dreams that an attack is made on himself, then that he
has left all behind and is waking up, again that he has made trial
of himself and has discovered the deception. In some such way
must the sons of Aloeus be suffering punishment for piling up the 25
mountains of Thessaly against the gods.‘ But there is no law of
Adrastea? in the way of the sleeper, to forbid him from rising from
earth more happily than Icarus, from soaring above the eagles,
or reaching a point above the loftiest spheres themselves. So one
looks steadily upon the earth from afar, and discovers a land not 30
visible even to the moon. It is also in his power to hold converse

CONSTITUTIO


INASMUCH as I have not chosen a philosophy that stands aloof
from public life, and inasmuch as the religion that most cherishes
humanity urges us to acquire a character devoted to the common


1576 weal, I have given ear to your summons, and I am glad to know


the reasons which have brought the two cities so speedily into

and in the future, that they are at once grateful and show their
gratitude towards those who initiated kind actions. I welcomed
therefore the united expressions of the people and at the same
time I extolled all individual speakers with praise. But I too
must needs be of the company of eulogists, and this also becomes
me more than all others. I even consider that I myself owe thanks
to those who have conferred any benefit, on behalf of every
one, whether an individual or a city. For how can the man whose
duty it is to pray for the common good, fail in gratitude to him
who has added to it by his military service and the rest of his
administration? How can I fail to treat with all honour the man
who has throughout laboured with the sweat of his brow, that
I may obtain the object of my prayers, that the accursed bar-
barians should perish evilly, in evil wise? It was I indeed that
prayed to God, but it was the hands of Anysius that carried out
God’s will. Of the cavalry who attacked us the other day, over
a thousand in number, not the fifth part survives, say those who
have suffered. They themselves yet live and have counted the
fallen. These results, too, have been attained with no great army
to lead the way; but the men who fought along with them
numbered forty. I will say nothing derogatory to the cavalry
and infantry we are supporting, but he, Anysius, thinks that we
ought to use the Unnigardae for everything. The rest of his

HOMILY I


I SHALL not make this festal assembly a silent one, nor again one 1561
of many speeches; for, although it is God whom I honour in my
speech, by bringing it to a speedy close I shall do what is pleasing
to the assembled company. But in order that you may be a partici-

s pant worthy of God in the festival, do not set your hearts on
the pleasures of the table, passing from fasting to drunkenness.
Offer to God a garlanded goblet of sober mixture. Our God is
wisdom and reason. A beaker that confuses reflection, that dis-
turbs the reasoning faculty, is quite alien to true reason. There is

10 a recreation that is befitting to God, and there is one that befits
evil spirits. ‘Exult ye in the Lord in fear’. When you feast, he
says, be you mindful of God, for it is then that most men slip into
sin. When the body is well nourished and grows fleshy, it deflects
the soul’s judgement. ‘In the hand of the Lord there is a cup

15 of unmixed wine filled with a mixture, and he pours from this
vessel into that, but the dregs of it have not been drained.’? Drink
thou of that cup, and thou hast become worthy of the banquet of
the bridegroom. That cup is beneficial, full of wine, and once
sought, 1s worthy to raise us to Mind. And indeed the passage is

20 quite clear, though many things fall a little short of compre-
hension. A drinking cup is full of a mixture in unmixed wine.
‘And he poured from this vessel into that’.? If it was of unmixed
wine, how is it full of a mixture, and if it is one, how did he pour it
from this to that? The words seem to be altogether nonsensical ;

25 not so, however, if really understood. God has no interest in
divinely inspired diction. The divine spirit disdains literary petti-
ness. Dost thou desire to behold the harmony of this discord? Con-
cerning what sort of cup is he speaking? It is the word which we
have from God, freely offered by God to men in the Old Testa-


1 Cf. Ps. ii. 11. 2 Ps. Ixxiv. 9.


370 HOMILY I


ment and the New, for by this drink is our soul watered. Inas-
much as it is a word, each of the two is unmixed, for even although
a double word it is mixed together, for what has been compounded
out of the two is one, a perfection of Gnosis. The Old Testament
contained the promise, and the New revealed the apostle, and the s
phrase ‘he poured from this into that’ shadows forth the succession
of the teachers of the law, that of Moses and that of the Lord, and
the cup is one, for one Spirit breathed both on the prophet and the
apostle, and like good painters, He sketched out, in days of old, and

HOMILY II


1564 IT is a holy night that brings light to those that are accursed,
a light greater than that wherewith any sun has ever illumined the
day. Lo, it is not holy that even the fairest thing upon the earth
should be compared to the Creator; but that light which illumines r¢

exists through the harmony of its present blessedness, that will

you will maintain the soul ina more enviable state for the present,
if not for your whole life. At this moment each one of you goes 20
about the city as an announcing messenger. Now believe ye that
the words of scripture refer to you, that being on earth ye have
a citizenship in heaven.! Beware of missing your deserts, for hard
to wash out is the stain that comes after cleansing.

Why then do these men think fit to overstep the limits that have
been assigned to them from time immemorial, and come against
us, who are more aflame than they. Why do they always sell the
rs Surplus to us, who are more parched than they and wronged by our
situation? Since there has been no profit this year, they insist that
our misfortunes should take its place. This is the object of the
writs recently issued, and their decrees have no other aim than
this. And they also make a second admission, which it is only just
20 that we should state first of all, and we alone; for it explains
their most unjust attempt. For having themselves long ago laid .
a foundation for their false accusations, to support their shameless
claims to make use of the water that does not belong to them,
they have now approached this most august court.

Page 245, 1.4. after risingin the morning &c. In regard to this chapter,
extending over about two pages, which Synesius quotes from the works
of Dio Chrysostom, I have to make the following observations. No work
of Dio concerning hair was known to Photius, nor has any such work
been noted by any other writer of antiquity. The chapter in question,
therefore, was, until the year 1839, always regarded as the introductory
part of a work by Dio, of which the rest has disappeared. In that year,
however, a distinguished Dutch scholar, J. Geel, the librarian of the Uni-


394 NOTES


versity of Leyden,and correspondent of the French Académie des Inscrip-
tions, who had been making a close study of the document in question,
published a letter on the subject, addressed to M. Hase, Conservateur
au Département des Manuscrits, at the Bibliothéque du Roi, Paris. In
this letter, which is full of very close and acute argument, he attempts
to establish, and it would seem with great success, the thesis that he
sets out to demonstrate, namely, that the two pages quoted here
from Dio are not a fragment of the lost essay, but the whole essay.
‘For my part’, he says, ‘I have come to the conclusion that Synesius in
saying at the beginning of his discourse that a work had been produced,
called a Eulogy on Hair, by Dio of the tongue of gold, has fabricated a
title that Dio himself had never thought of. This Eulogy of Hair,
which he pretends to offer us, is only an exercise in style, a study, one
such as I could point out in other of this author’s writings, as for
example, the nineteenth discourse, introduced in the same way by an
account of some event, and as little polished as the so-called “Eulogy”’.
The same thing may be said of the fifty-second discourse, one of the
most interesting bits in the collection of his works. They are nothing,
all of them, but thoughts jotted down on paper at the moment. At the
same time, I call your attention to the extraordinary resemblance be-
tween the commencement of this fifty-second discourse, and that of the
“Eulogy of Hair”... . If the Eulogy did not bear the marks of Dio’s
style even in its smallest details, one would be tempted to suspect
Synesius of bad faith, and to imagine that he had forged an imitation
in order to fight with a shadow’ (Leyde, Hazenberg, 1839). There is not
room here to go through all the points of this very interesting work of
Geel’s, which I recommend to any one desirous to form a definite opinion
on the question. The text is printed, with the readings of a Florence
manuscript of Synesius, in von Arnim’s edition of Dio (vol. ii [Berol.
1896], pp. 313-19).

Another interesting discovery in regard to this essay of Synesius was
made a little later. A French savant, E. Miller, published in Paris in
the year 1840 a Greek text entitled, ‘Eloge de la Chevelure, discours
inédit d’un auteur grec anonyme en réfutation du discours de Synésius
intitulé, Eloge de la Calvitie, publié d’aprés un manuscrit grec, &c.’
It seems that M. Miller came across this work of an anonymous Greek


A EULOGY OF BALDNESS 395


author in the Bibliothéque Nationale in Paris, where for some extra-
ordinary reason it had escaped the notice of other scholars. ‘The writer
whose work I publish to-day,’ says Miller in his Introduction,
“has struck a blow at Synesius’ reputation. . . . It is still more
extraordinary that this work has remained unnoticed until now,
when we observe that it is mentioned in the Greek catalogue (Art. 21,
no. 2953) with this notice, Anonymus de Encomtio Caluitss quod a
Synesio scriptum est. This title arrested my attention. .. . I commenced
reading it at once .. . and finally decided to publish it with a commen-
tary. I had hoped that the work itself would furnish me with indica-
tions that might be sufficient to decide its authorship. It is certainly
remarkable in many ways, but in this particular I was disappointed.
Not only does the author say nothing to throw any light on the question
of authorship, but he cites no poet of antiquity except Homer and
Hesiod.’ Miller means no doubt by this that we cannot assign a date
to him through the authors that he quotes; I have pointed out else-
where that there would be a similar difficulty in the case of Synesius, if
we were otherwise unaware of the exact time in which he lived. ‘Never-
theless,’ Miller continues, ‘there was abundance of opportunity for
quotations, and he could easily have brought upon the scene many
poets of antiquity. He contents himself, however, as a philosopher
with combating Synesius single-handed. In spite of this excessive
dearth of sources of information, I do not wish to leave the discussion of
this point of literary criticism without seeming to have arrived at some
sort of solution. I have therefore endeavoured to fix approximately
the period in which this champion of Dio must have written his essay,
and after a conscientious examination of his style, I have sought to
indicate to what class of writers he belonged.’ While admitting that a
decision upon this point must be more or less conjectural, Miller goes
on to point out that certain Greek writers of the fourteenth and fifteenth
centuries did succeed to a certain extent in rehabilitating their style in
Greek by a close study of the authors of the golden age. The anony-
mous work that he is criticizing he describes as showing considerable
purity of Attic style, an achievement which would have been quite
within the compass of such men as Demetrius Cydonius, Bessarion, or
Gemistus Plethon. And this alone is sufficient to make one hesitate.

From a palaeographical point of view the manuscript in question cannot,
he says, be more modern than the end of the thirteenth century, or the
beginning of the fourteenth. This seems to make it impossible, there-
fore, to attribute it to such fourteenth- or fifteenth-century writers as
those just named. After weighing all possibilities, therefore, the happy
discoverer of the manuscript has come to the conclusion that its author,
if he were not a contemporary of Synesius, which is quite possible,
must have lived in some part of the two centuries following. I shall
have occasion to refer to this anonymous work in the course of my notes
on this essay of Synesius. It is interesting to observe that the writer of
the pamphlet directed against Synesius does not seem at all to have
appreciated the irony and wit of the author he is criticizing. He shows
a tendency to take everything that Synesius says quite seriously and
literally, and answers him in like manner, training all the heavy artillery
of a philosopher upon him. He never seems to suspect that the essay
of Synesius is really a skit upon precisely such pompous people as him-
self, in other words, the sophists of his time. Muller describes his author
as a philosopher, but I should be more inclined to class him as a sophist,
who was trying to show his ingenuity at the expense of Synesius, just
as Synesius was trying to show his, although in a much lighter and more
jocose spirit, at the expense of Dio, whom, notwithstanding, he admired
so much. ‘Are you not ashamed, Synesius,’ says the anonymous author,
‘unless it is purely on account of your own baldness that you are
speaking, are you not ashamed, I say, to write an encomium upon the
work of a disease, and to leave out of consideration the praise of what is
becoming and healthy?’

A long discussion follows as to the number of the ‘spheres’ necessary
to explain the movements of the heavenly bodies. Synesius was an
astronomer, as we see from the famous Leter to Paconsus, and the
science, as he tells us in the letter in question, had made great strides.
He reminds us that Hipparchus in his day was prophetic, and that his
vague anticipations were fulfilled by the work of Ptolemy and ‘the
divine band of his successors.’ ‘Every allowance must be made’, he
adds, ‘for these men, inasmuch as the more important problems were
still unsolved, and geometry was still at the nursing stage.’ It would
be very interesting to know what these ‘important problems’ were. But
the exact history of astronomy in the time that elapsed between
Ptolemy and Synesius is lost in obscurity. We naturally scan the
allusions in Synesius here and elsewhere, but find nothing to tell us
whether the conceptions of Eudoxus as to the plurality of spheres in
the universe was still accepted in the fourth century. In the meantime,
at all events, astrology had come in to occupy a large place in the
popular imagination, though of this we hear little in Synesius. But
throughout all his wit and playfulness about the sphere we can easily
detect the same underlying conception that we find in the passage from
Proclus quoted above, namely that the sphere, being the most perfect
form, is the expression of Mind, in other words the second hypostasis of
the Neoplatonists, but it is worthy of observation that Synesius never
endorses in so many words the doctrine of the Neoplatonic hypostases.
For him the sphere is the most perfect form, and therefore the idea of
the sphere must dominate the cosmos. Beyond that he does not go.
He remains with the Platonic doctrine of the idea. In this respect he is
pre-Aristotelian, notwithstanding the fact that he has, as I have tried to
show, so frequently drawn on the works of Aristotle.

celestial bodies, or at all events had some connexion with astronomy.
