The above description of the Egyptians in general as ignorant and
grossly superstitious is rather in accord with what Synesius says here,
speaking of them as a people who were hoodwinked by their priests. It is
always of the priests that he speaks when he is extolling the wisdom of
the Egyptians. We must not forget that he expresses himself frequently
in favour of not enlightening the masses as to the mysteries of religion.
In letter 105, notably when on the brink of accepting the bishopric, he
writes: ‘Thephilosophic mind . . . admits the employment of falsehood.
...I consider that the false may be beneficial to the populace, and the
truth injurious. . . . I can take over the holy office on condition that I
may prosecute philosophy at home, and spread legends abroad... .
Divine truth should remain hidden: the vulgar need a different
system.’ Is it possible that Synesius’ views on these matters were in-
fluenced by his admiration for the Egyptian priests? The tradition
amongst Greek philosophers is as old as the time of Plato, who ts always
endorsing their wisdom, without, however, throwing much light on
their theology. Plutarch, on the other hand, gives us so many explana-
tions of the origin and interpretation of the myths of their religion, that
we are forced to conclude that in his time either the priests themselves
had become very ignorant about their own doctrines, or saw fit to throw
dust in the eyes of inquiring Greeks. We find elsewhere in Synesius
allusion to the fact that they were not able to interpret their own hiero-
glyphics (De Prov., p. 1256 c). Plutarch, in Jsts and Ostris, c. 72 ff.,
tells us that some men account for the heads of animals in the images
of gods as coming from military standards or ensigns, carried into
battle in the past, and each sacred to some single tribe, which after-
wards endowed its protecting deity with the emblem, and that others
say that they were used in war as portentous signs to terrify the enemy
with; or again, that they were the areas marked out by the priests, in
the celestial vault, and referred to the astral nature of their gods, as does
Porphyry in the letter quoted above.

Diogenes Laertius speaks of the philosophy of the Egyptians in the
following terms (i. 10): “They say that matter was the first principle,
next the four elements were derived from matter, and thus living things


A EULOGY OF BALDNESS 403


of every species were produced. The sun and the moon are gods bear-
ing the names of Osiris and Isis respectively: they make use of the
beetle, the dragon, the hawk, and other creatures as symbols of divinity,
according to Manetho.. . and Hecataeus. . . . They also set up statues
and temples to these sacred animals because they do not know the true
form of the deity. They hold that the universe is created and perishable
and that it is spherical in shape. They say that the stars consist of fire,
and that, according as the fire in them is mixed, so events happen upon
earth ; that the moon is eclipsed when it falls into the earth’s shadow ;
that the soul survives death and passes into other bodies; that rain is
caused by change in the atmosphere ; of all other phenomena they give
physical explanations. . . . They also laid down laws on the subject of
justice, which they ascribed to Hermes; and they deified those animals
which are serviceable to men.’ (Diog. Laer., translation R. D. Hicks,
Loeb Library.) It must be remembered that Diogenes Laertius was
writing probably in the early part of the third century, and was nearer
to the time of Synesius than was Plutarch.

the land. The rest of each army was to go away to its own country....
Having thus agreed, the armies drew off, and picked men of each side
were left and fought. Neither could gain advantage in the battle; at
last of six hundred there were left only three, Alcenor and Chromios of
the Argives, Othryades of the Lacedaemonians: these three were left
alive at nightfall. Then the two Argives, deeming themselves victors, ran

bore the armour to his own armies’ camp, and remained in his place.
On the next day both armies came to learn the issue; for awhile both
claimed the victory. .. . At last the dispute so ended that they joined
battle and fought ; many of both sides fell but the Lacedaemonians had
the victory. Ever after this the Argives, who before had worn their hair

should wear gold, till they should recover Thyrea; and the Lacedae-

Page 264, 1.2. Ptolemy, son of Lagus. Arrian explains in his
preface to his Ltfe of Alexander, that since Ptolemy, son of Lagos, and
Aristoboulos had both written concerning his campaigns, he himself
has adopted the course of accepting for his work all statements in which
these two writers agreed, and in case they disagreed of adopting the
more plausible version of the two. He further states that they both
seem to him the more trustworthy inasmuch as they both accompanied
Alexander on his campaigns, and as to Ptolemy, he of all men was the
least likely to falsify the truth, for deception is more disgraceful
in a king than in any other man. From this phrase it may be inferred


A EULOGY OF BALDNESS 407


that Synesius had Arrian’s work in his mind when he wrote this passage.
Certainly he would have agreed with Arrian. Compare his remark
in the address to the Emperor Arcadius, ‘Truth is the aristocracy of
language.’ The passage which he refers to here, or possibly quotes in
places, is not in the few fragments we possess of Ptolemy, whom, how-
ever, Arrian frequently refers to. Ptolemy seems to have enjoyed the
reputation of telling amusing anecdotes. If the one that he recounts
of the dragons with human voices who conducted Alexander’s army to
Ammon be taken as an example of his critical powers as an historian, the
amusing war episode that Synesius tells us here will find little credence.
There is, perhaps, a vein of irony in the manner in which he observes
that Ptolemy must be truthful because he is a king. It reminds us of the
passage in Letter 44, where he says: ‘This is the story which Rumour
has recounted, and it is not ordained that a divinity should lie.’

and succeeded thereby in getting his enemy out of the way, and in
making the task of Demosthenes more difficult. Demosthenes, how-
ever, won his case against Aeschines in the end, and the latter retired
from public life. Both these men became the butt of the comic poets.

Page 275,1.1. sons of Taurus. The phrase ‘written at the time’, or,as
Druon translates it, ‘under the reign of, the sons of Taurus,’ is obscure.
Petavius reminds us of a Taurus who was consul with Florentius under
the EmperorsConstantine, Constantius, andConstans. It is obvious that
Aurelian, ‘the better man’ mentioned in this passage, is the Osiris of the
story, and ‘the inferior man’ Typho. That Aurelian had a son Taurus
we know from Letter 31; he was consul in 428 (Socrates, vii. 29). He
comes into this story under the name of Horus. It seems not improbable,
as Crawford points out (Synessus the Hellene, p. 454), that the father of


410 NOTES


Aurelian, whose name is unknown, may also have been named ‘ Taurus’.
‘The Riddle of the Wolf’ marks the end of the first part of the story,
where it is alluded to as belonging to the mysteries that must not be re-
vealed, even in the disguise of a fable. Plutarch, in Ists and Ossrss, gives
all the information known to Greek antiquity as to the symbolism of
these names, which were identified by him in certain passages, as analo-
gous to Greek conceptions, as in cap. 78, where he speaks of the
Egyptian priests, hinting cautiously, and with the greatest reserve, at
the functions of Osiris in the under-world, as similar to those of Dis and
Pluto ("A:dov xai []Aovrwvos). In the same way Plutarch identifies Horus
with Apollo, and Bacchus with Osiris. Osiris was the son of Helios, and
Typho of Cronos, &c., &c. (cap. 12). Osiris, he tells us, was announced
by an oracular voice, as born to be a beneficent monarch (péyas
Baowreds evepyérns “Ootpis yéyove), and when he came to rule over the
Egyptians, he civilized them not by the use of arms, but by persuasion,
and by reason conjoined with song (er’ wos), and subdued them with
the charms of every form of musical art (dons povoucjs, ibid. 13). Thus
he seems to be to the Greeks identical with Dionysius. This account of
the rule of Osiris in Plutarch has an unmistakable likeness to the opening
passage in chapter twelve of this story, in which Synesius describes
Osiris as, ‘a marvel ill-suited to this earth, one who at once began
striving to banish the forces hostile to it, without employing any
violence at all,’ but who ‘sacrificed to Persuasion, to the Muses and to
the Graces, and made all willingly fall in with the law .. . he made it a
point of honour to conquer the most shameless man by the gentleness
of his mind, &c.’

It is difficult, in the face of this and other concordant passages, to
resist the conclusion that Synesius had Plutarch’s essay in mind when
he framed his story. Typho, in Plutarch’s version, is represented as
laying snares for Osiris, and compassing his destruction. The name
Typho, Plutarch tells us (cap. 62), signifies all that is perverse, preven-
tive, and contrary, in the light of the Egyptian words that are used to
designate him. But although Osiris and Typho are well and consistently
chosen by Synesius for the purpose of his allegory, in that they repre-
sented, in Egyptian mythology, the powers of light and darkness, we
cannot follow the historical side of the story at this distance of time with


THE EGYPTIAN TALE 4II


absolute certainty, for whom he meant to designate by Typho is still a
moot question. Otto Seeck made out a strong case for identifying him
with Caesarius, and this view, which has the endorsement of Bury, I am
inclined to accept, if it is necessary to fix upon a historical personage ;
but it is of course possible that Typho in this story is merely symbolic
of the evil political forces in general, which stood in the way of Aurelian,
the friend of Synesius, whom he so much admired, and whom he has
made the hero of his drama.

An analysis of the arguments advanced by Otto Seeck will be found
in the appendix 27 to Bury’s edition of Gibbon’s Decline and Fall,
vol. ili, p. 506. ‘It had long been recognized’, says Bury, ‘that Egypt
stood for the Empire, and Thebes for Constantinople; and the Prae-
torian Praefect Aurelian had been detected under the veil of Osiris. But
no likely conjecture had been made as to the identity of Typhos, the
wicked brother of Osiris. It was partly in consequence of this lacuna
that the able attempt of Giildenpenning to reconstruct the history of
the years A.D. 399 and 400, on the basis of the work of Synesius (com-
pare my Later Roman Empire, i, p. 79 sqq.) did not carry complete
conviction. But O. Seeck has recently made out a good case for the
identity of Typhos, and interpreted the allegory more fully (Phtlologus,
52, Pp. 442 sqq., 1894).’ Bury explains next that according to Seeck
there can be no doubt that Taurus, father of Osiris and Typho, is the
man who appears in the Consular Fasti of A.D. 361, who was quaestor
in 353, and Praetorian Praefect in 355. He held this office (the peyaAn
apx7 of Synes. De Prov.c. 2, p. 1213) till 361, and presided at the Council
of Ariminum (359). He then passes to Aurelian, whom Seeck describes
as having built a church in 383, having in 393 become Praefect of
Constantinople before Rufinus, and after the fall of Eutropius Prae-
torian Praefect of the East (399-400); and so on through his career,
which witnessed the revolt of Gainas in 400, and his recall to the office
of Praefect for the third time (402-404). Seeck has shown this by com-
paring Letters 31 and 38 of Synesius with the Cod. Th. 4, 2,1, and 5, 1, 5.
Now such being the history of Aurelian, Seeck explains the descrip-
tion of Osiris given on p. 1217 as émordrns Sopuddpwv yevopevos Kai
dxoas muorevfeis to stand for magister officiorum, and the word zoA-
apyyjoas to mean that he was subsequently Praefect of the city, &c.,

2878-3 Z


412 NOTES


showing that the account given by Synesius tallies with what we know
of the history of Aurelian. He observes also that what happened to
Osiris in the story after his fall corresponds even more strikingly to that
which happened to Aurelian, as we shall see in dealing with page 1252.
But the identification of Osiris with Aurelian was never in any doubt,
although Seeck and Giildenpenning have given corroborative evidence.
We now come to the Emperor Arcadius, who, it is natural to suppose,
would appear in the story. Seeck identifies him with the High Priest
(Crawford, however, rejects this identification, cf. Synestus the Hellene,
p.456. ‘The High Priest’, he says, ‘can be no other than S. Chrysostom’,
cp. Volkmann, p. 177, note). Is it not possible, on the other hand, that
in this bold political squib, as Bury describes it, Synesius wishes from
motives of policy to keep the Emperor entirely out of the narrative?
We next come to the identification of Typho. As this is the most im-
portant part of Seeck’s reconstruction, I will quote Bury’s account of it:
‘In the allegory, Typhos is in close alliance with the barbarian mer-
cenaries, and instigates their attack on Thebes in order to overthrow his
brother Osiris. When Osiris surrenders himself to the barbarian leader,
Typhos urges that he should be put to death. Typhos then receives the
kingdom and administers it tyrannically ; nor is his position shaken by
the fall of the barbarian leader. Before the first rise of Osiris to power
he had filled a post which gave him patronage in distributing offices, the
power of oppressing towns (p.1217),and the duty of regulating measures
in connexion with the payment of taxes in kind (p. 1219). These hints,
taken along with the mention of torch-bearing attendants, suggest
that the office was no less than that of Praetorian Prefect. It would
follow that Typhos was Praetorian Prefect before 399, and again in 400.

‘Eutropius had endeavoured to reduce the power of Praetorian Pre-
fect of the East by making it a collegial office; and Eutychianus ap-
pears as holding that office (1) along with Caesarius while Eutropius was
in power; (2) along with Aurelian 399-400; (3) along with Aurelian
when he was restored 402. It may be assumed that he also held it
between 400 and 402.

‘It would follow that Caesarius, whom we find Praetorian Prefect
from 396-8, and again in 400 and 4o1, was the prototype of Typhos, the
son of Taurus and the brother of Aurelian. Some other points may


THE EGYPTIAN TALE 413


confirm the conjecture. The tendency to Arianism, of which Typhos is
accused, is illustrated by C. Th. 16, 5, 25, and the passion of Typhos for
his wife by a notice in Sozomen, 9, 2. If Typhos is not meant for
Caesarius it would seem that he must be purely fictitious.’

It would be interesting to know what part the Empress Eudoxia
played in all this. Bury considers that there was a close political union
between Eudoxia and Aurelian, in which case an empress of German
origin must have allied herself with a statesman whose policy was anti-
German.

Volkmann held the opinion that Aurelian, as the result of some court
intrigue or in some other irregular way, had a brother who was the original
of the Typho in this story. This view is rejected by Crawford (p. 459), as
also by Miss Gardner, as resting purely on surmise. Quite apart from
the improbability of such a person escaping the notice of the historians
of the period, it seems an explanation too obviously derived from the
evidence of the story itself. This theory, however, was held by so
great an authority as Krabinger. (v. Volkmann, p. 72, note). If this
were the case it would make Synesius history perfectly consistent, but
on the evidence before us the view of Seeck seems to be the most
plausible one.

The point is an important one; for if Synesius did not adhere to
history in this case of the relationship of the two men in question,
there is no reason to suppose that he may not have recorded other
imaginary details in his story.

Plato, in the Republic, has a good deal to say concerning the influence
of legends upon the minds of children, as, for instance, the remarks of
Socrates (p. 3774). ‘You know, I said, that we begin by telling
children stories which, though not wholly destitute of truth, are in the
main fictitious. . . . You know also that the beginning is the most im-
portant part of any work, especially in the case of a young and tender
thing; for that is the time at which the character is being formed ...


414 NOTES


Let them (i.e. mothers and nurses) fashion the mind with such tales, even
more fondly than they mould the body with their hands.’ Plato is fre-
quently recurring to the value of first impressions on the mind of the
child, and insists that knowledge in the first stages should not come to
them through compulsion. In Republic, p.536D, he says that ‘Solon was
under a delusion when he said that a man, when he grows old, may learn
many things—for he can no more learn much than he can run much...
and, therefore, calculation and geometry. and all the other elements of
instruction which are a preparation for dialectic, should be presented to
the mind in childhood; not, however, under any notion of forcing our
system of education ... Then . . . do not use compulsion, but let early
education be a sort of amusement.’ All this is equally relevant to the
passage at the end of page 1236, where Synesius speaks of the value of
early education. It might be argued in this connexion that Plato
regarded all men as ‘children of an older growth’, for when he has
exhausted all the arguments that his dialectic method suggests, he
generally turns to the myth, and tells us some legend before abandoning
the subject.


Page 277, 1.21. The elder brother Typho. Plutarch, in his Ists and
Osiris, explains the symbolism of Typho in the following words: ‘In
the soul, reason and that understanding which is the guide and mistress
of all the best things is Osiris. . . in an opposing sense the passionate,
violent, unreasonable, brutish, rash and foolish part of the soul is
Typho ’ (Is. et Os. p.371 A-B). Again, he alludes to Osiris as representing
the beginning and principle, and Isis that which receives. Horus is the
compound of both. It would seem also, he says, that the poet Hesiod,
when he avers that all things in the first instance were Chaos, Earth,
Tartarus, and Love, has no other foundation than the significations of
these names, meaning by the Earth Isis, by Love Osiris, and by
Tartarus Typho (thtd. p. 374).


Page 282,1.9. There ts a sacred mountain, &c. The geography of the
valley of the Nile near Karnak, and the remains of the ancient city of
Thebes, does not help us much to reconstitute the picture that Synesius
draws here. The valley of the Nile is over six miles wide at Luxor, the
little town that has grown up on what was once the southern suburb of


THE EGYPTIAN TALE 415


the ancient city of Thebes, about 1,400 years B.c.; and the range of
mountains on one’s left hand when looking down stream is at least five
miles from the river. There cannot be said to be ‘a mountain’ near
Thebes, as Synesius puts it, for it is a high range of cliffs, a sort of
palisade that rises abruptly from the flat plain, and in which are the
celebrated ‘Tombs of the Kings’. On our right hand, still looking down
the river, and at a distance of some miles from it, there are ranges of
lower hills. What the ‘two opposite mountains’ are, it would be diffi-
cult to say; but the distance between any two elevations chosen on
different sides of the Nile in the neighbourhood of Thebes would be
some seven miles, and such a distance does not tally with the descrip-
tion here. The ancient town of Thebes, with its hundred gates, was said
to be about fourteen miles in circumference, and lay on both sides of the
river. The legend of its great magnitude has been rather confirmed by
archaeologists. Even in the days of Strabo, long after its decline, it seems
to have shown remains of outer walls of some eight miles in extent.
‘Vestiges of its magnitude still exist’, says Strabo (xvii. 1. 46), ‘which
extend to a length of eighty stadia. The site is at present given over to
villages. That part of it in which the city lies is in Arabia, another, in
which is the Memnoniun,, is on the other side of the river (i.e. the left
side, always looking down). Here are the two colossal figures near one
another, each consisting of a single stone.’ The Colossi which Strabo
mentions are still standing, although he speaks of one of them in his
time as having suffered from an earthquake, which threw down the
upper part.

Diodorus Siculus speaks of the city of Thebes as having been embel-
lished by the King Busiris and his eight sons. According to him it was
called by the Egyptians themselves the great city of Zeus (Aus wéAw
THv peydAnv), and only by the Greeks, Thebes. It is not clear what
Egyptian divinity he means to imply by Zeus. He goes on to speak of
the vast extent of the walls enclosing the city that extended to 140
stadia, and of the great palaces, and magnificent temples, and stately
shrines which adorned it in marvellous fashion. As to the hundred
gates of which Homer speaks, he tells us that some are of opinion that
these were not gates but vestibules of temples. All this, of course, was
legendary in his time. The great Thebes seems to have disappeared


416 NOTES


about the time of Cambyses. There seems to be little doubt that Syne-
sius had never visited the site, and the picture that he draws is a purely
imaginary one. It is interesting as showing how little known this part of
the valley of the Nile must have been, even at Alexandria, in the fourth
century. (See Diod. Sic., Lib. I, cap. xv.)

Page 286, 1.11. another and super-cosmic race of gods. This same idea
of the super-cosmic gods Synesius touches on in Dreams (cap. i). Ps.-[am-
blichus in his tractate on the Myséertes, a work written in answer to
Porphyry’s letter to the Egyptian priest Anebo, and which is in some

He tells us that demons are far distant from both the visible and
intelligible gods from their very essence. The demons, it is true, are
invisible, and cannot be objects of sense perception, but they do not,
like the gods, transcend rational knowledge and concrete intelligence.


THE EGYPTIAN TALE 417


In Dreams also Synesius speaks of gods who are within the confines
of the universe, and who may therefore be propitiated by offerings
of herbs, stones, and so forth, as distinguished from gods who are
without the confines of the universe. Synesius, says Petavius, indi-
cates here three grades of gods: the lowest those to whom the manage-
ment of the lower world is attributed and who fulfil a double function,
one an active and busy one, when they have time to administer the
affairs of this world; the other a happy and quiet one, when they lift
themselves up to the contemplation of the sublime divinity. The second
grade contains the medial gods, to whom I understand the phrase ‘the
hypercosmic race of gods’ (yévos Bedv drepxcopiov) to refer to, who do
not participate in the management of affairs below; and these have a
third divinity above them whom he calls the Source (zyyjv), in other
words, the fountain of the divine essence.

Page 286, 1. 21. action generated in their contemplation. Contemplation,


418 NOTES


in the case of the gods, was identified with action. It was by their con-
templative power, according to Synesius’ conception, that they gener-
ated the world, and kept successively regenerating it in their visits from
time to time, as he tells us a little farther on. The force that descended
in this way from one rank of deities to another, was a sort of emanation
from the fountain head which seems to have become feebler and
feebler, as it approached the realm of matter, and this necessitated the
actual descent from time to time of the beings who were nearer the
source.


Page 287, 1. 6. that does the demon. There is a good deal of confusion
in the conception of demons. The demon in the time of Plato is repre-
sented as an intermediate being between gods and men. Socrates, in the
Symposium, represents Eros as being, not a god but a demon, and as
therefore partaking of the nature of both god and man. The demon was
not understood asmaleficent. Even Ps.-[amblichusrepresents the demons
as ministers of the gods, as in the following passage from the Mystertes.
‘In short, that which is divine is of a ruling nature and presides over
the different orders of beings; but that which is daemoniacal is of a
ministrant nature, and receives whatever the Gods may announce,
promptly employing manual operation, as it were, in things which the
Gods intellectually perceive, wish,and command. The Gods, therefore,
are liberated from the powers which verge to generation ; but daemons
are not entirely purified from these’ (I. 20, Taylor, p.78). He appears to
give them functions somewhat resembling those of the demiurges in
Plato’s Timaeus, but in this story Synesius brings them in as purely
maleficent, and this conception grew in the fourth and fifth centuries,
and was no doubt strongly affected by Christianity, which in the Middle
Ages had come to recognize the existence of vast tribes of evil spirits.

Page 294, 1.5. Early education. The whole subject of early education
is gone into by Plato in detail in Laws, pp. 809-10. He says, for instance,
‘A fair time for a boy of ten years old to spend in letters is three years ;
the age of thirteen is the proper time for him to begin to handle the lyre.
... Hear, however, first of all what the young aught to learn in the early
years of life: . . . they ought to be occupied with their letters until they
are able to read and write; but the acquisition of perfect beauty and
quickness in writing, if nature has not stimulated them to acquire these
accomplishments in the given number of years, they should let alone.’
The ‘ Athenian Stranger’ in the Dialogue goes on to discuss the practice
of learning poets by heart, or making compendiums of their works, &c.
In page 819 of the same Dialogue he recurs to his favourite idea of
teaching children through their games: ‘All free men, I can see, should
learn as much of these branches of knowledge as every child in Egypt is
taught when he learns the alphabet. In that country arithmetical
games have been invented for the use of mere children, which they
learn as a pleasure and amusement. They have to distribute apples and
garlands for a larger and sometimes for a lesser number of persons. . . .
Another method of amusing them is to distribute vessels of gold, brass,
silver, and the like . . . and in this way make more intelligible to their
pupils the arrangement and movements of armies and expeditions .. .
and again in measurements of things . . . they free us from that natural
ignorance which is so ludicrous and disgraceful. . . . I, like yourself, my
dear Cleinias, have late in life heard of our ignorance in these matters ;


THE EGYPTIAN TALE 423


to me we appear to be more like pigs than men, and I am quite ashamed,
not only of myself, but of all Hellenes.’ It is possible that Synesius was
thinking of this passage in speaking of the attention that Osiris, his
Egyptian hero in the Tale, paid to early education. Another example
of Plato’s views on the subject may be found in the first book of the
Laws, p. 643: ‘The most important part of education is nght training
in the nursery. The soul of the child in his play should be guided to the
love of that sort of excellence in which, when he grows up to manhood,
he will have to be perfected. .. . We are not speaking of education in the
narrower sense, but of that other education in virtue from youth upwards,
which makes a man eagerly pursue the ideal perfection of citizenship,and
teaches him howrightly to rule and how to obey. This is the only educa-
tion which, upon our view, deserves the name.’ Again in Book IT, p.653.
“Now I mean by education that training which is given by suitable
habits to the first instincts of virtue in children; when pleasure, and
friendship, and pain, and hatred, are rightly implanted in souls not yet
capable of understanding the nature of them, and who find them, after
they have attained reason, to be in harmony with her. This harmony
of the soul, taken as a whole, is virtue; but the particular training
in respect of pleasure and pain which leads you always to hate what
you ought to hate, and love what you ought to love, from the beginning
of life to the end, may be separated off; and in my view will be rightly
called education.’

Turning now again to Book I, p. 641, we find the same note quite as
definitely expressed, ‘But if you ask what is the good of education in
general, the answer is easy—that education makes good men, and that
good men act nobly, and conquer their enemies in battle, because they
are good. Education certainly gives victory, although victory some-
times produces forgetfulness of education ; for many have grown inso-
lent from victory in war . . . and many a victory has been, and will be,
suicidal to the victors; but education is never suicidal.’ How much the
conception of education as a political end is in Plato’s mind may be
gathered from a passage in the Republsc, in Bk. VI, p. 498, where
Socrates, declaring that States should pursue philosophy, continues:
‘At present the students of philosophy are quite young, beginning when
they are hardly past childhood.’ (Cf. Synesius, supra, ‘the child’s philo-


424 NOTES

sophy’.] In childhood and youth their study, and what philosophy
they learn, should be suited to their tender years: during this period,
while they are growing up towards manhood, the chief and special care
should be given to their bodies, that they may have them to use in the
service of philosophy; as life advances and the intellect begins to
mature, let them increase the gymnastics of the soul; but when the
strength of our citizens fails and is past civil and military duties, then
let them range at will, and engage in no serious labour, as we intend
them to live happily here, and to crown this life with a similar happiness
in another.’ All this is interesting as showing the conception of Plato,
that the real object in education was a political one, and that the
developed mind of the philosopher was inseparable from the duties
towards the State. Synesius, however, although he was forced by his
destiny to become a shining example of the Platonic ideal, continually
complains of political necessity. But here again he is thoroughly in the
Platonic tradition, for elsewhere Plato admits that the true philosopher
will only take up the burden of government regretfully.


Page 294, 1.6. all education as a fountain-head of virtue. The ideas of
Synesius on education, as I have already pointed out, seem tohave come
from his reading of Plato, the intellectual side being inseparable from
the moral. Compare the passage in Timaeus, p. 87, when after repre-
senting madness and ignorance as diseases of the mind, due to a bad
condition of the body, he adds: ‘Further, when to this evil constitution
of body evil forms of government are added and evil discourses are
uttered in private as well as in public, and no sort of instruction is given
in youth to cure these evils, then all of us who are bad become bad
from two causes which are entirely beyond our control. In such cases
the planters are to blame rather than the plants, the educators rather
than the educated.’


Page 296, 1.29. the one virtue of a woman, &c. The conception of the
proper sphere and conduct of women would not seem to have changed
from the time of Homer to the time of Synesius, if we are to take
his statements as anything but a reflection of his favourite Greek
authors. Certainly here he is reminiscent of the famous passage in the
funeral oration of Pericles (Thuc. ii. 45): ‘And if I am to speak of


THE EGYPTIAN TALE 425


womanly virtue to those of you who will henceforth be widows, let me
sum them up in one short admonition: To a woman not to show more
weakness than is natural to her sex is a great glory, and not to be talked
about for good or for evil among men.’ Substantially the same point of
view may be found in Xenophon, as in Oeconomicus (cap. 7), where
Ischomachus describes how in the course of the conversations he had
with his young newly married wife, he took care to impress upon her
that her sphere was within the precincts of the house rather than out-
side, to be the steward of the possessions within doors, and to direct
the servants from there.

Plato is a decided cross-current to the conceptions of the sphere of
women that existed in Athens at his time, and this is perhaps the only
point in which Synesius does not seem to have followed his master.
Plato, as we see in the Republic and elsewhere, was what we should call
to-day an advanced feminist, and made an eloquent plea for the
equality of the sexes, both in education and in their occupying public
functions, and so forth (Rep. v. 451, 456; Laws, vii. 805). But even
Plato echoes the conservative tradition in the Meno, 71 E: ‘It isa man’s
virtue to be capable of managing the affairs of the city, and in managing
them to benefit his friends and injure his enemies. . .. The woman’s vir-
tue is to take good care of her house and to preserve the things within.’
This is the same language that Synesius employs in De Regno, cap. xiv,
q.v. Synesius would seem to have been anything but a feminist, in
spite of the fact that his mind had been largely formed by the great
Hypatia. Aristotle speaks in the purely conventional strain in the
Polstics, 1277 B, in which he alludes to the different spheres of the sexes
as follows: ‘For a man would be thought a coward if he had no more
courage than a courageous woman, and a woman would be thought
loquacious if she imposed no more restraint on her conversation than
the good man; and indeed their part of the management of a house-
hold is different, for the duty of the one is to acquire, and of the other
to preserve.’ It will be remembered how scandalized Synesius shows
himself in the third Letter at his niece driving in a mule-cart through
the crowded Forum, although she was both betrothed and in mourning.
Plutarch, on the other hand, commences his essay on The Virtues of
Women, with the following observations: ‘Concerning virtue in women,


426 NOTES


O Clea, I do not hold the same opinion as Thucydides, for he gives the
first praise to the woman concerning whom there is the least conversa-
tion amongst those without her doors, either in praise or in blame of her,
for he thinks that the repute of a good woman ought to be secluded in
her house with her person, and should not walk abroad. But Gorgias
seems to me to put the case more happily when he demands that the
good fame of the woman should be known to many, not her person.’
Coming down to the days of Philo, we find him expressing the classic con-
ception again, as in this passage in the Special Laws, III. 31,§ 171:
‘Let no woman busy herself about those things which are beyond the
province of household management, but let her cultivate solitude;
let her not be seen to be going about like one who walks the streets
in the sight of other men, except when it is necessary for her to go
to the temple, if she has any proper regard for herself; and even then
let her not go at noon when the market is full, but after the greater
part of the people have returned home; like a free-born woman, a real
and true citizen, performing her vows and her sacrifices in tranquillity
so as to avert evils and to receive blessings.’

Petronius, in the famous Saturae, 66, has a description of a banquet
in the house of Trimalchio, the rich freedman, which is worth reading if
only for the picture he gives of the manners of the time, which was that
of the Emperor Nero. One or two incidents at the feast are rather in the
same line of manners as that described here by Synesius. ‘I ate a lot of
the tarts,’ says one of the guests, in describing another banquet which
he has just come from, ‘and gave myself such a soaking of honey.
Pease and lupines were handed, a choice of nuts and an apple each. I
took two myself and I have got them here tied up in my napkin; for
if I do not bring some present back for my pet slave boy, there will be
trouble. Oh! yes, my wife reminds me.. . pickled olives were brought
round in a dish too, and some greedy creatures took three handfuls.
For we had let the ham go.’

Page 303, 1.13. Ostris ... gave himself up, &c. Synesius speaks of
Aurelian’s (Osiris’) conduct as if it were a case of voluntary self-sacrifice.
Zosimus, Sozomen, and Socrates seem to know nothing of this. As to the
chivalrous conduct of Gainas, the Gothic general, Griitzmacher
(pp. 48-9) calls attention to the fact that it was only owing to the inter-
cession of St. John Chrysostom that Gainas was contented to exact no


THE EGYPTIAN TALE 429


more than the deposition and banishment from court of the three
statesmen, Aurelian the Consul, Saturninus the Magister militum, and
Johannes the Comes. ‘Synesius’, says Griitzmacher, ‘has certainly
stated the case incorrectly in describing Gainas as a philanthropic and
high-minded Barbarian, and in laying the whole blame on Caesarius.
All the other writers who give an account of these events make the bold
and ambitious Goth, the ally and fellow-worker with Tribigild, answer-
able for the menace to the capital, and we must accept their evidence.
Cf. Zosimus, v. 13 ff. p. 230; Socrates, vi. 6, Migne, P.G. 67. 676 ff. ;
Sozomen, viii, 4, Migne, P.G. 67. 1521; Philostorgius, xi, 8, Migne, P.G.
65. 601 ff.’ He furthermore tells us, on the authority of Socrates (vi. 6),
that Arcadius was obliged by Gainas to take an oath not to lay an
ambush against him, and that this promise was extorted from him by a
threat. He acceded to it in order to save the capital from being sacked
by the Gothic army. Gibbon describes the surrender of Aurelian, the
Osiris of the story, and Saturninus his colleague, who is not mentioned
in it, with his accustomed dramatic power (Decline and Fall, iii. 371,
ed. Bury). I cannot do better than to quote his words: ‘While this
domestic revolution was transacted, Gainas openly revolted from his
allegiance; united his forces, at Thyatira in Lydia, with those of
Tribigild; and still maintained his superior ascendant over the rebel-
lious leader of the Ostrogoths. The confederate armies advanced, with-
out resistance, to the streights of the Hellespont and the Bosphorus ;
and Arcadius was instructed to prevent the loss of his Asiatic dominions
by resigning his authority and his person to the faith of the Barbarians.
The church of the holy martyr Euphemia, situate on a lofty eminence
near Chalcedon, was chosen for the place of the interview. Gainas
bowed, with reverence, at the feet of the emperor, whilst he required the
sacrifice of Aurelian and Saturninus, two ministers of consular rank;
and their naked necks were exposed, by the haughty rebel, to the edge
of the sword, till he condescended to grant them a precarious and dis-
graceful respite. The Goths, according to the terms of the agreement,
were immediately transported from Asia into Europe; and their
victorious chief, who accepted the title of master-general of the Roman
armies, soon filled Constantinople with his troops, and distributed
among his dependants the honours and rewards of the empire. In his


430 NOTES


early youth, Gainas had passed the Danube as a suppliant and a fugi-
tive; his elevation had been the work of valour and fortune; and his
indiscreet, or perfidious, conduct was the cause of his rapid downfall.
Notwithstanding the vigorous opposition of the archbishop, he impor-
tunately claimed, for his Arian sectaries, the possession of a peculiar
church; and the pride of the Catholics was offended by the public
toleration of heresy. Every quarter of Constantinople was filled with
tumult and disorder; and the Barbarians gazed with such ardour on the
rich shops of the jewellers, and the tables of the bankers, which were
covered with gold and silver, that it was judged prudent to remove those
dangerous temptations from their sight. They resented the injurious
precaution; and some alarming attempts were made, during the night,
to attack and destroy with fire the Imperial palace. In this state of
mutual and suspicious hostility, the guards and the people of Constanti-
nople shut the gates, and rose in arms to prevent, or to punish, the
conspiracy of the Goths. During the absence of Gainas, his troops were
surprised and oppressed; seven thousand Barbarians perished in this
bloody massacre. In the fury of the pursuit, the catholics uncovered
the roof, and continued to throw down flaming logs of wood, till they
overwhelmed their adversaries, who had retreated to the church or con-
venticle of the Arians. Gainas was either innocent of the design or too
confident of his success; he was astonished by the intelligence that the
flower of his army had been ingloriously destroyed ; that he himself was
declared a public enemy; and that his countryman, Fravitta, a brave
and loyal confederate, had assumed the management of the war by sea
and land.’ It is ‘this conventicle’ that Synesius has in mind on p. 1257,
when he speaks of ‘a certain evil stamp of religious observances ’, and
describes how Typho ‘sought to make a gift of a temple in the city,
breaking the laws of his ancestors’. It is interesting to remark in what
way Synesius, who presumably had not yet become a Christian convert,
speaks of all this schism in the Church. No doubt he was influenced in
his views on the subject by his friend Aurelian.

This riddle of the wolf and the lion is still unsolved. Griitzmacher (p. 58)

call in to the assistance of the Empire, not the lion, by which we should
probably understand the Goths, but the wolf, probably meaning the
Huns. Synesius may have adopted this outlook, because the Huns
had just put the Goth Gainas to death, had sent his head to Arcadius,
and had thus shown themselves obliging towards the Eastern Roman
Empire.’

Page 315, 1. 29. they decided to beguile Typho, &c. All this part of
Synesius’ story appears fanciful. Historical facts are inextricably
mixed in with romance and allegory. The picture he paints in the
ensuing pages of political corruption is plausible enough, but we have
no detailed evidence from the historians of the period already cited to
confirm it. All that we know is that Caesarius returned as Praefectus
praetorio Orientis, and held the office until the return of Aurelian. All
this about deciding to deceive Typho might be taken to mean that there
was a conspiracy on foot amongst the partisans of Aurelian to oust
Caesarius when a suitable moment should arrive, and that this party of
conspiracy was conscious of its superior power. But on this supposition
what can be made of the statement that the High Priest was in con-
spiracy? If we were right in identifying the priest with Arcadius, it would
mean that the Emperor was a conspirator. If, on the other hand, we

take Crawford’s view that the priest in the story is meant to represent

Eudoxia, his bitterest enemy, who finally secured his banishment. The
whole problem is beset with difficulties, for St. John Chrysostom was the
last man in the world to enter into secret machinations and plots.

The idea of humanity being destroyed by cataclysms, and new civiliza-
tions being evolved from the dust and ashes of the old, is recurred to
by Plato in several of his dialogues. It is evident that Synesius here,
as elsewhere, is saturated with the works of Plato, of which I will point
out a few passages:


Laws, p. 677.

Athentan Stranger. ‘Do you believe that there is any truth in ancient
traditions? ... the traditions about the many destructions of mankind
which have been occasioned by deluges and pestilences, and in many
other ways, and of the survival of the remnant. ... I mean to say that
those who then escaped would only be hill shepherds, small sparks of the
human race preserved on the tops of mountains. After the great de-
struction,... there was a fearful illimitable desert and a vast expanse of
land; a herd or two of oxen would be the only survivors of the animal
world; and there might be a few goats. . . . And out of this state of
things has there not sprung all that we now are and have: cities and
governments, and arts and laws, and a great deal of vice and a great
deal of virtue?’


Timaeus, p. 22.

Crittas. “There have been and will be again many destructions of
mankind arising out of many causes; the greatest have been brought
about by the agencies of fire and water, and other lesser ones by in-

Critias, p. 109.

Critias. ‘In the days of old the gods had the whole earth distributed

was naturally adapted for wisdom and virtue; and there they im-

planted brave children of the soil, and put into their minds the order of

Politicus, pp. 269-70.

Stranger. ‘There is a time when God Himself guides and helps to roll

Passing down now to pp. 271-3, the Stranger describes how in those
days human life was produced spontaneously ; how God Himself was the
Shepherd of men and ruled over them ; and he paints a picture of the
golden age. Beginning then on p. 273 he represents the world as
‘turning round with a sudden shock, being impelled in an opposite
direction from beginning to end, shaken by a mighty earthquake,
which wrought a new destruction of all manner of animals. Afterwards
... the universal creature . . . settled down to his ordinary and accus-
tomed course . . . executing, as far as he remembered them, the instruc-
tions of his Father and Creator, more precisely at first but afterwards
with less exactness. The reason of the falling off was the admixture of
matter in him; this was inherent in the primal nature, which was full
of disorder until attaining to the present order’.

It will be noticed how this last sentence contains the same doctrine
that Synesius is impregnated with when he writes on p. 1228 (c. 9) about
‘that which is erring in nature’. To resume the quotation from the

and the old discord again held sway . . . and there was a danger of

NOTES ON DREAMS


Nicephorus Gregoras, in the early part of the fourteenth century
in Constantinople, wrote a Commentary on this treatise of Synesius,
On Dreams. In a letter to Joannes Cantacuzenus (Ep. 23), the sub-
stance of which is repeated in one addressed to Demetrios Cavasilas
many years later (Ep. 155), he extols this work in the following terms:
‘You know, I think, that I wrote a book long ago inspired by my pro-
found gratitude towards the great Synesius. He wrote, as you are aware,
a most remarkable work on Dreams. Just as nature made every effort,


ON DREAMS 437


and with great success, to show in him a man of the highest order
among the Greeks, in like manner this work is the best of all that he has
written, and he made every effort that it should appear so. .. . He gives
us his own personal evidence in the matter. God inspired him, and he
had no recourse to his forces as a man, he tells us, in this work. He
simply lent his pen to it. God did all. Thus the work is the production,
so he writes, of a man possessed by a prophetic inspiration, and full of
the Divinity. For this reason the greater part of the book has been com-
posed in an obscure style, as were the oracles that the Delphic Tripod
gave forth, and that were, as you know, full of prophetic phrases
sedulously concealed and unintelligible to the ignorant, phrases which
screened them as if behind a curtain of heavy obscurity. Yielding to
numerous requests, we have sought to elucidate this work, to what
extent it was possible, by the help of a varied Commentary.’ (Nic.
Greg. Ep., ed. Guilland, Paris, 1927.)

There is nothing in this passage from the Letters of Nicephorus that
is not contained in the text of De Insomntis, and a Letter to Hypatia,
(Ep. 154), concerning the manner in which it was written. But it is in-
teresting as showing to what an extent the works of Synesius were
admired by the erudite of the fourteenth century, and also as indicating
that at this time the work on Dreams, which has been regarded by
modern commentators with less favour than the other essays, was
esteemed as the most important. One of the friends who urged Nice-
phorus to write a Commentary on it was Theodorus Metochites, the
Prime Minister of the Emperor Andronicus II, who was the most
learned man of the fourteenth century, and had instructed Nicephorus in
Greek philosophy as well as astronomy, and had become his patron at the
Court. Nicephorus, like Synesius, was an astronomer as well as a rhetori-
cian, and wrote a work on the construction of an astrolabe, which, he
tells his correspondent Cavasilas (Ep. 155), he laboured over with the
same ardour that he put into his study of Synesius. It seems that
Byzantium in the fourteenth century was not so far off in point of cul-
ture from Athens or Alexandria of the fourth and fifth.


Page 328, 1.8. .. . brothers 1n a single living creature, the cosmos.
The conception of the universe as an independent whole, and as forming


438 NOTES


a living creature, is an old conception in Greek philosophy. Plato has
touched upon it in the 7smaeus; there are allusions to it in the pre-
Socratic philosophers. Plotinus (En. 11. 3. 7) compares the stars and
other phenomena to letters, as Synesius does in this passage. He
continues:

‘It is thus that in a being animated by one unique principle we may
draw inferences as to one part from another . . .: just as our limbs are
parts of our body, so we ourselves are parts of the universe. .. . Every-
thing is full of omens, and any one is wise who learns one thing from
another, .. . and it is by reason of this that birds and other animals give
us prophecies. . . . One principle and one only there must be, to make this
multiple being one, to convert it into one universal animal. ... All
things proceed from one principle, each playing an allotted role and all
rendering mutual assistance. Each ts assisted or perchance hindered by
another, but their progress is not one of chance; they form a series of
which each is the effect of what precedes, because of what follows.’

Similarly Aristotle (Met. 1076*) blames those (the Pythagoreans ?)
who ‘make the substance of the universe a mere series of episodes (for
one substance has no influence on another by its existence or non-
existence), and they give us many governing principles; but the world
must not be governed badly.

‘The rule of many is not good; one is the ruler”’’ (tr. Ross).


Plotinus again in Enn. iv. 4. 35, states that ‘the universe is one
single animal suffering the same things throughout by reason of its
unity. Its course of life is regulated by its intelligence, it is in complete
accord with itself, has nothing of the nature of chance, and presents one
order, one harmony.’

whole universe, but they fulfil incidentally another function, namely,
that they who have knowledge of this sort of writing may, by looking
at them as written characters, read future events from their arrange-
ment and, according to their analogy, interpreting the thing an-
nounced; as if, seeing a bird flying high in the air, they were to
conclude that a lofty act were signified.’

The Chaldeans also regarded stars as letters written in the firma-
ment and the Cabala is full of the same imagery and belief. Plotinus,
while admitting the prophetic nature of the stars and auguries from
the flight of birds, attacks those who regard them as the causes of
events. For him they were simply symptoms. This seems to have
been the view of Synesius also.

Leibnitz, as Bouillet remarks (vol. i, p. 176), develops similar ideas in
his Monadology, cap. 61: ‘Each body is affected, not only by bodies
touching it ; but it is sensible in some way of all that happens to these,

that this communication extends indefinitely. Consequently each body
feels everything which happens in the universe, and to such an extent
that he who sees the whole can read in each thing that which is happen-
ing everywhere, and even that which has been or will be, by noticing in
the present that which is separated by time and by distance; this is
the ovpmvoa zdvra of Hippocrates.’

The following passage from Seneca (Quaestiones Naturales, li. 32, 4)
expresses the same thought: ‘Quidquid ratione fit, alicuius rei futurae

motu et occursu suo praedicat aliquid. Non omnia scilicet, sed quaedam
notantur. Auspicium observantis est: ad eum itaque pertinet qui in ea
direxerit animum.’ The same conception of the interdependence of the
parts of the universe was turned to account to explain any sort of magic

spells and witchcraft in general. Thus Plotinus (En. iv. 4. 26): ‘Magic

world of reason) who cannot be bewitched’ (iv. 4. 54).

Page 328, 1. 29. limbs of one entire body. The idea of the interpenetra-
tion of the parts of the universe is taken up by Proclus (On Parmentdes,

each other as they go up or down the scale. We must admit, he says,
that the mingling takes place in more than one way; for things which
are situated in the same rank are mingled with each other in one manner,
whereas things of superior rank are mingled with those inferior in a
totally different manner; just as the inferior with those better than
themselves. For the one sort enter into the others and communicate
their own powers to the others; the others penetrate through those
things which are beneath them and communicate their own individual
character to them, and are within them by participation; others again

Page 329, 1.10. tosome god of those who dwell within the universe. This
distinction between cosmic and hypercosmic deities occurs in several
Neo-Platonic writers, Cf. Sallustius, vi: ‘Of the gods some are cosmic
some are hypercosmic,’ he says, and then goes on to explain how their
various spheres and functions are divided. Zeus, Poseidon, Hephaestos
are those who have created the universe (zrovoivres tov Kdopov), whereas
Demeter, Hera, and Artemis have breathed life into it (suyoivres)
and Apollo, Aphrodite and Hermes have brought it into a state of
harmony. It is then guarded (fJpovpotvres) by Hestia, Athene, and
Ares. Now he tells us that these gods possess the universe in the first
rank, and that we must believe that other gods are contained in them.
He gives as an example of this that Dionysos is included in Zeus,
Asklepios in Apollo, and in Aphrodite the Graces. As the passage
reads, all the deities above would be included amongst the cosmic or
mundane. This whole system, in the mind at least of Sallustius, as
probably in that of Iamblichus and others, had to be conceived of in


442 NOTES


some way as existing underneath the soul of the world, the third division
of the Neo-Platonic trinity, from which the religious aspirant ascended
through Mind, to the One, leaving aside, it would seem, the whole
Olympian theogony.

Page 335, 1.11. The phrase tm such a life as this probably alludes to
the unpurified life. The conception dear to the Gnostics was that
demons took up their abode in the soul, and had to be exorcized by
magic, or some form of purification. Only the soul that is concentrated
within itself on the world of Mind (the second hypostasis) can, according
to Plotinus, be proof against sorcery (Plot. Enn. iv. 4. 43). He tells us
that enchantments (é7wéai) act upon the irrational part of the soul
and could only be met bycounter enchantments (avr¢5wv xai avrerqdwv).
Magic could therefore be used for good or for evil. It could be offensive
or defensive ; it could cajole the demons to render them quiet, or expel
them from their stronghold in the soul, or again attack the soul directly
in an evil sense. Man with magic in his hand could become demoniac ;
but the sage was exempt. Bouillet (vol.i, p. 536) quotes St. Clement of
Alexandria as comparing man with the wooden horse of Troy, inasmuch
as he contains within his breast a whole army of maleficent spirits
(rocovTwy mveupdrwy Siaddpwv orpards), and he quotes Valentinus as
comparing the godless soul to a hostelry disordered, soiled, and pro-
faned by thieving intruders (Stromateis, 409).

Page 335, 1.15. We do not form thought concepts without imagination.
vonoets ...movetv, to form thoughts or conceptions.

The passage seems to mean that we cannot have thoughts without
some image or words or objects of sense perception being presented to
us by the imagination. Modern psychologists are endeavouring to
experiment on the possibility of thinking without language; of making
the mind play upon thoughts directly and without this unconscious
intermediary. It is something of this sort that I take Synesius to refer
to when he speaks of grasping a form bereft of matter, i.e. of the image
of language that is before the mind of the thinker (eous avAov).

As an example of the suggestion of the image of language by the
imagination, any one who is equally conversant with two modern
languages must have noticed that he is apt to think in one or other of
them at a given moment, and that his thought is deflected to a certain
extent by the language in the channel of which the mind is running at
that moment, for a language influences thought just as thought in-
fluences a language. But to think without the agency of this imaginative
presentation of language is practically impossible or, as Synesius says,
a rare experience. Therefore, he would say, we imagine when we think.
Aristotle states in De Ansma (402°) his position in regard to imagina-
tion as follows: ‘The function that seems to belong most particularly
to mind is thought, but thought itself, whether it is a sort of
imagination, or whether #¢ cannot exsst without tmagination, could
never take place without the body. . . . The soul if it has nothing that
belongs exclusively to itself cannot be separated from the body.’ We
infer from this passage that in Aristotle’s conception the mind and soul
(‘the rational soul’ of Plotinus) could not work without the body. It is
true that in another passage (De Anima, 413°) he is less affirmative.
‘It is not clear whether the soul is the actuality of the body (évreAdxera)
as the passenger is the soul of a ship.’ Plotinus rejects the simile of
Aristotle. For him the soul pervades the body but is not enclosed in it
(Enn. iv. 3. 21-2). He distinctly says (Enn. ii. 3. 9) that ‘the rational
soul is not in the body, it is raised to the things intellective to the
beautiful, the divine, &c. The soul is present in the body as light
is present in the air.’ Synesius, in invoking the imagination as a
condition of the action of mind, seems to incline rather to the view of


454 NOTES


Aristotle. Bossuet (De la Connaissance de Dieu et de sot-méme, cap. 111,
20) observes that the body is not a mere instrument controlled from
without, nor a ship which the soul directs after the fashion of a
pilot. It would be such if it were intellectual and intellectual only, but
because it is in touch with the senses it is compelled to turn its attention
more especially to that which touches it and to direct this not as an
extraneous thing but as one naturally and intimately united with it.

Page 336,1. 23. the soul which has once been engrafted. Lang (Das Traum-
buch des Synestus von Kryene, p. 59) quotes a passage from Iamblichus
ITepi Yuyijs in Stobaeus (Ecl. i. 49) ‘which’, he says, ‘conducts us within
the very circle of those ideas that we are familiar with in Synesius.
Here we are told that the views of the Platonists relating to the union of
the soul and the body are divided. The majority admitted an immediate
union, the others assumed intermediate links. For some make the soul
come into immediate contact with the material body, as do most of the
Platonists. The others maintain that between the immaterial and the
material soul, ethereal, heavenly, and pneumatic envelopes are inserted,
which contain the rational life and which are the protectors of the soul.
These are the chariots of the soul, and they bring it into contact with
the solid material world, connecting the two by intermediate links.’
Whereas already the above quotation shows a distinct relationship to
our text, this is particularly clear in the last part. Here is expressed
briefly what Synesius describes as the ‘borderland between the rational
and the irrational’ (Dreams, c. 4). We must not be surprised if Iam-
blichus talks of two souls, corporeal and incorporeal. From Proclus
(In T1m. 214 A, f.) we know that in his view two souls emanate from the
creative soul. But, as Lang points out, here Iamblichus further com-
plicates the matter by assuming ethereal envelopes between the soul
(i.e. the immaterial soul) and the pneuma (i.e. the material soul), so that

458 NOTES


being moved, and only about that kind of substance which . . . is not
separable from matter.’ (Metaphysics, 1025, Ross.) He pointedly
excludes being that generates its own motion, irrespective of the forces
of matter; in other words that being which Plato finds in the soul. On
the next page (1026*, Ross) he goes on to say that, ‘it is clear... why it
belongs to the student of nature to study soul to some extent, i.e. so
much of it as is not independent of matter.’ The inference is clear. He
regards the soul as partly dependent on matter and partly independent
of it. We are far from Plato’s conception of the soul as the absolute,
metaphysical entity, self-moving and independent of material forces, as
explained in the Phaedrus. A little later, he continues, ‘physics deals
with things which are inseparable from matter but not immovable,
and some parts of mathematics deal with things which are immovable,
but probably not separable but embodied in matter; while the first
science deals with things which are both separable and immovable.’
Aristotle finally puts the case which concerns the uy as follows: ‘If
there is no substance other than those which are formed by nature,
natural science will be the first science; but if there is an immovable
substance, the science of this must be prior and be first philosophy, and
universal in this way because it is first.’

Plato then is conclusive as to the nature of the yvy7 coming under the
scope of the ‘first philosophy’. Aristotle assigns it partly to the physical
and partly to the metaphysical sciences. The atomists and Epicurus in
chief carried the material side of the fuy7 a step farther. The immaterial
side for them had ceased to exist. The Scholiast on Epicurus’ Letter to
Herodotus (c. 66, edition Von der Miihll), in commenting on the philo-
sophers’ statement that the soul cannot have the same sensations as
before, once separated from the body, because tts protecting envelope ts
not the same, remarks: ‘He says elsewhere that the soul is composed of
very smooth and round atoms quite distinguishable from those of which
fire is constituted. .. .” Epicurus himself goes on to say (c. 67) that ‘what
we call incorporeal . . . is that which cannot be self-conceived, but apart
from a vacuum it is impossible to conceive of the incorporeal. Vacancy
can be neither active nor passive; it only allows bodies to follow their
motion. Those therefore who say that the soul is incorporeal speak
senselessly.’

At this moment of Greek philosophy the sense of the dualism between
spirit the incorporeal and matter had become unintelligible, and the
metaphysical point of view defined by Aristotle in the passage above
was in eclipse. It seems to foreshadow the mavevparuc) yuy7 of
Synesius and the conception of Proclus.


Page 337, l. 27. Lethaean potion, &c. Synesius compares the well-
known image in poetry of death as the drinking of a lethal draught with
the drink that a soul was said to take in the astral zone of the universe,
before passing through the zones of fire, air, and water, in its descent to in-
habit a body upon this earth. Macrobius, in his commentary on Cicero’s
Dream of Scipio, describes at length (Bk. I, chap. xii, §§ 1 ff.), the route
that the soul takes in this voyage. The principal points are the following:
he tells us that the Milky Way cuts the Zodiac in two points, at Cancer
and at Capricorn, and that these two signs of the Zodiac are called the
Gates of the Sun. It is by these gates that the souls descend from
heaven to earth, and rise again from earth to heaven (‘per has portas
animae de caelo in terras meare et de terris in caelum remeare credun-
tur’). One of these doors, he tells us, is the gate of man, the other the
gate of the gods. The souls of men pass through the gate of Cancer, but
they come back through that of Capricorn, which is the gate of the gods,
and through this they attain the seat of the immortality which belongs
to them, and pass into the rank of the gods (‘in deorum numerum
revertuntur’). As long as the souls have not left the gate of Cancer they
are still in the rank of gods (‘adhuc in numero sunt deorum’). But when
they have passed down as far as the Lion they begin to make trial of the
condition before them. It is at this point that the soul descending from
the boundary of the Zodiac and the Milky Way leaves its spherical form,
that which alone is divine, and is attenuated into a conical form
(‘in conum defluendo producitur’). He next tells us that Plato in the
Phaedo means to make allusion to the soul first entering the zone of
matter, when he represents it as stumbling with intoxication (‘animam
in corpus trahi nova ebrietate trepidantem’), and that we have a symbol
of this in the so-called Cup of Bacchus, placed between the Lion and
Cancer. This represents that forgetfulness which is the companion of
intoxication, and all souls in descending drink of this cup of oblivion

(‘sed oblivionem quidem omnes descendendo hauriunt ; aliae vero magis
minus aliae’). It is evidently to this potion that Synesius alludes.
Macrobius goes on to say that the doctrine of reminiscence is used
among the Greeks to explain the greater or less forgetfulness in man
of the truths that were part of his knowledge before he had descended ;
but there is also the drink of the gods. This is no other than Hyle
(vAn), or matter, which stamped with forms, moulds the whole body
of the world (‘Hyle, quae omne corpus mundi, quod ubicumque cernimus,
ideis impressa formavit’). It is called nectar, and believed to be the
drink of the gods. But the drink of the souls is of a lower order, and it is
this that the ancients called the Lethean stream (‘inferior vero atque
turbidior, potus animarum’). The soul then, drawn down by the weight
of this drink, has next to pass through seven Zones. In its descent it takes
on a luminous body (by this no doubt he means the pneuma), and also
receives certain faculties for use in the life below, from the divinities to
whom the seven zones are respectively dedicated. Taking them in their
order, from top to bottom, it is from the zone of Saturn that they receive
reasoning power (‘quod Aoyiorixdy et Oewpnrixov uocant’), from that of
Jupiter the power of action (‘quod zpaxrixdy dicitur’), from that of
Mars the spirited element (‘quod @uy:«dy nuncupatur’), in that of the
Sun the faculty of feeling and thinking (‘quod aio@yrixcy et davracrixdy
appellant’), in that of Venus the movement of desires (émOupyrexov
vocatur’), in that of Mercury the faculty of expression (€ppnveurixdv
dicitur’), in that of the Moon the forces necessary for increase (‘durixdv’).

This passage is somewhat obscure. Mosheim, in his commentary on
Cudworth (vol. iii. 472), q.v., considers it to mean that the pneuma is
not the body of the soul but a sidereal element derived from the stars
or analogous to them, and inherent in the seed that produces the sen-
tient soul. But that Aristotle recognized a division of the soul into a
material and immaterial part would seem to be indicated in a passage
in Metaphysics (p. 1070* 24), in which he says that just as ‘the
shape of a bronze sphere exists at the same time as the bronze sphere,
we must examine whether any form also survives afterwards. For in
some cases this may be so, e. g., the soul may be of this sort—not all the
soul but the reason ; for doubtless it is impossible that al/ soul should
survive’ (Ross). Iamblichus, on the other hand, calls attention to the
difference of opinion that existed in his day on the nature of the pneuma.
The greater number of Platonists, he says, introduce the soul directly
into the body, while others consider that between the material body
and the incorporeal soul there are coverings of an ethereal, celestial, and
spiritual nature (the puyicov rvedua of Synesius) which, enveloping the
rational soul, are formed to hold it in place and to act as vehicles for
it in its journey down to the realms of matter, and once descended there,
to attach it to the material body by common intermediary links. This,
at least, is the sense in which I understand the passage quoted by
Bouillet (Plotinus, vol. ii, p. 656). It seems essentially to concord with
a citation from Proclus on the same page. ‘Every soul’, says Proclus,
‘has a vehicle immaterial, indivisible, and unmoved in its essence. . . .
The vehicle of every soul descends by the addition of envelopes more
and more material. It rises with the soul when it is purified of matter
and has returned to its own shape, as in the same degree the soul makes
use of it. In point of fact the soul descends in an irrational manner,
taking to itself irrational powers, and it rises by stripping itself of all
the functions that are the province of generation.’ (Elements of Theology,
CCVill.)

Page 355, 1. 22. phantasy ... things, which are . . . inconcesvable.
This is the last time that Imagination is spoken of in this treatise.
Plutarch, ‘the great’, is quoted by Johannes Philoponus in his com-
mentary on Arsitotle, De Antma (p. 515, ed. Hayduck), as follows: ‘Once
sense-perception has addressed itself to the perceptible object and
has registered its form, it preserves it. It is to this form then that
Imagination addresses itself, to form a representation of it, as Plutarch
asserts. He also defines Imagination as the movement of the soul which
takes its origin from active sense-perception. . .. According to Plutarch
Imagination is double. At one extremity it touches the higher faculty,
it ends where discursive reason begins. At the other extremity it touches
upon the senses, of which it forms the summit. Imagination gives
nothing to Mind and discursive reason, but it is purified and perfected
by them, inasmuch as under their guidance it reaches the possession of
truth, as far as its nature is capable of so doing.’ In the same vein of
thought Iamblichus (xxi) speaks of Imagination as giving to Opinion
the intuition of forms which proceed from the senses, and at the same
time the conceptions that come from Mind. ‘It receives itself’, he goes
on to say, ‘the images which the various powers of the soul furnish it
with, and its name well expresses its function in assimilating and


ON DREAMS 471


reflecting back all the phenomena of the intellectual faculties, whether
the vegetative or the intermediary. It transmits to the other powers
throughout the body the impressions which it received from Mind.’
Simplicius has the following (Commentary on Aristotle, De Antma,
p. 214 Hayduck): ‘Although Imagination, as Iamblichus says, repre-
sents all our rational operations, nevertheless it resembles the forms
of sensation which are divisible and have extension. It is for this
reason that it touches upon sense-perception.’ It will be seen that the
psychologists who preceded Synesius or were his contemporaries, as well
as Simplicius, who wrote at a later period, did not give imagination the
preponderant place in the organization of the human intellect that is
accorded to it by the Cyrenean philosopher. (See Introduction, p. 78.)
Plotinus also asserts (Enn. iii. 6. 16) that ‘Imagination has the same
relation to soul that form has to matter’. Plotinus in Ean. iv. 3. 29,
makes imagination responsible for memory. ‘We are free to admit that
a sense percept (atc@nyua) produces an image (¢dyracpa) in the memory,
and that imagination . .. has the power of keeping these images ...,
so when sensation is no longer present, imagination preserves the
thing represented (dpapya). . . . It is therefore to imagination that the
memory of things perceptible belongs.’ Plotinus in recognizing the two
souls, the rational (Acy.«7) and the irrational (dAoyos), is bound to divide
imagination into two categories, sentient imagination, and intellectual
imagination. ‘When there is peace in that within us which is capable
of reflecting the images of the Rational and Intellectual-Principles,
these images appear... . When, on the contrary, the mirror within us is
shattered through some disturbance of the harmony of the body, Reason
and the Intellectual-Principle act unpictured: intellection is unattended
by imagination. In sum we maysafely gather that while the Intellective
Act may be attended by the Imaging-Principle, it is not to be con-
founded with it.’ (Plotinus, Enn. i. 4. 10, Stephen Mackenna’s trans-
lation.) Again, in Enn. iv. 3. 30 he asks whether intellectual concepts
can also be preserved by the imagination. ‘If imagination’, he says,
“accompanies each thought (vénors), and if perchance it preserves an
image of it, it will thus have a memory of the object of the thought in
question. . . . Reason (Adyos), whose action accompanies thought, has
perhaps the office of receiving it and transmitting it to the imagination.


472 NOTES


... Reason unfolds it and, making it pass from the state of a thought
to that of an image, displays it in our imagination as it were in a mirror.
It is in this way that a thought is perceived, in this way that it remains
and becomes a memory.’ As to the souls and the two imaginations
which belong to them, Plotinus tells us (sbsd. 31) that when they are in
harmony their images are confounded in one, that when they are in strife
the one or other of them imposes its image on us and we are unconscious
of the image of the alternative; ‘just as we are unconscious of having
two souls, for the two souls are confounded in one, and the one serves
as a vehicle for the other.’

Aristotle had said (De Antma 431°, 17) that we cannot think without
images ; he adds that memory of thoughts cannot exist without images,
and that it is only indirectly that memory can grasp thoughts; of itself
it can only reach percepts of the senses.

NOTES ON CONSTITUTIO


This speech, called by Petavius Conststutio, was delivered, as Druon
thinks, in 411, just after the final disgrace of Synesius’ great enemy,
the roman praefect Andronicus, and recall of his friend Anysius,
the general who achieved several victories over the Ausurian tribes
of the Libyan desert who were attempting to besiege the cities of
Pentapolis. When Synesius returned to Cyrenaica, probably in the
vear 405, the guerilla warfare was dragging on under the incompetent
and corrupt general Cerialis, ‘a venal fellow and cheap at that’, as
Synesius describes him in a letter (ep. 130) to his friend Simplicius.
‘May the wretched Cerialis perish wretchedly ’, he says in the same letter,
‘he who. . . for once in his life lost faith in earth itself . . . embarked his
gold on double-sailed merchant-vessels and is now tossing about on
the high seas.’ From this position of vantage he sent all sorts of orders to
Synesius and his friends who were defending the city. ‘Instead of being
on the ramparts like me, the philosopher’, writes Synesius (#b1d.), ‘the
general keeps himself close to the oar-blade.’ In the same year, perhaps,
he writes to his brother (ep. 125): ‘the enemy has occupied Battia, he has
attacked Aprosylis, he has burnt the threshing-floors, ravaged the fields,
sold the women into slavery . . .; when shall we have done with our
useless chatter? when shall we act seriously? Let us collect our peasants
... to advance upon the enemy... .’ The philosopher, who in De Regno
urges upon the emperor Arcadius the creation of a citizen army, native
to the soil, is now putting his precepts into practice, and takes the first
part in the defence of Pentapolis.


Page 360, 1. 21. the hands of Anystus ... carried out God’s will. For
Anysius Synesius had the greatest admiration. We first hear of him in
the indictment of Andronicus (ep. 57): ‘And as against this pestilence
God has arrayed the south wind, so now has a leader been chosen by
Him against the Ausurians. Oh, may it prove that he is the holiest
and most just of all His generals!’ Events must have moved very
fast if the chronology of Druon (p. 605), approved by Crawford (p. 492),
placing this speech in the year 411, is accepted. Andronicus only
arrived at Cyrene, Druon thinks, in 410. Then we must allow time for


474 NOTES


the awful scenes of maladministration and carnage that Synesius re-
counts in his indictment pronounced in 411. Synesius attacks him in
this great Philippic—the so-called Letter 57—and excommunicates
him in the encyclical addressed to the bishops (ep. 58), all in the
same year (411) as that in which he wrote the document before us.
But in 411 he speaks of Anysius as if quite recently appointed to his
post as commander. Writing to Anysius (ep. 78) in the same year he
congratulates him on his brilliant successes. ‘The Unnigardae,’ he says,
‘in two or three engagements. . . assisted by God and led by you have
gained the greatest and most glorious victories.’ But, still following the
same attempts at chronology, in the same year (411) Anysius is re-
called. So he was nominated at the end of 410 and left the country in
411, during which brief period he conducted a campaign in the desert of
Libya, and transformed the whole situation. In Letter 59, which Druon
dates in the year 412, Synesius writes to Anysius that Pentapolis only
existed while he (the general) remained there. ‘The times since your
departure have betrayed us to our enemies.’ There are seven letters of
Synesius in all addressed to Anysius; in ep. 94 he seems to be watching
a long campaign, in ep. 78 he is begging his friend to write personally
to the emperor for one hundred and sixty more Unnigardae. In those
days of slow communication all this meant time. Again in epp.6 and 14
Synesius writes to him about a certain Carnas, some trivial affair con-
cerning the stealing of a horse, and rather as if Anysius was not on active
service. These two letters contain no allusion to the war. These diffi-
culties in chronology I call attention to without being able to offer a
solution.

Now when we turn from the epistolographoi to the orators, we observe

the authenticity of which is more than doubtful (ed. C. Hude, Or. xv).

On the other hand, the lack of any personal allusion to his correspon-
dent, if such there be, is unusual to Synesius in a letter of such a length,
and the tone is rather one of impassioned oratory. A third supposition
might be made, namely that the letter was written to some friend,
possibly in Alexandria or Constantinople, to be read by him at a public
meeting or a private group there, in an attempt to rouse public opinion
on the awful danger that threatened Pentapolis, with a view to bringing
pressure to bear on the court. It does not seem the sort of speech to
deliver at an acute moment of crisis, when the morale of the population
required sustaining.


Page 363, 1. 15. the great Anthemius. Anthemius is mentioned in

friend Theotimus the poet, playfully compares him to Simonides, and
his admirer Anthemius to Hiero I, the tyrant of Syracuse. ‘You re-

semble him (i.e. Simonides) in this’, he writes, ‘that it was Simonides

Page 363,1.22. Prolonging her agony to the seventh year. If we are right
in supposing that this document was written in 412, the disastrous
