moment of dawn Iam off on horseback, [amscouting as far out as possible.
... We need archery in defence of our wells . . . we must either conquer
now by fighting, or perish in hand-to-hand struggle with the enemy... .’
And this is only the first of the six years of ‘agony’! Again in Letter
130 toSimplicius he writes: ‘ Alas for the young men we have lost!. . .we
have planted our fields for the fires lit by our enemies . . . our cattle, our
herds of camels . . . all are lost, all have been driven away.’ Passing to

former governor of Pentapolis, that Cyrene owes its continued existence
to him alone. In the year 407 a letter to his brother (ep. 108) begins:
‘I have already three hundred lances. . . . To-morrow, I think, the battle
will take place. ... I hope that. .. by the aid of God I may vanquish the
enemy. ...I commend my children to you.’ Letter 107, to his brother,
contains the words: ‘Theenemy is holding the country, plundering every-


478 NOTES

thing, and slaughtering whole populations.’ Again, still in the year 407,
he tells his brother (ep. 122) of a victory gained by a priest of Axomis,
Faustus by name, who led a force of peasants against the enemy. Now
it is strange that after this letter, if we follow Druon’s sequence, we find no
reference to the war until wecome to Letter 94, addressed to Anysius him-
self this time, and written in 411. In the thirty-seven intervening letters
covering the years 408-g-10, one of which (67) is extremely long, he is
writing in a most peaceful strain, nor could any one imagine on reading
them that a war or any sort of disturbance was going on. Are we to
conclude from this that a lull in the barbarian inroads had taken place in
these three years, or that many letters have been lost, or again, that
Druon’s conjectural order is fundamentally wrong? I have always been
inclined to think that a great number of Synesius’ letters have been lost,
and the facts we are considering are the best evidence of this. How-
ever you may rearrange the chronology of the letters, there are not
enough letters alluding to the war to cover the seven years, 405-12.
It seems inconceivable that so ardent a patriot and one with the power
of dramatic expression evidenced in this Catastasis and letters quoted,
should write thirty-seven letters without a single allusion to what was
evidently nearest to his heart. But to proceed with year 411—the
hypothetical date—at this juncture he writes to Anysius: ‘As soon as I
learned the bad news from Cyrene the other day (that the enemy were
approaching) I thought of sending to you. . . but a messenger came to
inform us that the general had already occupied the high ground, &c.;
send back the two brothers to Cyrene,—they will fight for their country.’
Here is another to Anysius (ep. 78) of the same year, speaking of the
Unnigardae : ‘The barbarians had scarcely shown themselves when some
were killed. . . and others put to flight. They (the Unnigardae) still patrol
the heights, ever on the watch . . .: who would not admit . .. that they
would suffice, when commanded by you, to bring the Ausurian war to an
end...?’ Coming now to the year 412, we have a lurid picture of the
war in a letter to Theophilus, the Patriarch of. Alexandria, his oldest
friend (ep. 69): ‘He (the messenger) was sent to solicit military co-opera-
tion... but the enemy did not wait . . . they have already spread en
masse over the country. All is lost, all is destroyed ... there is nothing left
but the cities, nothing! What may befall to-morrow, God alone knows.’


CATASTASIS 479


This is the last letter in Druon’s order which speaks of the war; it might
well have been the last Synesius was to write.


Page 363, 1.29. not poured over the country in a compact mass. We
have just noted that in Letter 69 he describes the barbarians as having
done precisely this. I think the sense is, ‘ things were going better in
the days of Anysius, for he broke the barbarians up, but now they have
poured over the country.’ Letter 69 was written before the Catastasis,
evidently, but probably in the same year.


Page 364, 1. 13. shtelds of the Marcomant. As the Marcomani (v.
Gibbon, i, p. 235 n.) were a colony who from the banks of the Rhine occu-
pied Bohemia and Moravia, one can only conclude that they had been
sent at some time to Libya, possibly under Anysius himself. They are
mentioned in Strabo, vii. 290, and Tacitus, Ann. ii. 62, &c.


Page 367,1.4ff. Cythera ts opposite Pentapolis ... Dorian tombs, &c.
The island of Cythera is almost due north of Cyrene, but at a distance of
about 280 miles. It is off the southern extremity of Laconia to the east
of Cape Matapan. No doubt this means that he wishes to be near his
Lacedaemon. The idea of the Dorian tombs of his ancestors was always
haunting Synesius. In his indictment of Andronicus (ep. 57) he reminds
his hearers that he is descended from Eurysthenes, who settled the
Dorians in Sparta, and how all this has been engraved on public monu-
ments.

of Synesius, or after the year 410. They seem to be merely fragments,
and it is difficult to recognize his style in them.

This so-called homily is obviously two fragments joined together,

HYMN I
Page 372,1.22. song of the cicada. Philo in The Contemplate Ltfe,
cap. 4, in describing the life of the Therapeutae, the anchorites who lived
in a community of their own, near Lake Mareotis, compares their absti-
nence in regard to food to that of the grasshoppers, which insects, he

Page 372, 1. 26. born without birth : ddéyevros. This word is used by

describing the birth of Athene.


Page 373, 1. 4. leaping from out the centre, &c. Cf. Plotinus, v. i. 11:
“This Highest cannot be divided and allotted, must remain intangible
but not bound to space, it may be present at many points, where-
soever there is anything capable of accepting one of its manifesta-
tions: thus a centre is an independent unity; everything within the
circle has its term at the centre; and to the centre the radu bring each
their own. Within our nature is such a centre by which we grasp and
are linked and held; and those of us are firmly in the Supreme whose
collective tendency is There.’ (Trans. Mackenna, vol. iv, p.15.) See also
the note on Dreams, p. 446.


Page 373, 1. 6. reveal not the mysteries. Here we have a trace of Gnosti-


HYMN I 481


cism. Compare the passage in the book of Jedi, quoted in Hastings’s
Encyc. Relig. Eth. vi, p. 231: ‘This is the book of the yudces of the
invisible God, contained in the hidden mysteries which show the way to
the elect generation.’ In the same way the magical papyn contain
what they define as Gnosis. It was the privilege of the one initiated in
the mysteries of the Gnostics to have a knowledge of watchwords and
magical formulae that would enable his soul after death to pass through
the sentinels of the planetary zones. Cf. Hippol. v. 5, Hymn of the
Naassenes: ‘Then said Jesus: ... send me, O Father. With the seal will I
descend, travel through all Aeons, disclose all mysteries, show the forms
of the gods: the secrets of the holy path which are called ‘‘Gnosis”’ I will
impart.’ It will be seen from this to what an extent Gnosis was a super-
natural revelation of a mystical character, in the eyes of its earlier
exponents. The later Gnostics endeavoured to clothe their tenets in a
metaphysical and philosophic dress. Synesius is perpetually referring,
in his letters and elsewhere, to the danger of revealing the secrets shared
by the initiated to the world outside. Of these initiations and mysteries
there were many. The Gnostics derived them from Babylonia, from
Persia, from Egypt, and through the Greeks, from Phrygia. To which
cult of Gnosticism Synesius alludes is not clear, but it certainly seems
that he had the Gnostics in mind, probably Basilides and Valentinus,
their chief exponents. Bardesanes, the disciple of the latter, according
to Eusebius, flourished in the last part of the second century and the
first part of the third, and was the last great teacher of Gnosticism.
Both he and Marcion sought to envelop their doctrines in the beliefs of
the Christian Church, and seem to have largely adopted its ritual. In this
way a new syncretic type of Christianity was formed, and the forces of
Gnosticism, which had come into collision with the Orthodox Church,
continued to survive in certain heretical sects.


Page 374, 1. 2. light shall leap forth. There is a trace here of the cult of
Mithra. Wisdom, the creator and the unified flame mentioned below,
is the directing mind of the world. The religion of Mithra, as Cumont
has pointed out (cf. Les Mystéres de Mithra, p. 201, note), was anything
but Hellenic in its inspiration ; it opposed the culture of Iran to that of
Hellas.

HYMN II


Page 374, 1. 18. a blessed stlence. Here again is an expression which may
have a Gnostic derivation. The Valentinians regarded Sige (silence),
as co-existent with Bythos, the invisible, eternal, the not-begotten.
Bythos placed in the bosom of Sige the germ of production which he had
produced from Ennoia (thought). Sige, made fruitful by this germ,
bore Nous, like to his father, and equal to him, and alone capable of
understanding Greatness. The Valentinians give to Nous the name
Monogenes, i.e. the one son of the father and of the principle of all
things. With Nous was also born Aletheia (truth). Bythos, Ennoia,
Nous, and Aletheia form the Tetrad of the Pythagoreans, and this the
Valentinians called in addition the root of all things. This is the account
of the Valentinian doctrine as given by St. Irenaeus, to whom we owe
most of our information on the subject (cf. St. Iren.i. 1.) It will be seen
to what an extent the Gnostics had assimilated Pythagorean doctrines.

Nous, according to St. Irenaeus’ statement of the doctrine, under-
standing for what motive he had been engendered, produced by his
union with Aletheia, Logos (the Word), and Zoe (life), so that Logos
should be the father of all the Aeons that were to be born after him. He
was thus the principle and the artificer of what the Gnostics described
as the Pleroma (fullness or completion, vid. St. Paul, Rom. xi. 12).
From the union of Logos and Zoe were born Anthropos (man) and
Ecclesia (the Church). This is the primitive Ogdoad, the root and sub-
stance of all things. Synesius, it will be observed, is always returning
in the Hymns to this phrase, The Root.


Page 375, 1.11. Thou Male, Thou Female. St. Epiphanius cites a frag-
ment from one of the Valentinians in his work on the Heresies (xxxi,
cap.5) as follows: ‘In the beginning all things were contained as unknown
in Autopator, (the Father Himself), whom some call the Aeon, who is
exempt from age, who is always young, who is male and female, and
includes all things everywhere, without being contained in any of them.
In him was Ennoia (thought); this is the name that some give her, but
others call her by her own name, Charis (grace), because grace makes
part of the treasures of Greatness to those who were born to greatness ;


HYMN II 483


indeed those who make use of her real name call her Sige (silence) because
Greatness has made all things by conception and without a word.
Ennoia, the incorruptible female Aeon, desiring to break her chains,
seduced Greatness by the attraction of pleasure. Once united to him she
bore the Father. . . . By the will of Bythos, who contains everything,
Anthropos and Ecclesia, remembering the words of the Father, became
united and engendered the Dodecad. . . . Thereafter Logos and Zoe desir-
ing also to glorify Bythos, became united, that is to say had one will
in common, and by this union engendered the Decad, of which the male
Aeons Bythios, Ageratos, Autophyes, Monogenes, Akinetos, received
the names which they bear for the glory of that One Who contains all
things. The female Aeons, Mixis, Henosis, Syncrasis, Henotes, Hedone,
in like manner received their name from it for the glory of Sige.’

St. Irenaeus (I. iii. 1) remarks: ‘The Valentinians declare that the
things they tell concerning the Pleroma have not been clearly revealed,
because all men are not capable of understanding the Gnosis, but that
the Saviour indicated mysteriously in parables these things to those
capable of understanding their meaning. . .. (I. ili. 5) “This is what they
all say concerning the Pleroma’, he adds, ‘that they have imagined ;
they deflect from their obvious sense the most beautiful passages in
their attempt to render their ideas in them conformable to their
wretched invention.’

The union of Bythos and Ennoia reminds one somewhat of a passage
in Philo, as Bouillet points out (vol. 1, p. 505): ‘The author of this uni- -
verse ought to be called the Father of His works. We will give the name
of Mother to supreme Wisdom. It is to her that God united Himself in a
mystic manner, to bring about the generation of all things; it is she who,
made fruitful by the divine germ, gave birth at the time foretold, and
with sore travail, to that one dearly-beloved son whom we call the
World.’ (Philo, De Ebrietate, 8, § 30.) As to the part that Christ played in
the conception of the Gnostics (for it must not be forgotten that they
claimed to be Christians and the true representatives of the Christian
faith), St. Irenaeus (I. 11.6) describes it as follows: ‘Full of thankfulness to
Propator, the Aeons with one accord placed in common whatever each
one of them possessed that was most beautiful and perfect, the star and
the goodly fruit of the Pleroma, in a word, Jesus, or the Saviour, to

28782 li


484 NOTES


Whom they give His patronymic names of Christ, the Word, and the All.
With Him were born in honour of the Aeons themselves, the angels, des-
tined to serve Him as attendants.’

Bouillet again remarks (vol. i, p. 510) that the Valentinians pre-
tended that their doctrine about Jesus was indicated in various passages
in St. Paul. ‘In ipso habitat omnis plenitudo divinitatis corporaliter.’
But the Valentinians cut out the last word from the text (Col. ii. 9).
He also quotes the Epistle to the Romans xi. 36, ‘Omnia ex ipso et in
ipsum omnia.’ St. Irenaeus and Tertullian also say with some reason
that, in the Gnostic system, Jesus is a sort of Pandora: ‘The myth
in fact of the birth of Jesus, and of the angels who accompany Him, is
very like the myth of Pandora in the sense in which the Neoplatonist
understood it. Plotinus, for instance, expresses himself in this way:
‘Prometheus having formed a woman, the other gods adorned her,
and hence she was called Pandora. ... This myth evidently indicates
the gifts that the world has received.’ (Emm. lib. IV, iii. 14.)

‘In the Gnostic myth’, continues Bouillet, ‘the intelligible gods are
the Aeons; the intelligences, which are the givers of souls, are the angels
who accompany Jesus, or, again according to St. Irenaeus, the lights
which surround Him.’ We may compare in this connexion the phrase
‘ plucking flowers of light to be hymns unto Thee’ (Hymn III. 138 ff.),
and in this Hymn (45 ff.) the passage ‘an ageless army of angels, now
looking upon Mind, plucks therefrom the principle of beauty’, which
last is very much like the conception of the Valentinians as presented
to us by St. Irenaeus.

This hymn may be compared with the Orphic verses quoted by the
pseudo-Aristotle, De Mundo, 401*», and translated by E. S. Forster:

Zeus of the flashing bolt was the first to be born and the latest,

Zeus is the head and the middle; of Zeus were all things created ;

Zeus is the stay of the earth and the stay of the star-spangled heaven ;

Zeus is male and female of sex, the bride everlasting.

De Mundo was probably written as late as the beginning of the second
century A.D.

Page 375, 1. 27. weaving a crown. Pindar, in the eighth Isthmian Ode,
68 (148), speaks of presenting to Cleander, the victor in the pancratium,
a crown of myrtle. In the same way Hippolytus in Euripides’ drama (73)

Page 376, 1.5. that mighty witness, the sun. Here again is a touch of
Mithraism.

Page 376, 1.24. the demon of matter .. . soul-devouring hounds, &c. It is
very interesting to trace the different functions that Synesius assigns to
demons in his various works. The terrors that came from demonology
were ever present to the minds of the fourth and fifth centuries and after.
They passed into the conceptions of the Middle Ages, and we find them
in full force in Byzantium in the eleventh and fourteenth centuries, if
we turn to the works of Michael Psellus, or Nicephoras Gregoras, or of
Anna Comnena. In the Egyptian Tale we find a more ambitious and
lofty réle assigned to the demons (1228¢). They remind us of the Titans
in Hesiod (Theog., 392, 648, 668, &c.) who storm Olympus and fight with
the immortal gods. They display in the Egyptian Tale malice, cunning,
and resource. As in Hesiod they were finally imprisoned in Tartarus,
so here the demon of matter is represented as sinking beneath the earth,
cf. Theogony, 729 ff., where the poet says: ‘There by the counsel of
Zeus who drives the clouds the Titan gods are hidden under mystic
gloom, in a dank place where are the ends of the huge earth. And they
may not go out; for Poseidon fixed gates of bronze upon it. .. .’ (trans-
lation Evelyn White). All this is very like the view of the demons pre-
sented in the Essay on Dreams. The allusions to the demon or demons
of matter in the Hymns point rather to a vaguely destructive agency.
The prayers that Synesius is always sending up rest upon a haunting
fear of their power to do him harm, not merely to the soul but to the
body, a fear which was present to the Christian mind at this period, as
well as to the pagan. Both the neo-Platonists and the Christian writers
agreed in this point at all events, in their terror of the demons. We find
it in Proclus as well. Lang (Das Traumbuch des Synesius von Kyrene,


486 NOTES


p. 85) traces the influence of Porphyry (De Abs. ii. 40) upon Synesius
in the following quotation: ‘This and similar things they (the demons)
do to turn us away from the true knowledge of God, and to direct our
glance towards themselves. For they derive their pleasure from all
contradictory and unreasonable occurrences, and advantage from our
indecision, and in this way they hide themselves behind the masks
of the other gods. They approach the great mass of people and inflame
ambition in men. They suggest to them especially a love and longing for
riches, power, and fleshly gratification, and imbue them with love for
fame, from which arise insurrections, wars, and the like.’ Above all (13d.
42), hesays: ‘they wish to be gods, and to arouse the impression of being
the power which rules these, that is to say the highest god himself.’
Lang further remarks that this “wallowing in matter”’ as a charac-
teristic of the demons, may also be found in the commentaries on
the Chaldean Oracles. “The beasts of the earth’’ spoken of in the
Oracles are interpreted by Psellus (1140*) to mean the demons which
thus wallow on the earth. ‘These animals’, says Psellus, ‘exist in our
own life, which is full of passions, for they are present abundantly
in the passions, and their dwelling-place is that of matter, as is their
rank and degree. For this reason they are also subject to passions and
fettered to them... .’ Again in 1140c.: ‘the Oracles call them demons of
the earth because they have been thrown down from heaven and sprawl
upon the ground.’ It is certainly interesting in regard to the unity and
tradition of Greek sentiment to see how the same conception may be
traced from the days of Hesiod to the days of Synesius and Michael
Psellus, little disturbed practically by the waves of the Persian, Jewish,
and Christian religions that had come into contact with it.


Page 377,1. 11. Father of Thyself... Son of Thyself. Here Synesius
uses the phraseology dear to the Valentinians, who affirmed that there
exists on the unseen heights an eternal Aeon of all perfection, which
was pre-existent to everything. This they called Proarche, the first
principle, or as Synesius in this passage, Propator, i.e. the first father or
Bythos, the abyss. He is invisible and incomprehensible. The mytho-
logy of the Valentinians turned largely upon this invisibility and in-
comprehensibility of the Almighty.

Page 378,1. 29. starry intelligences. Plotinusattempted to take up some
of the ideas from Plato’s Tsmaeus regarding Mind, the rational soul, and
heavenly bodies (Enn. ii. 3. 9): ‘In the Timaeus, the creating God
bestows the essential of the Soul, but it is the divinities moving in the
kosmos (the stars) that infuse the powerful affections holding from
Necessity—our impulse and our desire, our sense of pleasure and of pain
—and that lower phase of the Soul in which such experiences originate.
By this statement our personality is bound up with the stars, whence
our Soul (as total of Principle and affections) takes shape; and we are
set under necessity at our very entrance into the world: our tempera-
ment will be of the stars’ ordering, and so, therefore, the actions which
derive from temperament, and all the experiences of a nature shaped to
impressions.

‘What, after all this, remains to stand for the ‘‘ We’?

‘The “We” is the actual resultant of a Being whose nature includes,
with certain sensibilities, the power of governing them. Cut off as we
are by the nature of the body, God has yet given us, in the midst of all
this evil, virtue the unconquerable, meaningless in a state of tranquil
safety, but everything where its absence would be peril of fall..... ;
(Stephen Mackenna, vol. ii, p. 167-8.)

Plotinus, according to Bouillet, doesnot admit, as one might be inclined
to think at first on reading this passage, that we actually receive our
souls from the stars. All that the soul receives from the stars is the
pneuma, that is to say the aerial or fiery body that it puts on before
descending to the world of sense. The ‘starry intelligences’ mentioned
by Synesius here seem to be the ‘divinities moving in the kosmos’
mentioned by Plotinus. These gods who add to the immortal principle
of the soul the passions of the irrational soul are, according to Synesius,
the protectors of man also.

seem to have an echo from The Song of the Three Holy Children in the

except what time I spent as an ambassador. Would that I had not been

Page 380, 1.23. as many temples as were builded for Thy holy ceremontes,
O King,...I supplicated gods that labour, &c. Here is another curious
instance of the polytheistic tendencies of Synesius. The temples in
question it would not be easy to identify, but from his description of
them they seem to allude to tutelar divinities that protected Thrace
and Chalcedon. This passage is the more interesting, in view of the
syncretism that appears in so much of his writings, because here at
least one cannot explain the polytheistic note as a piece of imaginative
or poetical imagery. This appears to be a statement of something that
he actually did. So we might infer that at this period of his life he was
adopting more than aconventional form of paganism. On the other hand
the address to the emperor Arcadius reflects purely monotheistic con-
ceptions. It will be noticed at the same time that he speaks of the
temples in question as having been specially appointed by the One
God whom he is addressing in this Hymn, and whom he regards as
having inspired the minor gods in question.

HYMN IV

Page 384, 1.23. I sing unto Thee... with silence. Sige (silence) was, as
we have seen, one of the principal personages in Valentinian theogony.
Here and there in these hymns, Synesius seems to emphasize silence,
as in Hymn III, 1. 82, ‘Let silence hold the caverns of the universe while
these sacred hymns are offered up.’ Whether he attaches the meaning
to Sige that was dear to the Valentinians is not clear.

Page 384, 1. 31. Mother, Sister,and Daughter to Thyself. This might seem
to refer to the Holy Virgin, although where she is mentioned in the other
hymns, as in Hymn V and Hymn VII, he uses a direct and unmistak-
able phrase, as ‘the sacred travail of a Bride’, or, ‘Offspring of the
Virgin, Jesus of Solyma’. ‘The Secret Root’, on the other hand, could
scarcely be taken to refer to Christ, for Synesius is always using
the expression ‘Root’ as an attribute of the Father. A few lines
above he addresses Him as ‘Root of Roots’, and again in this
passage he speaks of ‘a Shoot’, which might be taken to refer to ‘the
Root’ as its origin. It is impossible to reconcile these extraordinary
contradictions. Farther down, p. 385, I. 12, he speaks of the ‘Root of all
things that came after Thy illustrious Birth,’ presumably then after
the Nativity. ‘

If we could omit lines 12 f. (p. 383, 29, ‘Giver’ &c.), which after all
might be an interpolation, the sentence would be quite consistent. After
this passage he seems to go on addressing the Son, until we get to p. 386,
1. 4, where he speaks of a second great Luminary, or Sun, the perceptible
impression of Mind. If we take this to mean the Holy Ghost, as I suggest,
we can explain this Hymn as a Jaudation of the Christian Trinity. It
might, however, be explained in another way, and the continual allusions
tothesunand light andso forth might beregardedas touches of Mithraism.

Page 385, 1.9. This Word I hymn, in unison, Gc. This whole hymn
seems to be addressed tothe Holy Trinity. He begins in the first lines by
addressing the Father, and so continues, as for instance in line 60, where
he uses the expression ‘Unit of units, Father of fathers’, and so on to
line 87, where he addresses the Son: ‘I sing to the Offspring,’ and so on.
In line 98 he mentions for the first time the Holy Spirit, described as the
‘Centreof theCreator, Centre again of the Son’. The phrase which follows


490 NOTES


‘Mother, Sister, and Daughter ’, as I have just said, is somewhat obscure.
We now come to line 130 (p. 385, 9), where he speaks of ‘the Word’.
This passage again might be taken in several senses, according as we con-
ceive the metaphysical or theological basis of Synesius’ thought. The
text as it stands seems to place the ‘Word’ in opposition to Mind. As
the Greek reads, it is then the Word which has begotten (ce) ‘Thee,’
presumably the Son. It is also the Mind of the ineffable Father which
has effected this parturition, and continuing to speak of the same person
(the Son?), he addresses Him as the ‘Word of the Father’. All this
involves either a contradiction or an attempt to place the existence of
the Persons of the Godhead on a metaphysical plane.


Page 385, 1. 18. seven planets dance in harmony. He may be
alluding here to the conception of the planetary zone which is found
in Gnostic literature, each of these zones having a guardian divinity.
To allow the soul to pass by these without danger, the initiated in the
Gnostic mysteries were supplied with magical formulae and pass-words.

HYMN V


Page 387, 1.22. The patriotic vein in Synesius, that always couples
Cyrene and Sparta, is present even here.


HYMN VI

Page 388, 1.22. Thou dividest the indivisible Spirit (pneuma) throughout
the earth. We have seen already, in commenting upon the Essay on
Dreams, how important a place the conception of the Pneuma occupied
in the philosophy of Synesius. He does not, however, seem to make
much play on it in the Hymns. Wolfram Lang, in his commentary
on the Essay on Dreams (Das Traumbuch des Synesius von Kyrene,
Tubingen, 1926), p. 57, makes the following remark on the part that
the term played in later Greek philosophy: ‘The idea of the Pneuma
is one of the most many-sided in the whole of Greek philosophy,
although it only began to play an important part when the climax
of Greek culture had already been passed. The Stoics considered
the Pneuma to be the material substance of the soul, and an emanation
of the all-penetrating divine power. In their view the soul of man was
an €vOeppov mveipa. The various powers of the soul were located in
Pneumata proper to each. Thus there was one that perceived, one that
represented, another that thought, and so on. . . . The sense in which
Synesius understands Pneuma is not this of the Stoics, or of Philo. ...
To the Greeks in pre-Christian days Pneuma meant the prophetic
substance which enters into man. To this conception the Delphic
Oracle had accustomed all Greeks. The Pneuma is a combination of
material and immaterial elements. It has, as Synesius explains in
140B, absorbed a part of the elements.’


HYMN VIII


Date of Hymn VIII. Druon considers that this Hymn was written in
the year 405 or 406; his reason for this is that Synesius speaks of only
having two children. Crawford (p. 505 n.) points out the fact that,
as the children are mentioned immediately after his sister, it is not
clear if they are not her children, although it is more natural to suppose
that they are his own. He goes on to say: ‘the second son does seem

2878.2 Kk


492 NOTES


to have been born about 405 or 406, and we have a shrewd suspicion
that the second and third were twins .. . if they were not twins, what
is there to show that the third was born before 408 or thereabouts?
Again, there is noclear evidence that the hymn may not have been written
after the death of one of the children. If there were twins, it seems almost
certain that the composition must be placed at a time when one of the
three boys had died, and consequently during our author’s episcopate.
In that case, one passage in the hymn would provide a strong argument
in favour of the theory that he retained his wife. . . .". Crawford points
to the fact that the hymn is entirely Christian in thought, and doubts,
for this reason, whether it could be placed as early as 405. Wilamo-
witz-Moellendorf, however, on the ground that the hymn was written
when Synesius had two sons, and consequently before the birth of the
third, considers that it was written long before he was made a bishop.
But he warns us in another place that, although a Christian of to-day
would scarcely recognize Synesius as a brother in the faith, the opposi-
tion between monotheism and polytheism was rather an inheritance of
the arrogance of the Jews, and was void of any meaning in the eyes
of the fourth century when applied to Christianity and Hellenism. In
Hymn III, where I pointed out the discrepancy in the prayers that
Synesius offered to the gods who watch over the lands of Thrace, &c.,
Wilamowitz is inclined to see temples to Christian saints rather than
to Hellenic deities.


P. 390, 1.15. the house of the sons of Hesychius. (‘Hovydav Sdpov.)
This precious reading has been recovered by Terzaghi. Hesychius was
the name of a dear friend of Synesius, to whom Letter 93 is addressed.
In his honour Synesius gave the name Hesychius to his eldest son
(cf. Letter 53, with my note).


HYMN IX


This hymn opens with a direct invocation to Christ, unmistakable
this time, as the offspring of the Holy Virgin. Druon supposes it to
have been written in the year 407 or 408, in other words shortly before
he was consecrated, if we agree with Druon in placing that event in the
year 410. It is replete with pagan imagery, although Christian in form.


HYMN IX 493


Wilamowitz-Moellendorf considers this one of the finest. ‘Hymn IX,’ he
says, ‘dealing with Christ’s descent to Hades, is more successful (than
Hymn VII). The description of his leading back to the Father the souls
He has delivered, and all the elements praising the victor who returns
to His kingdom, is not without grandeur; one must do justice to the
language which borrows so much from a foreign mythology, and the
syncretism of the philosophical ideas.’ He goes on tosuggest an interest-
ing comparison to the imagery of this Hymn in Correggio’s great paint-
ing of the Assumption of the Virgin in the Duomo of Parma, where the
central figure is borne up bycountlessangels. ‘Itis not difficult’, hecon-
tinues, ‘to find from an artist’s point of view, a sort of mood that would
respond to this sort of mingling of the clerical and the worldly, as also
of the Christian and the pagan. Is it too much to ask the same licence
for Synesius as for the painter? Is not this transcendental picture in the
province of real poetry, this in which he describes how the Son of God
descends to the material world, and how after His victory He wings His
way across the outmost spheres of the Cosmos into the transcendent, His
home; from the sea of light and from the harmonies of the spheres into
eternity, where there is neither time, motion, nor intercourse?’ This
hymn, says Wilamowitz, has been mutilated in most editions, and he
suggests a certain rearrangement of the lines (Die Hymnen des Proklos
und Synestos, Preussische Akademie der Wissenschaften, 14. Marz 1907,
Berlin). In Professor Terzaghi’s text six lines are introduced, lines 7-12
inclusive, which are not in Migne’s edition. Again, after the eighth line
in Migne he inserts a line (numbered by him 15); after the fourteenth
line in Migne, Terzaghihas inserted another, the twenty-second, accord-
ing to his numeration, and after the nineteenth line in Migne, he intro-
duces three more. This brings the total number of lines in the Hymn
to seventy-one.


Page 391, 1.10. hts hound, the devourer of man. It would almost seem
as if Synesius identified Cerberus with the demon of matter mentioned
in the fourth hymn, lines 245 ff., ‘the shameless hound of the nether
world, the demon of earth.’
